title: UMaine men’s hockey lose in OT to Holy Cross
text:
The University of Maine men’s hockey team settled for a split of its season-opening series against Holy Cross, falling 4-3 in overtime Saturday in Worcester, Massachusetts.

title: Katahdin Rolls, Two Games Go to Double OT in Saturday County Soccer
text:
The County Scoreboard: Katahdin Teams Combine for 16, full Saturday Soccer Slate, Festival of Champs recaps
It was a full Saturday of high school soccer across Aroostook County and beyond, with Katahdin putting together a huge day on both sides of the field, two games requiring double overtime, and several other County teams picking up key wins.
The Katahdin boys and girls combined for 16 goals in a sweep of East Grand, while the Fort Fairfield boys battled Bangor Christian to a scoreless draw and the Fort Kent girls played Penobscot Valley to a 1-1 tie.
Here is a look at Saturday's action, and if you missed the Festival of Champions results, you can find FULL COUNTY RESULTS here!
Boys Soccer
Katahdin 7, East Grand 0
Conor Schmidt powered the Katahdin offense with a hat trick and an assist as the Cougars rolled to a 7-0 win over East Grand.
Leighton Rodgerson added a goal and two assists, while Bryten Hartsgrove, Ben Rivers and Ralph Heath also found the back of the net. Blake Rush and Chandler Libby each contributed an assist.
Gage Phillips made six saves in goal to preserve the shutout for Katahdin.
East Grand goalkeeper Dylan Napoli faced plenty of pressure throughout the contest and finished with 16 saves.
Mattanawcook Academy 7, Houlton 4
Houlton put four goals on the board, but Mattanawcook Academy came away with a 7-4 victory over the Shires.
Beckett Koehler turned in another big offensive performance for Houlton, recording a hat trick. Cam Smith scored the other goal for the Shires.
Mount Desert Island 4, Caribou 2
Mount Desert Island earned a 4-2 victory over Caribou in Saturday's Class B matchup.
Bangor Christian 0, Fort Fairfield 0, 2OT
Neither side could find the deciding goal as Fort Fairfield and Bangor Christian battled through regulation and two overtime periods before finishing in a 0-0 tie.
Van Buren 3, Schenck 1
Van Buren picked up another victory on Saturday, defeating Schenck 3-1.
Piscataquis Community 10, Ashland 3
Ashland found the net three times on the road, but Piscataquis Community pulled away for a 10-3 victory.
Fort Kent 3, Old Town 1
Fort Kent came away with a strong road result, knocking off Old Town 3-1.
Girls Soccer
Houlton 4, Old Town 2
Ava Ezell and Raina Ezell supplied all four Houlton goals as the Lady Shires earned a 4-2 victory over Old Town.
Each scored twice in the win, while Reagan Wright and Emilee Cram added assists.
Gwen Ramsay finished with nine saves in goal for Houlton.
Caribou 4, Mount Desert Island 0
Caribou turned in a strong performance on both ends of the field Saturday, shutting out Mount Desert Island 4-0.
Van Buren 8, Schenck 3
The Van Buren offense erupted for eight goals in an 8-3 victory over Schenck.
Penobscot Valley 1, Fort Kent 1, 2OT
Fort Kent and Penobscot Valley could not be separated after regulation or two overtime periods, finishing in a 1-1 draw.
Wisdom 11, Woodland 0
Wisdom continued its high-scoring season with an 11-0 shutout victory over Woodland.
Katahdin 9, East Grand 1
The Katahdin girls completed a big day for the Cougars with a 9-1 victory over East Grand.
Combined with the boys' 7-0 victory earlier in the day, Katahdin's two varsity soccer teams scored 16 goals Saturday.

title: 7-year-old girl stabbed to death while walking along sidewalk in broad daylight
text:
CHICAGO (WLS) - Police in Chicago say a 7-year-old girl was walking along a neighborhood sidewalk when she was stabbed to death in broad daylight. Witnesses to the attack chased down the suspect and held her until officers arrived.
Chicago Police say a 7-year-old girl was walking along a sidewalk in the city’s Chatham neighborhood when a woman approached her just before noon Saturday. Investigators say the woman stabbed the girl multiple times in the back with a sharp object.
The victim was taken to the hospital, where she was pronounced dead. The Cook County Medical Examiner’s Office has identified her as Edimari Hernandez Chacon.
Bystanders who witnessed the attack chased down the suspect and held her until officers arrived. She is now in police custody, and charges are pending.
Authorities have not said whether the stabbing was a random attack or if the suspect knew the 7-year-old. They are still trying to determine a motive.
Residents expressed outrage and grief following the attack.
“I just don’t know what this world is coming to ... for a 7-year-old like that to be getting stabbed,” resident Denesta Freeman said. “I never thought it would come to this point. I never did. These kids nowadays are not getting to live their life.”
Alderwoman Michelle Harris of the 8th Ward released a statement following the attack:
“I am deeply saddened by the senseless stabbing of a 7 year old child in our neighborhood. My heart goes out to her family, friends, and everyone who is affected by this horrific incident. No child should ever have to experience violence or fear while simply walking down the sidewalk.
“I also want to recognize and thank the bystanders who quickly intervened—helping to detain the suspect and get assistance on the way. Their quick actions may have prevented further harm.
“I urge anyone with information to contact the Chicago Police Department. Our community must come together to support the victim and hold the perpetrator accountable.”

title: Florida appears set to tumble while Bama hopes to rise
text:
A week after a huge promotion in the poll, Florida is bound to come down in the newest AP Top 25 after a lopsided loss.
The No. 8 Gators fell 45-17 to No. 25 Missouri on a Saturday while other ranked teams generally won in workmanlike fashion.
Elsewhere in the rankings, No. 8 Alabama put a 56-23 beating on No. 16 Mississippi State. Both teams entered the week undefeated.
No. 2 Georgia, No. 3 Notre Dame, No. 4 Miami also remained unbeaten — and mostly untested — as top-10 teams. No. 1 Texas was idle Saturday.
Stick around for projections and live updates when the latest rankings drop at 2 p.m. EDT.
Six Top 25 teams were idle
By MAURA CAREY
Six AP Top 25 teams had the week off.
No. 1 Texas was idle after beating Tennessee in a hard-fought Week 4 road victory. No. 9 Ole Miss had a week to regroup following its first loss of the season to Florida. No. 13 Utah was off after a 31-17 win against Big 12 foe Iowa State.
No. 15 Oregon’s bye week came at a good time, giving quarterback Dante Moore a week to focus on recovering after a scary hit to the head.
Two of last week’s poll newcomers were also idle: No. 19 Oklahoma State and No. 23 UCLA.
How the votes are counted
By THE ASSOCIATED PRESS
For decades, voters called, emailed and faxed their votes to the AP and ballots were tabulated by hand.
Now voting happens online, and the count is automated first before AP checks for miscues.
The poll operates on a 1-to-25-point system, with the No. 1 team receiving 25 points down to the 25th team receiving 1 point. In between, the poll lists the teams with the most points from 24 down to 2. Teams that receive votes but not enough to make the top 25 are noted separately.

title: Trump names national intelligence director Jay Clayton to lead a new federal AI task force
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Sunday tapped Jay Clayton, his director of national intelligence, to lead a new government task force on artificial intelligence.
Trump is calling it the “Super Intelligence Force,” because he has tried to rebrand AI as “super intelligence.” The announcement comes after Trump hosted top executives of AI companies at the White House last week and said they had signed a voluntary accord that would effectively self-police the development of the technology.
The task force will coordinate the federal effort “to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans,” Trump in a post on social media Sunday.
The task force will reach out to consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers and AI companies, the Republican president said.
Others on the task force include the Federal Trade Commission’s chairman, Andrew Ferguson; Emil Michael, the Pentagon’s chief technology officer; and Scott Kupor, the director of the Office of Personnel Management.
The group will report to Trump and his chief of staff, Susie Wiles.

title: Maine Marathon winners soak in atmosphere, experience
text:
PORTLAND — Dylan Stoltzfus made a heart shape with his hands as he made his way to the finish line.
It was evident how much winning the 35th annual Maine Community Bank Maine Marathon meant.
“I spent a really long time with an injury in college,” said Stoltzfus, 24, a Portland resident. “I thought I would never run again, never race again. This is the first big race I’ve ever won. It feels like years in the wilderness and this is like coming out.”
Stoltzfus finished with a time of 2 hours, 23 minutes, 59 seconds, easily out-distancing runnerup Steven Fritzsche of Kennebunk (2:31.12). Will Faden of Somerville, Massachusetts (2:32.02) placed third.
Betsy Burke, 42, of Rye, New York finished first in the women’s field with a time of 2:54.08.
This was her second time running the race.
“I was really surprised,” Burke said. “It was fun. I had people to run with and felt pretty good until about (mile) 21 and then just tried to turn my brain off.”
Burke’s husband and his family are from Blue Hill, so she visits Maine often.
“I felt really good in the hills, like (miles) 12 to 18, then started feeling much worse,” Burke said, laughing. “But I felt good for a while and was like, ‘this is great,’ and then I knew I could just get to the end.”
Alyssa Carreau of Old Lyme, Connecticut (2:55.39) and Linnea Maynard of Portland (2:57.32) followed in second and third places, respectively.
On the half marathon side, winners JP Flavin and Megan O’Neil broke new ground.
As teammates who train out of Rochester, Michigan, not only was this the pair’s first time in Maine, but they earned course records in the men’s and women’s half marathon races.
“Oh my gosh, it’s gorgeous,” O’Neil said said of Maine. “I’m from Michigan. All my friends are super jealous I got to go to Maine in October. … Beautiful day for running, perfect temperature, not too windy.”
O’Neil, 30, finished in 1:14.34. Her time was 32 seconds faster than Cliodhna O’Malley’s record-setting run last year.
Flavin, 28, finished with a time of 1:03.00, beating previous record holder Colin Cernik’s 2025 time by 1:39.
“I’m in the middle of preparing for (the) New York City Marathon, so it’s kind of more of a workout, but it was fun,” Flavin said. “It was (a) good group of guys to work with for 10 miles and I was going to pick it up the last 5K and got rolling down those hills. The crowd was awesome, running past everyone was so much fun, so it was a blast.”
Next to finish were two Massachusetts runners — Cameron Dickson from Jamaica Plain (1:03.30) in second place and Ned Farrington of Cohasset (1:03.48) in third.
Heather Gallant of Wayne (1:15.38) and Isabel Seay of Hanover, New Hampshire (1:16.28) joined O’Neil on the podium in second and third place, respectively.

Obituary: Norman Albert Dean
text:
MADISON – Norman Albert Dean, 87, of Madison, Maine, passed away peacefully on Sept. 16, 2026, at his home in Madison with his devoted wife, Eleanor, by his side.
Norman was born on April 29, 1939, the son of Raymond and Alberta (Mantor) Dean, and was the eighth generation of the Dean family to make Madison home. Norman’s roots in the community ran deep. He graduated from Madison High School in 1957 and the University of Maine at Orono in 1961 with a B.S. degree.
On Aug. 5, 1961, he married the love of his life, Eleanor R. Wing. Together, they built a life on the Dean family farm and raised their two sons, Steven and Randall. Family was at the heart of Norman’s life. He took great pride in watching his family grow and especially in being “Papa” to his grandchildren. He rarely missed a game, graduation, birthday, or family celebration. His steady presence, encouragement, and genuine interest in their lives meant more to his family than words can express.
Norman dedicated 34 years to teaching at Madison High School, where he taught Vocational Agriculture, Driver’s Education, Biology, and several other science courses. He shared with generations of students not only what he knew, but also his love of the outdoors, agriculture, and the community he called home. Teaching was an important part of Norman’s life, and the relationships he formed with students and colleagues remained a source of pride throughout his life. Many students will remember “Mr. Dean” well beyond the classroom.
Legendary among family, friends, and students are the stories from the many Florida senior trips he chaperoned with longtime colleague and dear friend Ron Paquette. Just as memorable were the end-of-year teachers’ gatherings at Norman and Eleanor’s home, and later at Norm’s hunting camp, where stories were told and friendships were strengthened.
Alongside his teaching career, “Norm” owned and operated the family farm, Ray’s Dairy, delivering milk door to door. Farming was never simply a job to Norman; it was part of who he was. He loved being on his tractor, working the fields beneath the summer sun, and especially enjoyed the years when his grandson Thomas worked beside him during hay season. Special times were also shared with Norman’s cousin, Donald Morse, who came up from New Hampshire, every summer, continuing a tradition that began in childhood.
After his dairy farming days were behind him, Norman found new enjoyment in raising red deer in his pasture. Even at 85, he could still be found working the fields.
Norman believed deeply in giving back to Madison and the State of Maine. He served on the Madison Board of Selectmen from 1979 to 1991, including seven years as chairman. He served on Madison’s Charter Commission from 1979 to 1980 and was appointed by Governor John McKernan to the Maine Board of Environmental Protection.
In 2000, Norman agreed to serve as Madison’s interim Town Manager in what was expected to be a 30-day appointment. Those 30 days turned into 11 years. During his tenure, Norman helped guide a number of projects important to the town, including the development of the Madison Business Gateway and construction of the Preble Avenue Fields. He also worked with the developers of Backyard Farms, helping bring new investment and jobs to the community.
Norman was a member of the Kennebec Valley Grange, the Odd Fellows, and the Wood Turners Association of Maine. In retirement, he spent many joyful hours at his lathe. He made beautiful wooden bowls, salt-and-pepper shakers, music boxes, and countless other pieces, often giving them to family and friends. Each piece was made with care and became a lasting reminder of Norman’s generosity and the pleasure he found in making something special for someone he loved.
Whether he was teaching in the classroom, working a field, serving the Town of Madison, or standing at the lathe, Norman found purpose in being helpful to others. He was proud of his family, deeply connected to his community, and grateful for the life he and Eleanor built together. His legacy can be found not only in his accomplishments, but in the family he loved, the students he taught, the community he served, and the many people whose lives were better for having Norman in them.
When Norman was once asked what he would change if he could do it all over again, he thought for a moment and said, “Well, I guess I wouldn’t change a thing.” For a man who found happiness in his family, his work, his farm, and his community, perhaps nothing could say “a life well lived” better.
Norman and Eleanor were especially grateful to reach their goal of having a beautiful summer together and getting to celebrate their 65th wedding anniversary on the coast of Maine.
Norman is survived by his loving wife of 65 years, Eleanor W. Dean of Madison; his son, Steven Dean and his wife, Gloria, and their daughters, Erika and Jessica, and great-granddaughter, Layla; and his son, Randall “Randy” Dean and his wife, Charlene, and their children, Allison, Jennifer, and Thomas.
So, whether you knew him as “Mr. Dean,” “Norm,” “Dad,” or “Papa,” and whether he taught you how to drive, dissect a frog, or do math at the dining room table, please know he enjoyed every moment.
There will be no public funeral services. Norman’s wish was that his ashes remain with Eleanor on Thurston Hill until she joins him and then they will leave together.

2 shot dead, dozens injured in shooting at neighborhood block party in southern Georgia
text:
2 killed and dozens injured at large neighborhood block party shooting in south Georgia
Law enforcement officials are still working to determine just what happened when a chaotic homecoming party spanning a four-block radius of a southern Georgia town erupted in gunfire early Sunday, leaving two people dead and nearly three dozen others injured.
Dooly County Sheriff Craig Peavy identified the two people killed as 21-year-old Jaquevion Jackson of Cordele and 23-year-old Macaleb Jackson of Hawkinsville, Georgia.
Some of the three dozen injured had gunshot wounds, Georgia Bureau of Investigation Chris Hosey said Sunday evening, but he could not provide a number.
“We’re still trying to work through that,” Hosey said during a news conference Sunday evening.
No arrests had been reported hours later, and authorities gave no possible motive for the gunfire.
The injured ranged in age from 14 to 51, and they were taken to several regional hospitals, Peavy said. Some were in critical condition Sunday evening and others were stable, he said.
More than 1,000 people attended the party
More than 1,000 people had gathered at the site, and more than 50 shots were fired in at least two locations about a block apart in Vienna, Peavy told WMAZ-TV. Vienna is a small, rural community about 130 miles (about 210 kilometers) south of Atlanta.
Deputies were near the scene when the shooting began, Peavy said, and after they arrived more gunfire erupted about a block away.
“We don’t know if it’s coming at us or someone else,” he said. “You just have to keep doing what you’re doing and hope you don’t get hit by gunfire.”
The incident took place over homecoming weekend for Dooly County High School.
One woman recalled rapid-fire shots and people running
Ashley Gee, 30, who lives in nearby Turner County and came to Vienna for the party, described to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution a constant barrage of gunfire, imitating the sound of rapid-fire shots.
“Like a machine gun,” she said. “One person ran, and everybody started running.”
The AJC said the party drew in people from other surrounding counties in south Georgia following a local high school football team’s victory at a homecoming game Friday night.
The shooting was not at a school-sponsored event, said Sherrod Willaford, superintendent of the Dooly County School System.
“We recognize that its impact may reach many of our students, families, and staff,” he said in a statement. Schools will open Monday, he said, but additional safety measures have been put in place. He did not specify what they are.
Peavy said the festivities began Friday night, and that it had “gone well” with “respect from the community” that evening as deputies patrolled the event.
Sheriff says deputies were on hand as shots were still being fired
But the party Saturday night was a “different story,” he said.
“We’re still working through the investigation to see what went wrong. But at large parties with people from different places, not just your locals, sometimes problems come,” he said.
"Our deputies were just about on the scene when it happened. They were at the end of each, most directions of where the block party was being held. But it was so many people. And it was just hard to figure out what was going on,” he said.
Peavy said the shooting was “a learning experience,” for his law enforcement team.
“There's just hardly no way to know how to operate when something like that happens on the scene," he said. He later continued, “We thought we'd been involved with a lot of stuff. But sometimes it surprises, and it was overwhelming.”
Vienna is about a 50-mile (80-kilometer) drive south on the Interstate 75 corridor from the central Georgia city of Macon, where authorities say 12 teens were wounded by gunfire during a confrontation between people at a birthday party the previous weekend a city park.
Deputies in Vienna found two people dead at the scene and multiple others who had been shot, officials said. Police also did not specify how many of the injured had been shot. The victims were taken to several hospitals for treatment, the GBI said.
Dooly County Coroner Brett Walls said the two men were pronounced dead at the scene with fatal gunshot wounds. He said multiple other people were also shot, calling the scene “horrific.”
Walls told the AJC that multiple people were struck by bullets and roughly a dozen others were hurt while trying to flee.
“This doesn’t — it’s not supposed to — happen in a small town like that. It’s something you hear on the news in bigger cities,” Walls told the newspaper, adding hospitals were flooded with the injured. “And even in bigger cities, you don’t hear that kind of a number.”
Investigators are seeking suspects and a motive
Authorities have not said whether any suspects are in custody or being sought. No motive has been given for the shooting.
Vienna Mayor Eddie Daniels said the shooting was about a block from his house and he “saw a lot of blue lights.” Daniels said he hadn’t spoken with law enforcement officials yet and had no details about what had happened.
Daniels said the city hadn’t issued any kind of permit for the block party and he didn’t know if it was a homecoming party.
Georgia Bureau of Investigation spokesperson Lydia Bullard declined to answer questions about the shooting, saying it was an ongoing investigation.
___
Associated Press reporters Rebecca Boone in Boise, Idaho, and Anthony Izaguirre in New York contributed to this report. Bauer reported from Madison, Wisconsin.

title: Bateschella Comes Back to a Slow Start
text:
On Saturday, Sept. 12, Campus Activities and Traditions (CAT) brought Bateschella back to campus, giving students an evening of music, food, and games to kick off the school year. First introduced in 2022 and most recently held in 2023, Bateschella returned this year after a two-year break, bringing a Coachella-inspired music festival atmosphere to the Commons Quad.
Modeled after Coachella, the well-known music festival held annually in California, Bateschella transformed the Commons Quad into a mini-festival of its own. The event ran from 7:00 p.m. to 11:00 p.m., and the music could be heard from across campus. As students approached the tent, they were greeted by food trucks, colorful bounce houses, Spikeball, Frisbee, a variety of lawn games, an inflatable jousting game and a dance floor that would gradually fill as the night went on.
Luke Allen, coordinator of Campus Life programming and First-Year Experience, commented on the two year pause. He talked about the replacement event “A Great Night To Be A Bobcat,” and with lower attendance rates and enthusiasm he decided it was time for a change. “This was the last year any current student would have attended Bateschella 2023, so if it was going to return, it had to be this year,” Allen said.
One of the biggest draws was the promise of free food. The first 600 students to attend received free poutine from Pinky D’s Poutine, while North East Ice Cream handed out free ice cream bars and novelties. Both food trucks were at the previous Bateschella events. The food quickly became one of the most popular parts of the event.
“I am not a big poutine person, but it was way better than I expected, and I really appreciated the ice cream,” said Francesca Stamney ‘30. “The best part was watching people joust on the inflatable stage with bouncy batons.”
Music, however, remained at the center of the event. Adien Habas ‘28 was one of the student DJs who performed at Bateschella this year. After other student DJs asked whether he was interested in performing, he immediately said yes.
Habas said one of his favorite parts of the night was, unsurprisingly, the inflatable jousting game.
“My favorite part of the event was fighting my friends on the stick fight one. I didn’t lose once,” he said. Habas also praised the event’s sound system, adding, “it was so nice!”
While Habas enjoyed the event overall, he did have some suggestions for future Bateschella events. He thought the four-hour event started a little too early and that he would have preferred a schedule running from 8:00 p.m. to midnight. He also wished more students had been on the dance floor earlier in the evening.
His comments point to one of the main challenges of the event: getting students to dance. Although Bateschella officially began at 7:00 p.m., the dance floor remained relatively quiet for much of the evening, with more students beginning to dance around 10:00 p.m.
Despite this, Habas said he would happily participate again.
“I wish more people were on the dance floor, but I would definitely do this event again,” he said.
With free food, inflatable games, lawn activities and student DJs, Bateschella offered students a chance to spend the evening together outside of the usual rhythms of campus life. Bateschella’s return after a two-year hiatus may also have provided a glimpse of what students can expect from CAT in the years ahead.

title: Obituary: Nancy (Doran) Lambert
text:
WELLS – Nancy Doran Lambert, 81, of Wells, went home to be with her Lord and Savior on Sept. 29, 2026.
Nancy was born May 23, 1945, in Boston, Mass., the daughter of Albert John and Lucille Totman Doran. Moving to Maine in her childhood, she is a graduate of Farmington High School, Class of 1963. Nancy worked at Poore Simons in Rochester, N.H., The Kennebunk Copy Center, and during the years George H.W. Bush was president, worked as head of housekeeping at the Rhumb Line Inn, where she enjoyed meeting the many Secret Service members who stayed there.

She was predeceased by her husband, Jon; parents, Albert and Lucile; and a sister, Elizabeth (Doran) Averill.

title: Check your freezer: Frozen berries sold in dozens of states recalled over possible E. coli concerns
text:
FDA expands recall of frozen berries sold in dozens of states over E. coli concerns
A recall of frozen berries sold at popular stores and that may be contaminated with E. coli has been expanded, the FDA announced.
The recall now includes Great Value frozen organic blueberries and its triple berry blend, as well as Trader Joe’s frozen organic mixed berry blend, the FDA said in sharing a recall announcement from Frutas y Hortalizas del Sur S.A. on Friday, Oct. 2.
Related video above: Check your fridge: Recalled foods could already be in your home
The Great Value berries were sold in Walmart stores in 30 states and Puerto Rico in 10-ounce bags. Those affected products have best buy dates of January 2028 and February 2028, and the blueberries also list a best buy date of June 12, 2028, the announcement states.
The recalled Great Value product was shipped to select Walmart stores in 30 states, including Alabama, Arkansas, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, North Dakota, Nebraska, New Jersey, New York, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia, Wisconsin, and West Virginia, along with the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico. Consumers should check their freezers for the affected product, the FDA said.
The Trader Joe’s organic mixed berry blend was sold in 26 states and Washington, D.C., in 12-ounce bags. The product lists a best-before date of Feb. 20, 2028.
The recalled Trader Joe’s product was shipped to select Trader Joe’s stores in 26 states: Alabama, Arkansas, Colorado, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia, and Wisconsin, along with the District of Columbia.
“Consumers who have Great Value Organic Triple Berry 10 OZ with lot code 6 031 01, 6 041 01, Great Value Organic Blueberries 10 OZ with lot code 6 019 01, 6 040 01 and 6 163 01 and Trader Joe’s Organic Mixed Berry Blend 12 OZ with lot code 6 051 01 should not consume those products. The product should be discarded or returned to Walmart or Trader Joe’s for a full refund,” the announcement states.
The recall expands on a previous recall issued by Frutas y Hortalizas in July and September, CNN reported.

U.S. Coast Guard locates debris from missing plane off Massachusetts, search for passengers ongoing
text:
Coast Guard finds debris off Nantucket as search continues for 6 missing on medical plane
The U.S. Coast Guard located debris that was confirmed to be associated with the missing aircraft off Nantucket, the U.S. Coast Guard confirmed to Boston, Massachusetts, sister station WCVB on Saturday.
The search is still ongoing for the six missing passengers who were on board, the Coast Guard said.
The Gulfstream G-100 aircraft departed L.F. Wade International Airport in Bermuda and was traveling to Boston's Logan International Airport.
A Massport spokesperson confirmed that the aircraft did not arrive at Logan Airport as scheduled.
The Bermuda government said it has been in contact with the families of those on board.
“My thoughts are with everyone on board and their families during this deeply worrying time," said Premier David Burt. "We are praying that all six people will be found safe, and we thank the search and rescue crews for their continuing efforts.”
In a statement from Skyport, the company that manages Wade International Airport, a spokesperson said that the aircraft was a Canadian-registered air ambulance that left its airport for Boston at 12:41 a.m. on Saturday.
The company said there were four crew members and two passengers on board. The passengers were traveling to Boston for medical care.
"The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has advised that air traffic controllers subsequently lost contact with the aircraft off the coast of Nantucket Island, Massachusetts, and a search is currently underway," the spokesperson said. "Skyport has no further information to provide at this time."
The Federal Aviation Administration said it issued a search and rescue alert for the plane at 1:20 a.m.
The FAA notified the U.S. Coast Guard that it lost contact with the plane, which is registered to Canadian-based Latitude Air Ambulance. The company confirmed that the missing plane is among its fleet.
The Coast Guard's response includes crews from Air Station Cape Cod, a 47-foot motor lifeboat crew from Station Brant Point and the USCGC William Sparling -- a fast response cutter.
The search is about 13 nautical miles off the coast and extends from about 30 nautical miles wide and 20 nautical miles long, according to the Coast Guard.

title: An opinion section study in contrasts
text:
It was a delight to read William Smith’s elegant op-ed on the promise of trickle-up economics (Sept. 13), indistinguishable from democratic socialism, that made clear the differences between what we in this country have: extreme disparities in wealth and opportunity, and what we would enjoy with trickle-up economics. It is no surprise most of our politicians disparage democratic socialism; it is not in their interests.
On the other hand, the op-ed next door in the section, by Charles Todorich (“Western civilization is dying and Europeans don’t seem to care”), contained a number of mistaken assumptions and conclusions.
For example, Todorich says that a majority of Europeans are pessimistic about the future and believe life will be harder for their children. In the EU, 70% are pessimists; in the U.S., that figure is roughly 70-75%, not much different. It is interesting that in Denmark, with the highest taxes in the EU, only about a third of parents are pessimistic about their children’s economic future. After all, they do get something for the taxes they pay: universal healthcare, free university education, a highly developed social security and welfare system and a high degree of income equality.
Todorich, who seems to believe that the Crusades were a moral high point for European Christianity, expressed concerned about Muslim emigration to Europe, but seems ignorant of its cause: wars initiated by the Bush/Cheney administration in the Middle East destabilized the region and made life there unbearable; emigration to safety is the result. He also believes that concerns about global warming are simply mass hysteria. I could only shake my head in disbelief.
Jonathan Mitschele
New Gloucester

title: Obituary: Michael Edmund Saucier
text:
FREEPORT – Michael Edmund Saucier passed away in July after 73 years of a reflective, quietly joyful life. Born between Christmas and New Year, Michael was the oldest of Edmund E., Jr. and Joanne I. (Joler) Saucier’s ten surviving children.
After degrees from Waterville High School and Boston College, Michael graduated from the University of Maine School of Law. His admission to the Maine Bar preceded his joining the state’s public prosecutorial offices for six years. He then entered private practice, primarily for civil rights, municipal liability, product liability and family relations as a practicing member of the Maine and New Hampshire bars. During his career, he appeared in more than 100 civil and criminal jury trials with over 60 combined appearances before the Maine Law Court and the U.S. Court of Appeals in Boston.
Michael’s thoughtful approach to trial and appellate advocacy was recognized through his long service on the Maine Supreme Judicial Court’s Rules of Evidence Advisory Committee. The reputability of his practice was acknowledged with an appointment to and service on the Professional Ethics Commission of the Maine Board of Overseers of the Bar.
Michael contributed his time to both the professional and broader community. He chaired the Maine Juvenile Justice Advisory Group (JJAG) and then became National Chair in 1994 for the Washington D.C.-based Coalition for Juvenile Justice. He co-authored the Commentary that appeared with the Juvenile Code as a member of the Maine JJAG. His advocacy for the national organization was recognized by his alma mater with a Boston College Alumni Association Award for Excellence in Law. He also served as a member and chair of the Criminal Law Advisory Committee to the Maine Legislature and as an officer on the Board of Directors of the Cleaves Law Library in Portland. He served for many years on the governing board of First Parish in Portland Unitarian Universalist Church.
A life-long and capable athlete, Michael enjoyed playing baseball, football and hockey while growing up in Waterville. He started skiing while in college and found great pleasure in heading to the top of Sugarloaf and then making the long run down to the base lodge. He played tennis, racquetball, and squash as well as hockey during law school. Later, he enjoyed his time sailing the Maine coast with family and friends. An alumnus of the Portland Industrial hockey league, he sought out various indoor and outdoor venues on skates, including Snow Pond with family in Belgrade; the Kent’s Hill Rink for a significant birthday bash; the canal in Ottawa, Canada; Rockefeller Center; Boston Common; “The Whale” at Yale University; the Natural History Museum rink in London at Christmas; and most recently the Royal Victoria Park in Bath, England.
Michael’s joy came from joining extended family gatherings, building and maintaining home garden paths, golfing anywhere in Maine especially with a brother or two, listening to live music performances from classical to fiddle, and painting the Maine landscape. His keen sense of humor charmed family, friends and colleagues, who shared delight in his sudden broad smiles and understood his nature in the kindnesses he showed them.
Michael is survived by his spouse of 45 years, Paula Craighead, and their child Jillian; also by siblings, Jon (Nancy), Sandra Bard (Andrew Heckler), Cathy Kershner (Dirk), Daniel (Brenda), James (Jean), Peter, Patty Bearce and Paul (Cindy); 15 nieces and nephews, Matthew (Erika), Andrew ( Kate), Kelley Estrella (Norwin), Joshua Kershner (Angie), Britney Michaud (Jake), Liza, Lexi (Wade Cooper), Kelsey, Jodi Chase (Jared), Sarah Deslandes (Chris), Christopher Jacques (Lexi Lint), Aaron, Jericah Hart (Cooper), Abigail Lauter (Jay), and Nathan Surette (Saige Brickett), and numerous great-nieces and great-nephews. Both parents, sister Susan Surette, and brother-in-law John Bearce predeceased him.
A private memorial meditation was held in August at Spurwink Church in Cape Elizabeth. His memory may be honored with support for a Maine youth hockey program and, for his legal colleagues, by becoming a member of the Cleaves Law Library in Portland.

title: Good Shepherd Food Bank, local pantries see more demand: ‘We’re going to see the gap get bigger, not smaller’
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Rising prices and cuts to federal food assistance are forcing more people to seek out help from food pantries, local operators and an official at Good Shepherd Food Bank in Auburn said last week.
The organizations providing the help are also feeling the pinch.
Good Shepherd itself saw a major source of government funding cut this year, hindering its efforts to provide food for pantries across the state, Robin McCarthy, chief advancement officer, said.
And the state’s network of small, largely volunteer-led pantries are feeling those cuts amid rising costs.
“There just isn’t a safety net,” McCarthy said. “So as fuel becomes more expensive, as heating the pantry becomes more expensive, as buying the food becomes more expensive, it all starts to pressurize and the end result is less food.”
‘MORE AND MORE PRESSURE’
Good Shepherd Food Bank partners with about 600 food pantries, meal sites and community programs across the state, distributing about 35 million pounds of food a year.
The pantries, McCarthy said, are reporting a 10% increase in new visitors over last year, with visitors often returning more frequently.
Eligibility changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, better known as food stamps, that were part of President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill have led an estimated 18,000 Maine families to lose benefits, McCarthy said.
At the same time, McCarthy said, the U.S. Department of Agriculture scaled back a program that formerly provided funding for a quarter of Good Shepherd’s food, leading to a gap of about 4.5 million pounds — and a reduction in what they were able to provide around the state.
“Our sense, anecdotally, is that our partners are feeling more and more pressure,” said McCarthy. “We don’t have as much variety as we used to have. It’s getting harder for us to purchase the same volume of food to backfill what we lost from the government given rising needs.”
The Poland Community Food Bank is one of the partners that has seen how the issues facing Good Shepherd are trickling down. There have been fewer options lately, a food bank representative said, specifically for peanut butter, canned meat and cereal.
There’s also been an uptick in use of the food pantry in Poland. Typically, the food bank, which serves Poland, Mechanic Falls and Minot, helps between 25 and 30 families the two days it is open. Busier weeks see upward of 35 to 40 families.
There’s more demand at the Seventh-day Adventist Church in Auburn’s pantry, too, where on a normal day, they’ll see about 23 families, said Carol Holmes, co-director. Busy days will have upward of 40 families.
They see new families every week, Holmes said. And they welcome everyone.
“This is why we’re here,” she said. “If there was not a need, we wouldn’t be operating. I have a saying I tell everyone: everybody has a mouth, everyone needs to eat.”
‘WE ARE GRATEFUL’
Ibrahim Dubai of Lewiston goes frequently to the Seventh-day Adventist Church’s pantry to get fruits and vegetables for his family.
Dubai comes from a big family, with his parents, four brothers and two sisters.
“Every time I go to a store I walk out, the bill is $150,” said Dubai. “We’re having to spend more than we receive at places like Hannaford’s and Shaw’s. We are grateful for resources like this food pantry, as it helps us get more food into the house for little to no cost. “
The savings help Dubai, who works in Portland, get back and forth. It used to cost $30 to fill his car, he said; now, it’s $50.
McCarthy fears that additional changes proposed for SNAP in the coming years could make matters worse. As it is now, she said, Maine will have to spend a lot just to make up what’s been lost.
“The state is going to have to provide somewhere between $50 (million) and $70 million a year in our annual budget in order to keep providing just the level of SNAP benefits that we’re currently providing,” said McCarthy.

title: Man accused of kidnapping woman he met on dating app, keeping her captive in attic for weeks
text:
MALDEN, Mass. (WFXT) - A Massachusetts man is being held without bail after he pleaded not guilty to keeping a woman he reportedly met on a dating app captive in an attic for weeks.
Jordende Piere, 29, pleaded not guilty to multiple charges in court Sept. 25 after he was arrested in a human trafficking investigation. He was ordered held without bail.
Prosecutors say Piere is accused of keeping a woman in the attic of a Malden apartment building for weeks, where authorities say she was sexually abused and living in poor conditions. The woman had not eaten, was covered in scabs and was using a bucket as a toilet, according to prosecutors.
Malden Police Chief Marc Gatcomb said the investigation began when an officer noticed something out of place at the apartment building, which led officers to the victim.
The woman told police she met Piere on a dating app. Investigators say he forced her to have sex with him and arranged sexual encounters with other people.
Gatcomb says the case is a reminder that human trafficking can be happening anywhere.
“[These cases] are very disturbing. There are a lot of moving parts to them. Sometimes, these types of crimes are hidden in plain sight, right under your noses in neighborhoods, hotels and whatnot,” he said.
Piere is charged with kidnapping, human trafficking and indecent assault and battery on a person over 14. Authorities say he was on release at the time of his arrest on assault and battery and weapons charges out of Somerville.
Piere is scheduled to return to court Tuesday.
Police say the investigation is ongoing, and there could be more charges involving other people.

Nolo becomes a Category 3 Hurricane in the remote Pacific Ocean
text:
Nolo becomes a Category 3 Hurricane in the remote Pacific Ocean
Nolo strengthened into a major hurricane Saturday in the remote Pacific Ocean, far to the west of Hawaii's main islands and population centers.
Related video:
The storm's maximum sustained winds rapidly intensified to 115 mph (185 kph), the Miami-based National Hurricane Center reported, meaning it was a Category 3 hurricane.
As of the evening, Nolo was located about 200 miles (320 kilometers) south-southwest of Lisianski Island and moving westward at 20 mph (31 kph).
A tropical storm warning was issued for the Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument — a massive and remote federally protected area with islands, atolls, seamounts, shoals and coral reefs — from Maro Reef to Lisianski Island.
The hurricane center said large surf associated with Nolo “will likely inundate some of the low-lying atolls.”
No threat was in the forecast for any populated islands, however.
The hurricane center said Nolo was expected to cross the international date line Sunday.
Nolo skirted Hawaii as a hurricane a week ago. It then lost some of its punch and became a tropical storm, before regaining hurricane strength Friday.
Meanwhile another Pacific hurricane, Category 1 Rachel, continued heading westward on a path away from the west coast of Mexico.
Dangerous swells were forecast through the weekend for the coast of west-central Mexico and through Monday for the Baja California Peninsula, according to the hurricane center.

title: UAE had shared details about FlyDubai flight with Israel, including pilots' names and nationalities
text:
UAE had shared details about FlyDubai flight with Israel, including pilots' names and nationalities
Authorities in the United Arab Emirates shared with Israel a list of passengers and crew ahead of the FlyDubai flight on which a pilot attempted to seize control of the Israel-bound aircraft and crash it, regional officials said Sunday, raising new questions over how the attacker evaded detection.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu later told the head of the National Security Council to appoint an examiner to review “all security aspects regarding foreign civil aviation to Israel.”
With the investigation into the FlyDubai incident underway, preliminary details have highlighted several major security lapses. Officials already have said the Omani co-pilot had been barred from flying by his own country because of concerns about his extremist views. It also remains unclear how a citizen of Oman, an Arab country that has no diplomatic relations with Israel, was allowed to fly a planeload of Israelis to Tel Aviv.
The UAE, which is leading the investigation, said the co-pilot attacked the flight's captain with the cockpit’s crash ax and tried to take control of the plummeting plane in a “terrorist attack” Wednesday. His actions nearly crashed the plane with 182 people on board before the Indian captain managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and others to rush in and subdue the attacker.
Israel did not raise concerns about passengers and crew
The regional officials said Emirati authorities had shared information about the passengers and crew, including their nationalities. Israel hadn’t raised red flags on any passenger or member of the crew, said the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to reporters about the probe.
The Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security agency, said the Transportation Ministry is responsible for vetting passenger lists from foreign flights. Transportation Minister Miri Regev on X said the security agencies are responsible for flight security and that her ministry wasn’t given a list of passengers or any warnings.
Sharing the list is standard aviation procedure. But the head of aviation security at the Transportation Ministry, Dvir Rubinstein, told Army Radio that the ministry relies on local security checks and does not have the tools or the ability to run checks on each passenger on every flight.
Netanyahu said Thursday that Israel has long-standing agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots from flying into the country if they are citizens of nations that don’t maintain diplomatic relations with Israel.
Australian police said Sunday that counterterrorism investigators were looking into the attacker's possible connections to Australia.
The passengers who halted the attack and helped regain control of the aircraft have been hailed as heroes in Israel.
Questions being raised about security failures
But as the initial euphoria of the rescue has subsided, officials have begun to raise difficult questions and trade accusations about the security blunders that could have led to a major disaster.
Ahead of the elections at the end of the month, some opposition candidates have seized on the security failures to highlight what they perceive as negligence on the part of Netanyahu and his supporters. Transportation Minister Regev is a member of Netanyahu's Likud party and a staunch supporter.
“This is exactly what system collapse looks like,” Yair Golan, head of the opposition Democrats party, wrote on X. “A transportation minister who completely abandons our skies, and a prime minister who abandons national security.”
It also remains unclear how FlyDubai, a low-cost Emirati airline that operates flights between Israel and the UAE, had failed to identify the Omani pilot as a security risk.
Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England who wrote a book about aircraft hijackings and bombings, said background check systems differ from country to country and there are limits on what types of information can be shared.
“In terms of aviation security itself, obviously we want to have as robust background checks as possible. But there are huge limitations on doing background checks in any case, especially in cross-border checks,” he said.

title: Frozen berries sold at Walmart and Trader Joe’s recalled. Here’s what to know
text:
(Gray News) - Frozen berries sold at Walmart and Trader Joe’s have been recalled because they may be contaminated with E. coli, according to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.
Packages of Great Value brand frozen organic blueberries and frozen organic Triple Berry Blend have been recalled. They were sold in 10-ounce bags at Walmart stores in 30 states. Also recalled are packages of Trader Joe’s frozen organic Mixed Berry Blend.
The Great Value frozen blueberries have a UPC code of 7874211213 and lot codes of 6 019 01, 6 040 01 and 6 163 01. They also have best if used by dates of Jan. 19, 2028; Feb. 9, 2028; and June 12, 2028.
The Great Value Triple Berry Blend contains strawberries, blackberries and blueberries. These packages have a UPC code of 7874211226 and lot codes of 6 031 01 and 6 041 01. They have best if used by dates of Jan. 31, 2028, and Feb. 10, 2028.
The affected states are Alabama, Arkansas, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Nebraska, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia, West Virginia and Wisconsin as well as Puerto Rico.
The Trader Joe’s Mixed Berry Blend includes strawberries, blackberries, blueberries and raspberries. It was sold in 12-ounce packages at stores in 26 states. The recalled products have a UPC code of 00977654, a lot code of 6 051 01 and a best before date of Feb. 20, 2028.
The affected states are Alabama, Arkansas, Colorado, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia and Wisconsin as well as the District of Columbia.
Anyone who bought the recalled products should not eat them but instead throw them away or return them to the store for a full refund.
Those with questions may contact Comfrut through email at Info.foodsafety@comfrut.com or by calling 336-899-5612 on weekdays from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. Eastern.
This recall is related to a larger recall of frozen organic blueberries produced and sold by Frutas y Hortalizas del Sur S.A. of San Carlos, Chile. The FDA says a total of 17 people were infected with E. coli. between May and August 2026, including six who were hospitalized.
An E. coli infection can cause severe stomach cramps, diarrhea and vomiting. Some infections may result in a serious complication known as hemolytic uremic syndrome, particularly in young children, older adults and those with weakened immune systems.

title: Teen accused of mixing toxic chemicals in cafeteria faces attempted murder, terrorism charges
text:
PORTLAND, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - A 15-year-old Oregon high school student accused of mixing toxic chemicals in the school cafeteria is facing attempted murder and terrorism charges.
Portland Police say a Benson Polytechnic High School student brought common household chemicals from home and mixed them in the school cafeteria on Sept. 8 before passing out due to inhaling the toxic gases. Investigators identified the mix as hydrogen sulfide and hydrogen cyanide.
The 15-year-old appeared in court Friday afternoon, facing a first-degree domestic terrorism charge in connection with the incident. Later Friday, the Multnomah County District Attorney’s Office also announced 12 counts of attempted murder.
Teen allegedly linked to violent extremist group ‘764′
Multnomah County Deputy District Attorney Eric Zimmerman said at least seven students and staff needed medical care after the Sept. 8 incident, and more than 100 people were checked at the school that day. He said investigators believe more people could have been harmed.
“It was really confusing. For one second, I’m in class, and I’m eating the school breakfast then next, I’m out on Buckman getting evacuated,” said Benson junior Eva Branstetter.
Zimmerman said surveillance video shows the suspect arriving in gloves and dark clothing and pouring chemicals from a white jug. A search of his home turned up many dangerous chemicals and reactive substances, including materials that can be used in thermite-type mixtures, along with social media posts about making acetone peroxide.
Prosecutors also pointed to social media posts referencing a “kill/death ratio,” along with language about self-harm and wanting to cause death to himself and others.
Benson Vice Principal Joe Metassik said the teen had been a responsible student before but said the impact on students has been “terror,” and it has been hard to get kids to return to school.
Zimmerman said the FBI is reviewing seized papers, hard drives and computers found Friday morning, including what he described as extensive references to “764,” a violent extremist group. He said the review is ongoing.
The state asked that the teen be held at the Donald E. Long county detention center until investigators better understand the full scope and asked that he be taken into custody right away.
Teen needs mental health treatment, defense attorney says
Defense attorney Norah Van Dusen acknowledged the seriousness of the allegations and submitted letters from the teenager’s personal psychiatrist and a psychiatrist at the Perry Center. Both recommend continued psychiatric care.
Van Dusen said the Perry Center is locked and secure with no access to the outside world or social media. She quoted from one letter: “Failure to provide this level of mental health support currently is estimated to come at high risk.”
She said the teen remains at high risk of suicide, has a serious depression diagnosis and is cooperating with treatment but has a long road ahead.
Van Dusen said the teen has strong family support, with his father present in court and visiting daily at the Perry Center. She said he appeared voluntarily, has made no effort to run, has no prior court history and has a stable placement at the Perry Center. She asked that he be released to his father to return to the Perry Center to continue treatment his doctors described as medically necessary.
The teen’s father said the current placement at the Perry Center is best, noting his son is only one week into a program that normally lasts six to eight weeks.
Some parents said they just want whatever gets the 15-year-old the help he needs.
“To me, I just feel like he needs the help, and a program would be better,” said Benson parent Loressa Williams.
“I hope he gets help, and I think that’s the most important thing and he doesn’t hurt himself or others in the future,” said Benson parent Ryan Branstetter.
The judge followed the recommendation from the Juvenile Department and ordered the teen released to his father, with the expectation he return immediately to the Perry Center. Conditions include attending all future hearings, not running away and not leaving the program. The judge set another hearing in about six weeks, after treatment, to decide future custody status.
Prosecutors immediately asked the judge to reconsider. A re-hearing is scheduled for Tuesday afternoon with a circuit court judge.

title: Obituary: Nelson David “Dave” Stevens
text:
CHEBEAGUE ISLAND – On Sept. 21, 2026, Nelson David “Dave” Stevens passed away, leaving behind his beloved family, a steadfast island community, and too many boats to count. While it is impossible to list everything he will be remembered for, the twinkle in his eye, his mischievous humor, and his heart of gold will be missed most.
Dave was born to Hermine and Nelson Stevens on Jan. 6, 1948 in Belmont, Mass. While he was raised in Massachusetts, his Maine roots ran deeper. His true home was Chebeague Island, where he spent childhood summers with family and the following decades making lifelong friends and a bit of mischief.
Before making Chebeague his permanent home with his sweetheart (wife) of 35 years, Cheryl, he spent his glory days in Portland riding his Triumph motorcycle. He raised his family in Yarmouth, just close enough for a quick commute to the island. Dave was a proud father of two and grandfather of four who all inherited his sharp sense of humor and strong spirit. He was a sucker for dogs and doted on his many English Cocker Spaniels over the years.
If you were looking for Dave, there were three places to look first: the garage, the boat, or Doughty’s Market. In 1995, he opened Stevens Mechanical Services, repairing island vehicles for 11 years. Though he enjoyed his work as an auto mechanic, his happiest days were spent later in life working as a marine mechanic at Chebeague Island Boatyard and spending every waking moment maintaining his pride and joy (after his children, of course): his 1971 Grand Banks wooden motor trawler boat, Luca.
In retirement, Dave and Cheryl spent the warmer months cruising the coast from Schoodic Point to Cape Cod. Through flat calms and high seas, they shared some of their best adventures aboard Luca—with the stories and T-shirts to prove it.
Chebeague was Dave’s favorite place in the world, and he was deeply invested in the community. You could always count on him to bail you out, whether it was engine trouble or a tow. He served as president of the Chebeague Transportation Company, was instrumental in lobbying for the island’s secession from Cumberland, and served as chair of the Board of Adjustment and Appeals and on the Coastal Waters Commission. Dave was also a dedicated lieutenant of Chebeague’s volunteer Fire Department for as long as he was able.
Dave was one of the most loyal, kind, and genuine people you could ever meet. He loved his family and the Chebeague Island community beyond words and will be deeply missed by all who knew him.
Dave is survived by his loving wife, Cheryl Stevens; his daughter, Jessica Wallace and her husband, Adam, along with their children, Henry and Olivia; and his son, David Stevens and his wife, Kathryn, along with their children, William and Sofia.
He was predeceased by his parents, Nelson and Hermine Stevens; and his brothers George and Alan Stevens.
A celebration of life will be held on Oct. 24, at 1 p.m. at the Chebeague Community Church, with a reception to follow.
Arrangements are under the direction of the new Conroy-Tully Walker Cremation, Funeral, and Gathering Center, 300 Allen Avenue, Portland.
In lieu of flowers, donations may be made to Chebeague Fire & Rescue Department.

title: On the Road Review: Dodge Charger R/T Plus
text:
Hand washing a new car often reveals the many subtleties of its design. You get to feel shapes and contours, you touch how various lines and seams blend together, plus you get a greater sense of a vehicle’s size — whether it be a full-size SUV, a compact crossover, or a refreshed muscle car like this week’s Dodge Charger.
Stellantis has experienced a rocky road over the last few years. Under previous CEO Carlos Tavares, retail prices escalated faster than inflation while there was a decided emphasis to build products that consumers were not asking for — shifting to EVs that lacked demand. Stellantis’ market share dropped swiftly, both in the North American market as well as in Europe.

title: Caribou City Council candidate wants to lower taxes and support those who struggle
text:
New to municipal government, Jeff Whitney is running for Caribou City Council because he wants to lower taxes, keep skilled people local and be a voice for those who are overlooked.
Whitney, 47, described himself as a Republican in the Abe Lincoln tradition who embraces smaller government, with an eye toward taking care of the elderly and those with mental challenges.
Caribou residents will elect three council representatives in November. Whitney is running unopposed for a three-year term. He is joined by Tamara Lovewell and George LaCasse Jr., who are also running unopposed.
Colleagues inspired him to enter the race, Whitney said. He works at Facilities Inc., a nonprofit that oversees 45 residential and five commercial properties in which tenants either provide or have a relationship with mental health services.
“I have familiarized myself with past debates, meetings and articles and come to the conclusion that like so many communities, drugs, unemployment and crime plague this area,” he said. “My current employment puts me right in the thick of knowing residents trying to repair their lives.”
Whitney believes it’s important to support mental health agencies as they work to help residents overcome hurdles.
He’s explored many career paths, but credits his past community work for influencing his desire for public service.
He served as a teen volunteer with his local police department, then advanced through police cadet academies and obtained a criminal justice degree, he said. He’s also volunteered as security at Special Olympics events.
If elected, Whitney’s top issues include taxes and retaining youth and skilled workers. But he also wants to be a voice for the city’s Public Works and emergency personnel, who frequently miss out on family time as they tend to accidents, fires, crime and problems that come with cold weather, he said.
“I am passionate to be a voice for the heroes in our community that are often overlooked, but keep us going all year long,” he said. “When we all want snow for holidays, adventures on our trails, hunting and just visits to see the uniqueness of this area, these hard workers make it possible for our business folk to open their shops, restaurants and outdoor venues.”
Whitney said he, like most people, has had moments of struggle and cares deeply about community. He hopes he can strengthen Caribou, his adopted community in which he wants to retire.
Fatherhood and homeownership happened early in his life at 18, and family is everything to him, he said.
He knows stepping up to serve means he’ll be in the public eye, and he welcomes hearing from others on topics they care about. Whether people agree or disagree, conversations are needed to help the city resolve issues and thrive.
“I would love to hear fresh ideas for motivating the whole community,” Whitney said. “I will dedicate 100% of myself to the City Council and I will do everything in my power to make this area a better, more welcoming community.”

title: Quality of life in Maine is high — why do people say it’s getting worse?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The ground was still frozen eight years ago when Maggie Hoffman’s husband came to Bangor for a job interview. They left a charmed and vibrant life in New York, just outside the city, and eventually landed in Hampden, an 18th-century town of 8,000 in Penobscot County with few sidewalks.
In some ways, life is good — the way it should be.
Hoffman marvels at the Cooper’s hawks and the red foxes and the bald eagles circling above the ever-nourishing Penobscot River.
“Look, I got to learn how to pee in the woods when I came to Maine,” she said.
The Maine Trust for Local News partnered with the Siena Research Institute to survey 824 residents and take a snapshot of life in Maine. Although three out of four respondents described an overall positive quality of life, only 20% said life in the Pine Tree State is getting better or much better.
And 38% said life is getting worse or much worse — that’s more than double the share of people nationally who said things are getting worse in their communities, according to polling Siena conducted last year.
Mainers are more likely to feel safe and secure in their home than the average American. The state’s outdoor spaces, as Hoffman noted, as well as its schools (particularly higher education) and sense of community scored highly.
But they say healthcare is hard to find, housing costs are high and the likelihood a young person will get a job with opportunity for advancement is low. All of that contributes to the disproportionately high number of people feeling that things are getting worse.
“I haven’t seen anybody really doing anything toward fixing any of those problems,” said Justin Crockett, who grew up in Franklin County and is worried about the high cost of living and the scourge of drug addiction.
It’s not surprising to Bill Nemitz, a retired journalist who for decades wrote a column for the Portland Press Herald/Maine Sunday Telegram, that Mainers are simultaneously fond about the place they live and yet pessimistic about its future.
“Maine has always had a really strong self identity of — the slogan says it all — ‘the way life should be.’ And I think Mainers have always taken pride in that,” Nemitz said.
It’s a state with a tempered resistance to change.
With the deluge of thousands of new-comers who have moved to Maine since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, change can feel inevitable.
And, Nemitz added, it’s difficult to look at the contours and trend lines of the world “and not feel a tinge of pessimism.”
“The fact that Mainers feel that way more strongly, perhaps, than other people in the country might be reflective of the fact that they value what they have so dearly,” he said.
It’s not all pine trees and soaring raptors for the Hoffmans either.
Their 38-year-old son, Jake, lives at home and has developmental and intellectual disabilities. He is a rock music aficionado and a dog whisperer, his mom said, but requires a high level of support. Finding caretakers who can help meet Jake’s needs is increasingly difficult. Maggie blames the high cost of living and childcare, and the lack of affordable housing.
“I believe that our scarcest resource are human beings, and that we’re really forgetting what we need to do to keep Maine alive,” she said. “What are we, 1.4 million people in this vastness of beautiful forestry and great waters, and people can’t live here?”
JUMPING TO HELP OUT
When his neighbor fell and broke her arm, Joel Katz brought over a healthy portion of potato leek soup.
That’s the way their community on the Blue Hill peninsula in Hancock County works, he said.
As Katz, 74, considers what he loves about living in Maine, his neighbors come to mind first. “The people we live around are just outstanding,” he said.
Down East, 52% of those polled said that quality of life, lifestyle and sense of community was the No. 1 best thing about their life in Maine, and 46% said the same statewide.
Katz moved to Maine full time when he retired a decade ago from a career leading performing arts centers, but has lived on and off in the state for 41 years. He was the first executive director of UMaine’s Center for the Arts, now known as the Collins Center for the Arts.
In the last decade, Katz and his wife have taken up some typical pastimes of the retired: they garden, for both flowers and food; on Mondays, he’s part of a team of that delivers soup to about a hundred residents of the peninsula; and on Thursdays he volunteers at the Tree of Life Food Pantry.
He’s found a community in Penobscot unlike anything he’s ever seen before.
The way life should be, for a long time, evoked the way in which life in Maine was different from other places, said Bill Green, the retired TV reporter who hosted “Bill Green’s Maine,” a program about Maine’s outdoors.
Mainers’ sense of community identity becomes “really the glue that binds this state together through thick and thin,” added Nemitz, the former columnist.
“Day to day, you can go to Hannaford, you can go to the hardware store, and, like, people really are nice to each other, and that’s something to celebrate,” said Hoffman, of Hampden.
Patricia Smith, a Lewiston resident, raised her son in Buxton and always appreciated the little things, like how neighbors check on each other during storms and power outages, or her landlord hiring the 8th grader down the block to mow the lawn.
“What we need is that type of community support,” Smith, 63, said.
NO SMALL PRICE: MAINE’S RISING COST OF LIVING
Katz is fortunate, he recognizes, to have stable housing and a reliable way to feed himself.
But with the costs soaring, he and his wife have opted to forgo some luxuries of retirement: a trip to Europe is off the table right now; the couple is waiting on a plan to add a second utility room to their 1,000-square-foot home; and they’ve put off adding solar panels to the house since the tax credits dried up.
“We don’t think it’s wise to spend our reserves,” Katz said. “We plan to live a little longer and we don’t know what’s going to happen, quite frankly.”
More than any other issue, Mainers surveyed said affordability was the worst thing about living here.
At the food pantry and thrift shop where he and his wife volunteer, there’s been a sharp increase in the number of people walking through the door.
“The rich have been doing very well, and the poor even worse,” Katz said.
Down East, the rising cost of fuel and bait has slimmed profit margins in Washington County’s $100-million commercial fishing industry, said Charles Rudelitch, executive director of the Sunrise County Economic Council.
Diminished services, the dearth of emergency medical care and specialists chief among them, makes the rural county a hard sell for those looking to settle long term. The median home price in Washington County has more than doubled in the last decade, while wages have only risen 54%. That said, it’s still one of the more affordable places to live in the state.
But what it giveth in housing, it taketh away in jobs, said Sean Thomas, who moved to Calais four years ago from Brockton, Massachusetts.
“It’s taken me a long time to get established in having enough work,” he said. “I was under-employed for a long, long time.”
Thomas was among those who said things were getting somewhat worse. He also quite likes living in Maine.
“Calais reminds me of when I was a kid,” he said, adding, “It’s a bit like stepping back in time.”
In Maine, 32% of those polled said a young person in their community was likely to find a job with opportunity for advancement and 27% said it was unlikely, while 39% said it was a tossup. Down East, a third of respondents thought it was unlikely.
Now, Thomas works as a janitor cleaning a supermarket and office buildings a few nights per week. He got another part-time job, but it meant his Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits were cut “down to nothing.”
At 57, starting over in a small town, it’s hard to see how he might move up, professionally speaking.
The Woodland Pulp Mill, in Baileyville, is Washington County’s largest employer and is considered the county’s economic anchor. It’s the kind of place where employees can work for decades.
But those large-scale economic development projects are few and far between these days, Rudelitch said, given that political opposition can threaten a project and scare off investors. It’s hard to find the community consensus needed to swallow the downsides of something like that — the blows it could strike to quality of life and the environment, for example.
Rudelitch can envision a world in which rural Maine resembles something of its past: a place with economic opportunity where people want to move to start a family.
“But it’s hard to really imagine how that would actually happen right now,” he said.
NATURE: ‘THE GREATEST THING EVER’
Justin Crockett’s ancestors landed in Kittery in the mid-1600s and they never left.
“Every grandfather I ever had from that time until present day lived and died in the state of Maine,” he said.
Now 44 with two teenage kids of his own, Crockett isn’t sure he wants his grandchildren to grow up in Maine.
He was raised in a small town in Franklin County and now lives in central Maine. Crockett left 25 years ago to join the Air Force and returned in 2022, stunned by what he described as the state’s 180-degree turn for the worse.
Four childhood friends have died from drug overdoses, including one last winter. The sawmills buzzing in his hometown when he left are all gone and the quality of public education has dropped precipitously.
“How much worse is this drug problem going to get? How much worse is the housing crisis going to get?” Crockett said.
He, along with Smith, the Lewiston resident, were among the small minority of poll respondents who felt that crime and public safety were major problems in Maine, and it contributed to their perception that things were getting much worse.
It’s when he’s alone in the woods, hunting and watching the seasons change, that Crockett is reminded of why he loves Maine.
He and Hoffman, the New York transplant, are unlikely to agree on much, at least politically. But on this, they, and many others, stand on common ground.
Some 69% of respondents said the quality of the environment was better than in other places they’ve lived or know. Nature and the environment was the second-most popular pick (22%) when respondents were asked about the best thing in their community.
“If you want to go out and grasp the goodness of Maine, you can still do it,” said Green, the retired local TV personality.
Maine has vast forest lands and craggy coastlines, and ample opportunity to play and hunt and even make a living.
“It’s just the greatest thing ever, being out in nature,” Hoffman said.
Mainers say it’s a large part of what makes life here the way it should be.
And because Maine is a place where your neighbors will bring you soup.
Reuben M. Schafir is a Report for America corps member who writes about Indigenous and rural communities for the Portland Press Herald.

title: ‘A hero’: 13-year-old killed shielding younger sister from gunfire at apartment complex
text:
SHREVEPORT, La. (KSLA/Gray News) - A 13-year-old Louisiana boy who was killed while shielding his younger sister from gunfire at an apartment complex’s basketball court is being hailed as a hero.
Sha’michal Russell, 13, was among three children shot last Monday on a basketball court at a Shreveport apartment complex after a shooter fired multiple rounds from a distance, according to Shreveport Police. He later died from his injuries at the hospital.
Jessica Haley, who serves as the Shreveport Police Department’s chaplain, is Sha’michal’s aunt. She says the 13-year-old was trying to protect his younger sister when the gunfire erupted.
“He was shielding his 3-year-old sister at the park to keep her from being hit by the bullets,” Haley said. “He is a hero, a loving heart. He is a hero. He shielded his own sister.”
Thanks to her brother, Sha’michal’s sister was not among the children injured in the shooting.
Family remembers Sha’michal as a playful boy who loved his sister
For his actions, Sha’michal will posthumously receive the Youth Heroism Award from the Youth Peace & Justice Foundation, also known as the Uvalde Foundation. The award recognizes young people nationwide who demonstrate exceptional courage, compassion and a willingness to help others in moments of crisis.
The 13-year-old will be the first teenager to receive the award posthumously.
Family members remember Sha’michal as a loving, playful boy who was quick to help neighbors, loved sports, made others laugh and cared deeply for his sister.
“Sha’michal’s family has told us about a boy who loved his little sister and tried to protect her,” said Daniel Chapin, founder and president of the foundation. “He was only 13 years old. He should still be here growing up with his family. We want to recognize the courage his family described and make sure people remember Sha’michal for the life he lived and the person he was.”
The foundation has launched an emergency fundraiser to assist Sha’michal’s family with funeral and memorial expenses. Additional funds may provide emergency support to the two surviving victims, ages 2 and 17, and their families once their needs are verified.
“We want the money raised for these families to actually get to these families,” Chapin said. “We’re going to take the time to verify who we need to work with and how the funds should be delivered, and then, we’ll get the assistance where it is needed.”
Police charge 19-year-old cousins in shooting
Shreveport Police say two cousins – Javion and Alonzo Abbott, both 19 – have been arrested and charged in connection with the shooting that killed Sha’michal.
Javion Abbott is charged with second-degree murder and two counts of attempted second-degree murder.
Alonzo Abbott is charged with one count of principal to second-degree murder and two counts of principal to attempted second-degree murder.
Police say the investigation is ongoing, and additional arrests are possible.
