title: An opinion section study in contrasts
text:
It was a delight to read William Smith’s elegant op-ed on the promise of trickle-up economics (Sept. 13), indistinguishable from democratic socialism, that made clear the differences between what we in this country have: extreme disparities in wealth and opportunity, and what we would enjoy with trickle-up economics. It is no surprise most of our politicians disparage democratic socialism; it is not in their interests.
On the other hand, the op-ed next door in the section, by Charles Todorich (“Western civilization is dying and Europeans don’t seem to care”), contained a number of mistaken assumptions and conclusions.
For example, Todorich says that a majority of Europeans are pessimistic about the future and believe life will be harder for their children. In the EU, 70% are pessimists; in the U.S., that figure is roughly 70-75%, not much different. It is interesting that in Denmark, with the highest taxes in the EU, only about a third of parents are pessimistic about their children’s economic future. After all, they do get something for the taxes they pay: universal healthcare, free university education, a highly developed social security and welfare system and a high degree of income equality.
Todorich, who seems to believe that the Crusades were a moral high point for European Christianity, expressed concerned about Muslim emigration to Europe, but seems ignorant of its cause: wars initiated by the Bush/Cheney administration in the Middle East destabilized the region and made life there unbearable; emigration to safety is the result. He also believes that concerns about global warming are simply mass hysteria. I could only shake my head in disbelief.
Jonathan Mitschele
New Gloucester

title: The choice is simple in Maine’s Senate race
text:
This paper has printed several letters that explain why the authors are voting for Susan Collins or Troy Jackson. It is interesting to hear the different perspectives, but when it really comes down to it, this is not about who has more energy or who has done more for the state. It comes down to the fact that our Republican-controlled Congress has done nothing to rein Donald Trump in.
They are allowing him to degrade free speech, massively cash in on the presidency, sell pardons, illegally deport and detain (and kill) innocent people and lie about election fraud. Most strikingly they are allowing him to waste taxpayer dollars on a needless war, ballrooms and arches and on and on.
In my view, Collins (who also no longer appears to have the power of the purse strings in Washington, D.C.) has consistently voted in a way that has allowed Trump’s agenda to move forward. The proof is there for anyone to see. Collins only votes against her party when they do not need her vote for an issue to pass. When they need her, she is right there for them.
A vote for Collins is a clear vote for Trump’s agenda. If people disapprove of what Trump is doing to this country, then they should not be voting for Collins, period. Jackson will call out Trump’s nonsense, something Collins has not been willing to do.
Margaret Duhamel
Woolwich

title: Hearts of Pine overcome 3-goal deficit to earn draw
text:
Diego Gonzalez’s penalty kick right before the final whistle kept the Portland Hearts of Pine’s slim playoff hopes alive.
The Hearts of Pine nearly scored on a stoppage-time corner kick, but after the ball was deflected, Diogo Barbosa was fouled in the box in the 97th minute. That gave Gonzalez a penalty kick, which he buried in the back of the net to secure a 3-3 draw with Spokane Velocity FC in a USL1 soccer match Saturday in Spokane.
Hearts of Pine (7-12-10) now have 31 points, putting them eight behind Fort Wayne FC for the eighth and final postseason spot.
Heading into halftime, the Hearts looked headed for their 13th defeat of the season. Spokane scored three goals in a 10-minute spurt at the end of the opening half. Nil Vinyals netted the first goal and set up scores by Neco Brett and Andre Lewis.
Portland played much better in the second half and got on the scoreboard in the 64th minute whenFelipe Rodriguez Gentile scored off an assist from Matteo Kidd. The Hearts of Pine cut their deficit to 3-2 on a goal by Aboubacar Camara.
The Hearts of Pine, ranked 13th in the league, next host fourth-ranked Athletic Club Boise, which has already clinched a playoff berth, Saturday at 5 p.m. at Fitzpatrick Stadium in Portland.

title: Closure of Surry ice cream shop among changes in Blue Hill-area dining scene
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Changes are rippling through the Blue Hill-area food landscape as some new eateries are opening, others are moving to new venues and at least one is shutting down for good.
In Surry, Pugnuts ice cream and gelato shop will close Sunday, Oct. 11, after a decade of operation as its owners, Eric Treworgy and Karl Holmes, retire, according to the Island Advantages newspaper. The business and property on busy Ellsworth Road was listed for sale in recent years for $1.1 million as they prepared for retirement; no active listings appeared online Friday.
Stowaways, a family-style restaurant that operated in downtown Bucksport for the last year, is moving to Main Street in Blue Hill. It plans to reopen in a space formerly occupied by Sandy’s Blue Hill Cafe, which closed last winter, in the next two weeks, according to the Island Advantages newspaper.
Owner Rob DeGennaro previously owned similarly styled, generally short-lived restaurants in Stonington, Castine, Deer Isle and Northeast Harbor, along with establishments in Florida.
Since July, locally owned Blue Hill Deli has sold sandwiches from the former home of a Subway sandwich franchise, which closed earlier this year after its regional franchise owner filed for bankruptcy. The business added pizza on Thursday through Saturday nights starting in late September, according to its Facebook page.
“Good food, good sandwiches,” local owner Ashley Munroe told the Rising Tide online newspaper when the deli opened in June. “This is something for the community.”
Across the peninsula in Brooksville, the Old Post Office opened this summer serving coffee, baked goods and ice cream next to Buck’s Market in the center of Buck’s Harbor. It closed for the season last Sunday, the business posted on social media.
A new place to eat also came to the center of Brooklin this summer in Astro, a takeout focused on hot dogs, fries and ice cream in the former home of the Morning Moon breakfast restaurant. It will close for the season on Saturday, Oct. 10, according to an Instagram post.

title: A Black community in Louisiana faces a future without a champion in Congress after redistricting
text:
SCOTLANDVILLE, La. (AP) — If you cross the Mississippi River on the Huey P. Long-O.K. Allen Bridge, pass the Exxon Refinery, then head north for a few minutes, you’ll find a pocket of Louisiana that’s unlike any other place in America’s never-ending battle over what it means to have equal representation.
Here is Scotlandville, which was once its own unincorporated town but is now part of Baton Rouge. It’s a nearly all Black community of 10,000 people that has been, for the second time, shuffled around on the state’s congressional map to make it part of a majority white district. Both times it was during the term of the same representative.
The first time was 1996, when a group of voters sued to redraw the lines. The second time was earlier this year, after the U.S. Supreme Court decided that a core part of the Voting Rights Act intended to protect minorities’ political rights was unconstitutional.
The ruling led to cascading changes around the American South, but the case originated in Louisiana — specifically the 6th Congressional District that included Scotlandville. This is where Democratic Rep. Cleo Fields, 63, grew up poor and attended local schools before graduating from nearby Southern University A&M, eventually climbing the ranks to the U.S. House.
Now he plans to leave Washington and return to the Legislature instead of running for reelection in a race that he sees little chance of winning because the district boundaries have been altered dramatically. Scotlandville will no longer be represented by a native son, someone who people believed instinctively understood their challenges and offered a direct line to power and influence in the nation’s capital.
“We’re back to where we were right after Reconstruction,” said Press Robinson Sr., 89, who has spent years working on issues involving the congressional map. “When they redistrict, they are not concerned about the effect it has on those of us who are people of color.”
The methods have changed over the years, he said, but the intent has not.
“They disenfranchise people of color and they’ve done it again,” Robinson said.
Field’s career echoes legal battle for representation
Congressional districts are core to debates over racial equality in the South, where white leaders spent decades using gerrymandering to ensure Black people couldn’t gain enough power to elect their own representatives.
The Voting Rights Act signed by Democratic President Lyndon Johnson in 1965 was supposed to fix that. Among other things, it required states and jurisdictions with a history of racial discrimination to get approval from the U.S. Department of Justice before congressional maps could take effect. It also allowed people to sue to challenge laws and procedures that would deny them the chance to elect candidates of their choice.
That didn’t settle the issue, however, and there has been a series of legal battles since then. Fields’ political career has tracked those twists and turns over the years.
He first came to Congress in 1993 when Scotlandville was part of the 4th District, which had been redrawn to create a majority Black seat. A federal court said in 1996 the boundaries that zigzagged from northwest portion of the state to the Baton Rouge area were unconstitutional.
Scotlandville shifted to the 6th District, which was then predominantly white, and Fields became a state senator. But he had an opening to return to Washington when Robinson and other plaintiffs challenged how the state drew its maps following the 2020 census.
A 2023 court decision involving Alabama also affected Louisiana, requiring the state to draw new district lines to achieve fairer representation for minorities. The district became majority Black again, and Fields won the seat in 2024.
Another wave of litigation was already starting, and the issue soon reached the U.S. Supreme Court once more. The new lawsuit by a group of non-Black voters dovetailed with a separate effort by President Donald Trump to push Republican-led states to redraw their maps to help his party keep control of Congress in this year’s midterms.
The high court’s conservative majority said Fields’ district was unconstitutional. Louisiana, Alabama and Tennessee raced to redo their U.S. House districts in time for the November elections.
In Alabama, Democratic Rep. Shomari Figueres is fighting to hold onto his seat, where Black voting age population dropped from 50% to 40% under the new political lines, according to an Associated Press analysis of the citizen voting age population in his redrawn district. In Tennessee, the majority Black district anchored by Nashville was split between three others.
Fields’ district went from being 53% Black to 25% in the new one. He announced in July that he wasn’t going to run for reelection.
Blocks from the main entrance to Southern University A&M, a small crowd hung around a convenience store but people were unwilling to talk about politics, eyeing strangers suspiciously. One younger man said he didn’t know who represents the area on the city council, let alone in Congress.
Frank Levy, 56, the cashier, said people’s apathy created the political environment that allowed for gerrymandering to occur again.
“A lot of people don’t even think about politics like this,” he said. “They don’t understand.”
About five minutes away, Dakasha Caulfield Leonard, 48, sat in the chapel of Scott’s Bluff Morticians, a nearly century-old fixture in the business community. Leonard returned two years ago to take over the funeral home when her father, who purchased it in the 1990s, became ill. She is worried about what will happen when Fields is no longer in office.
“The community is small and everybody knows everybody. Cleo is a member of our community,” she said. “If he doesn’t speak up and carry our voices, there’s nobody else to do that for us.”
Scotlandville has struggled for investment
Scenic Highway is one of the main thoroughfares in Scotlandville, and it once featured family businesses and restaurants as part of a prosperous self-contained Black community.
It’s faded overtime. The centerpiece boulevard has become blighted by empty lots and vacant buildings.
But deeper into the community is the Louisiana Leadership Institute, a sprawling complex that includes a full-scale gymnasium, classrooms, a fine arts center, a football field and a stadium with artificial turf. A thousand-seat amphitheater is being built.
The campus is the legacy of Fields, who founded the institute as the Congressional Classroom in 1993, during his first stint in Washington, and secured a mix of public and private funding for it. Over the decades since, it has hosted government, civics and leadership classes, and it’s created opportunities to travel and experience art and music and see government work in Washington.
“I wanted to engage young people,” Fields said. “Everything you see with the institute is result of me being a member of Congress.” The goal, he said, was to bring the workings of the federal government and other experiences to kids who had grown up like him.
Baton Rouge Councilman Anthony Kenney Jr 29, is one of the human legacies, taking advantage of the course offerings, training and opportunities at the center as a young student.
“Congressman Fields is someone I’ve known my entire life,” Kenney said. “I actually grew up in the Louisiana Leadership Institute. I was talking about civics, how to get involved in government, how to do policy, how to move legislation as a young child.”
Kenney is now responsible for improving the roads, plumbing, drainage and sidewalks around Scotlandville, describing it as essential for attracting new businesses.
He said it was “devastating” to see what happened to Fields.
“It’s important for us to have representation that not only is from here, raised here, but actually lived through that same experiences,” Kenney said.
____
Associated Press data reporter Hannah Recht in Washington contributed to this report.

title: What makes a ‘good’ grouse season in Maine?
text:
This was originally published Oct. 3, 2025.
As I got out of the truck and grabbed my shotgun, the cold, crisp air filled my nostrils, and I welcomed the scent of balsam fir like an old friend. I loaded my gun, snapped the action shut and headed up the old logging trail.
There are still too many leaves on the trees to see into the woods well, but I trudged uphill with the shotgun in my hand. The pungent smell of decaying leaves and damp earth replaced the fir aroma as I went further up the trail.
I heard a soft “putt putt” and stopped. I scanned the forest for the source, knowing it was a grouse. Remaining motionless, I played the familiar waiting game that usually elicits movement. It worked: the grouse craned its neck, betraying its position and gave me an easy shot.
A flood of emotions came over me. I harkened back to first hunts with my dad, adventures between classes with college buddies and hunts with my longtime hunting partner who passed away a few years ago.
I slipped the warm bird into my game pouch and continued on. It’s bird season again — my happy time of year.
October is prime time for hunting what’s probably the most popular game species in Maine, aside from the white-tailed deer. Colloquially known as “partridge” to many, the ruffed grouse season is open through December 31, but most of us hunt them in October.
While I saw a good number of birds on my first two days of hunting above Rangeley, the jury is still out on whether this will be a good grouse year.
A good grouse year, in my book, is one with plenty of sightings — singles and groups of two or more. Nothing gets your blood pumping faster than rounding a corner and bumping into a covey of four or more birds.
Outside the woods, the conversation starts in rural “mom-and-pop” country stores when you walk in wearing orange gear and boots: “How do the birds look this year?”
My answer is complex. We had a wet spring, which is never ideal for nesting birds, followed by a very dry summer. Grouse can have a second hatch and conditions were perfect for one. However, second-hatch birds typically result in fewer overall numbers. You can often identify them by their smaller size and uneven tail feathers.
Cover also affects success. With heavy leaf cover, it’s hard to spot and hit birds. Without a first frost, grass and roadside ferns hide birds from view. Hunters likely pass over more than they see.
Using dogs improves success, especially early in the season. To help understand bird behavior, I examine their crop — the sack below the throat where they store food before digestion. One crop was filled with mountain ash berries, but the rest consisted of alder leaves and ferns.
After two days of hunting, we saw 15 birds and bagged five. Skittish birds and missed shots explain the difference.
All in all, I had an enjoyable first two days in the grouse woods and look forward to many more, even with a moose hunt in between.
My prediction: It will be a decent bird year, likely featuring a second hatch and some good holdover numbers from last year.
But even if it’s deemed a “bad” bird year, you’d still find me walking that old logging road, shotgun in hand, smiling all the way. A “good” grouse season isn’t just about bird numbers — it’s about being out there in the colorful, brisk October woods.

title: Why even resilient forests are struggling to regrow after wildfires
text:
Why even resilient forests are struggling to regrow after wildfires
As Monica Turner trekked across the western hills of Yellowstone National Park, the cold rain was inescapable. Even the constant movement of putting one foot in front of the other as she fought through a slew of dense branches could not warm her body. It was easy to forget it was July.
Four years later in 2017, Turner made the same journey. But instead of fighting the once compact forest, she was met with a desolate clearing as the sun pounded above her. After the Maple Fire the year before, all that was left of the towering trees was a smattering of survivors looking over a sea of skinny, pencil-like sticks sprouting from the charred dirt.
In Turner's time as a researcher, she has seen massive destruction and its subsequent regrowth as she studied the impacts of Yellowstone's 1988 fires, which left a crown jewel of the national park system scorched. This made the level of destruction Turner witnessed in 2017 even more shocking — especially as the area had burned before without this level of loss.
Researchers across the U.S. are seeing a similar trend — forests that are historically adapted to fire are now often being obliterated by the fast-moving, high-temperature wildfires that are becoming increasingly common with climate change. These researchers are grappling with what it will mean for our world if the trees that are the centerpiece of these landscapes we love don't recover like they once did.
The fire itself is not inherently the problem. Every scientist CNN spoke with emphasized the need for fire on the landscapes they researched. But the lack of prescribed burning, a practice long used by indigenous people to clear out dead plants and to keep landscapes healthy, has left these trees vulnerable. It means their futures — when they encounter hotter, more vicious fires — are uncertain.
As these ecologies start to shift, it's unclear if or when these different areas around the U.S. will hit a tipping point where the trees won't come back. Instead, researchers say it's more likely there will be a gradual conversion over time, with once towering forests becoming robust scrublands or large fields of grassland.
Here's how some places around the country are changing, and how one state is succeeding in preserving its native wildlife.
Yellowstone National Park, Wyoming
As Turner stood on the dirt field, the air was hot — much hotter than during her previous 2013 visit. Cool summers and rain had been the norm for Yellowstone during her years of research. The heat was so intense this time that a field assistant was hospitalized for dehydration during the trip, said Turner, who works at the University of Wisconsin-Madison as the Eugene P. Odum Professor of Ecology and a Vilas Research Professor.
The ash coating the former forest floor reminded her of the ash she walked through during the 1988 fires — ash that covered her face and caked her socks. For a long time, Turner thought the wildfires from that summer 38 years ago represented how forests could and would recover. Despite miles of charred trees, the research in her field showed the forest would come back, and with a high density of trees, she said.
But Turner said she didn't appreciate "how much things could change in a relatively short time."
"We could see what we call ghost logs, which is where there had been large logs on the ground, and they were completely combusted," she said. "And then you can see their shadows where the white ash is left behind from the hot temperatures."
Only about 5% of the tree seedlings have grown back so far from the 2016 fire, compared to what burned. In place of the trees, grasses blow in the exposed meadow, now dotted with wildflowers that commonly sprout after a wildfire. Turner said she is seeing "a slow but detectable shift" to plants that are "more tolerant of warmer, drier conditions" and can grow back more easily if more wildfires come.
Slowly but surely, these changes could impact visitors to the park, Turner said. People like trees, for both how they look and the practical element of shade during hikes, she said, and the changes the forest is undergoing could impact how and when people visit the park.
The repercussions are seen in more unexpected ways as well — at one point, the park had a temporary ban on fishing, including catch and release, because the fish were already too stressed out from low water levels and the high water temperatures that were partially due to the lack of shade, she said.
"What will be the consequences for lots of other values that people care about in that region?" Turner said. "That could be wildlife habitat. It could be water availability. It could be shade if you're hiking."
But ultimately, it's not yet clear what the future Yellowstone will look like.
Plumas National Forest, California
About 100 miles northeast of California's state capital, Derek Young stood in the middle of a clearing in Plumas National Forest. The carcasses of burnt trees that surrounded him felt like a graveyard, the remains left in the wake of the 2021 Dixie Fire.
An occasional bird would chirp in the distance, but the forest emanated an eerie stillness, said Young, a research ecologist at the University of California, Davis. Fifteen years ago, Young started studying these landscapes as a PhD student. Many of them are now unrecognizable compared to the thriving forests they once were.
"It's really actually crazy to how much change has happened," he said.
Many of the areas Young studies are changing from dazzling emerald trees to fields of shrubs — even years after the wildfires.
The shrubs, ranging from deer brush to white thorn shrub, are incredibly good at resprouting, Young said. While fire might lop off the shrub tops, their roots remain, helping the plants return quickly, he said. It's stiff competition for trees to endure, which need specific conditions to grow back compared to the hardy, drought-tolerant shrubs, he said.
In just a few years, the shrubs can grow to be as tall as a person, covering the entirety of an area, Young said. "It can really feel like you're swimming in a sea of shrubs. You can't see more than a few feet ahead of you."
There are a couple of factors required for trees to successfully reemerge. Some species of trees can grow in the shade, but those species are also more likely to be destroyed during a high temperature fire, he said. Others need the heat of a fire to release their seeds, while many others don't, Young said. Those seeds then need to land in an area where they can grow and survive, which can be impacted by wind and wildlife, he added. A lot needs to happen in a short window of time in order for them to regrow.
As he sees these landscapes shift, it's hard to weigh if this is inherently a bad change — although he noted the important services forests currently provide humans, namely capturing and holding carbon dioxide through carbon sequestration.
"As forests burn up, they release carbon, contribute to climate change, which makes it more likely for more fires to burn and convert more forests," he said. "You could say, if you care about humanity's well-being, that that's actually a reason to favor maintenance and restoration of forests in place of post-fire shrub fields."
"I do sometimes try to think from the perspective of like, what if there were no humans, and there is no society to decide what our values are," he said. "In that scenario, I think the sort of definitive answer is the most valuable ecosystem is the one that is adapted to the site in the absence of all the human intervention."
But he notes this change to shrubs is not happening in that theoretical vacuum without humans.
"It's not that the system naturally wanted to be shrubs. We created that condition by suppressing fires for 100 years," he said.
Sugarite Canyon State Park, New Mexico
On the border where the Great Plains meet the Rocky Mountains, the flat-top mesas of Sugarite Canyon State Park frame the indigo blue lake nestled at the bottom of the canyon.
But the Track Fire had interrupted this picturesque scene, charring the thick tree trunks that peppered the canyon wall in New Mexico. "You look up on the hill slopes, and it's just these charred stems of old Douglas fir trees," said Chris Guiterman, a research scientist at the Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences at the University of Colorado Boulder.
Guiterman went to the park to research how forests recover from wildfires, inspired by the 2011 Las Conchas Fire, which burned over 156,000 acres in what was at the time the largest wildfire in New Mexico's history, according to the National Park Service. As the areas impacted by the fire started to recover, new life sprouted where the trees had previously been — the thorny New Mexico locust, bright green thickets of Gambel oak, clusters of dandelions and other types of herbs and shrubs, Guiterman said.
Like California, many areas of the Southwest are also seeing forests slowly transform into shrubland — specifically, many pine-dominated forests changing to drought-resistant oak shrubs, Guiterman said.
Those shrubs, in some circumstances, can act like kindling during wildfires, adding more fuel to an area that is already in extreme drought. This contributes to the high intensity of fire, in turn killing more trees that had previously survived, he said.
Many of the areas Guiterman studies have a long history with fire. In 2011, the Wallow Fire burned over half a million acres of forest in New Mexico and Arizona, the biggest wildfire in modern Arizona history. But Guiterman's research shows large-scale fires happened in this area about every 20 years going back millennia. What has changed recently is the growing intensity of these fires.
"The fires in the past that we recorded, the trees survived those fires to record the scar and kept going," he said. "But now those forests, like the trees that we sampled, were dead."
These intense wildfires are fundamentally changing the landscape, but in a way that he says isn't inherently good or bad, but just different.
"In Sugarite, you feel that sense of loss," Guiterman said when talking about losing 400-year-old trees. "At the same time, there's beauty to it because you have all these vibrant colors and everything (from other plants). But instead of wanting to wander aimlessly through this (forest) and have a picnic, it's this thicket of shrubs, and you can't leave the trail."
Austin Cary Forest, Florida
While for many, the charred remains of trees and dirt feels like the end of life, to Rae Crandall, it is just a beginning.
After a fire, a pine savanna ecosystem can look "almost impossibly black," she said. But the blackened landscape is anything but lifeless at the University of Florida's Austin Cary Forest, which is used for Crandall's research.
The gray spiny fence lizards blend into the singed ground, the movements of the dark scales of the pygmy rattlesnakes can look like an optical illusion.
Within two to three months of a prescribed fire, the scene is transformed. The previously burned landscape transforms "into a sea of grasses, wildflowers, butterflies, and other species that depend on fire to persist," said Crandall, an associate professor of fire ecology at the University of Florida and the principal investigator at the Southern Fire Exchange. When you hear her describe it, it feels like she is describing a small miracle — even though it happens all the time around here.
Like many places around the country, ecosystems in Florida have adapted to fire over time, and it's needed to help these places thrive, according to Crandall. While there might be different burning needs for different areas, like Everglades National Park versus Big Cypress National Preserve, both do better with occasional fire, she said.
"Fire has been shaping those landscapes for millennia," Crandall said, adding that they are "so, so resilient."
Florida has about 2 to 2.5 million acres of land undergo prescribed burns per year, according to Rick Dolan, the director of the Florida Forest Service, which issues about 85,000 burn authorizations a year. Not only does prescribed fire have an ecological benefit, but it also "helps enhance wildlife and habitats for wildlife," he said. It also means there is less plant material to burn when an unplanned fire comes through the area.
The state has unique conditions that allow for an easier prescribed burn culture, such as distinct wet and dry seasons, flat topography and a long history of private landowners burning their land to maintain it, Crandall said. And while they have these things on their side, state officials being proactive about prescribed burning has put Florida in a better position than other areas of the country.
"We don't see a tipping point," Crandall said. "Very rarely do we have any sort of catastrophic fire that's going to fundamentally change the plant and animal communities that are there."
One of the biggest hurdles the state faces is communicating to the public the importance of these fires.
"Florida is growing, and people that are native Floridians understand prescribed fire because they've grown up with it, you know, their whole lives," Dolan said. "The challenge that we have is when folks move into the state, and we are growing, you know, from areas of the country that maybe don't do prescribed burning. And I think education is the key."
Crandall said this isn't a one-size-fits-all approach to burning: "We're evaluating the land. We are writing a prescription like the doctor would for a patient."
One of the remarkable parts of the low-intensity fire used during prescribed burns is that even when something is left blackened on the plains of the pine savannas, it isn't irreversibly damaged — the same plants return and life goes on, said Crandall.
"By fall after a prescribed burn, it can be difficult to take a step without brushing against a flowering plant or sending a butterfly or grasshopper into the air," she said. "Gopher tortoises graze on the tender new growth. And beneath all that apparent renewal is remarkable continuity."
The uncertain path forward
Many of the trees that these researchers are studying don't seem to have a strong chance of returning. In the hot and progressively drier areas of the Southwest, the conifers — such as ponderosa pines or Douglas fir — are having difficulty growing back compared to their hardy competition.
"The conifers just don't really have much of a chance to get back in there," Guiterman said. "The oaks (shrubs) are going to hold it, and they're very persistent."
While Guiterman can't say these areas that have turned into shrub won't ever go back to the forests they previously were, climate change has made it more likely that the shrubs are here to stay. But despite what seems like a monumental change, life here continues.
"I remember we were eating lunch and we watched an osprey dive into the lake, pick up a trout," he said, which was an amazing moment to witness on its own. But then, they saw a bald eagle chasing the osprey until it dropped the fish, then the eagle stole the fish. The moment illustrated how despite all the change, life keeps going, he said.
"There's probably other loss because of the fire, but I couldn't feel it in that moment," he said.
In Yellowstone, it's hard to say when the landscape will change from forests to grassland permanently. It's unlikely there will be a single tipping point, Turner said. "There's going to be multiple of them," she said. "The forest is responding to many things at the same time, and so it's, that's why it's just difficult to predict."
Turner acknowledges that while we can observe what is happening now, we have no idea what the future holds, and we might be surprised by the landscape's resilience.
"The Greater Yellowstone area is our largest intact ecosystem in the lower 48 states," Turner said. "I have been surprised at some of the things that we have seen there. Where again, we thought, we thought everything was dead and everything recovered. We thought the soils would be sterilized, and they weren't."
"I think it's going to be very interesting to see how this ecosystem adapts to the changes that are coming, and they are coming," she said. "There may be more capacity to adapt than we give it credit for."

title: Obituary: Marlene M. O’Leary
text:
EAST GRANBY, Conn. – Marlene M. O’Leary, 88, of East Granby, Conn., passed away peacefully on Friday, Sept. 25, 2026, at St. Francis Hospital. Born in Lewiston, on June 29, 1938, she was the daughter of the late Joseph Cornelius and Lucyann (Paradise) O’Leary.
Marlene was born into a large and loving family as one of 12 siblings. She was a resident of East Granby, where she made her home with her nephew, John D. Ivanisin, and his wife, Mariann.
Marlene was predeceased by 10 of her siblings. She is survived by her sister, Nancy Davis and her husband, Joseph, of South Paris; and many other nieces, nephews, extended in family members, and friends.
After high school, Marlene followed a calling, as “Sister Marceline” with the Sister’s of St. Joseph, in Lewiston for nine years. Her life’s journey then lead her to become a respected legal secretary at Pratt and Whitney for nearly 30 years.
Marlene’s family will receive relatives and friends on Saturday, October 10, 2026, from 8:30-9:30 a.m., at Leete-Stevens Enfield Chapels, 61 South Road, Enfield, Conn. A Mass of Christian Burial will follow at 10 a.m. at St. Catherine Church, 6 Windsorville Road, Broad Brook. Burial will follow in St. Catherine Cemetery, Broad Brook.
For online condolences, please visit leetestevens.com.
In lieu of flowers, memorial donations in Marlene’s memory may be made to Shriners Children’s New England, Office of Philanthropy,
516 Carew St.,
Springfield, MA 01104.

title: Obituary: Joan Dawes Litteer
text:
BALDWINSVILLE, N.Y. – Joan Dawes Litteer, 94, formally of Liverpool, N.Y., passed away Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026, at Syracuse Homes in Baldwinsville, N.Y., surrounded by her loving family.
Joan “Jo” was born in Lewiston, to Forest E. Dawes and Celia Adams Dawes. Jo was raised in Auburn, with her sister, Betty and brother, Forest. Growing up on Lake Auburn, Jo’s childhood was filled swimming, boating, ice skating and fishing. She was an accomplished fisherwoman. Jo earned her BA Degree from Colby College. While on a weekend home, Jo met the love of her life, John Litteer, a member of the U.S. Coast Guard. Jo and John’s love bloomed through letters and visits, culminating in their 1954 marriage. After 70 years of marriage, Jo was predeceased by John in 2025.
Jo’s love of travel was the driving force for family camping trips to the family’s beloved Adirondacks, Jo’s home state of Maine, and adventures throughout the Canadian Maritime Providences, Canada and beyond. Jo toured England and Europe with her eldest daughter, Ireland, the Mediterranean and Australia with her sister. After a brief teaching career, Jo was a full-time homemaker and dedicated mother of five children. Jo was a great mom who never missed an opportunity to support her children at countless sporting and musical events, even being a Den and Girl Scout leader. Jo was a talented seamstress, knitter, and baker. When Jo’s grandchildren, and eventually great-grandchildren came along, her life was complete. She could be counted on for sticky buns on Christmas and pancakes for sleepovers and camping. Best Nanna ever!
Surviving to cherish her memory are her sister, Elizabeth Davis (Jerry Janell) of Auburn, and her brother, Forest E. Dawes Jr. (Dayle) of Catonsville, Md.; and her children, Linda Litteer-Ormond (William) of Durham, N.C., John S. Litteer (Julie) of Pennellville, N.Y., Barbara Schikora (Paul) of West Terre Haute, Ind., Andrew A. Litteer (Diane) of Clay, N.Y., and Rebecca P. Mounce (Martin) of Baldwinsville, N.Y.; nine grandchildren, Jamie (Shawn), Kelly (Eric), Lindsey (Michael), Paige, Kari (Lyra), Erin (Daniel), Sarah, Andrew (Kelly), and Zachary (Rudy); along with eight (soon to be nine!) great-grandchildren, Cecily, Bennett, Vivienne, Penelope, Corinne, Jonah, Beckett, and Eleanor; and many nieces and nephews.
Calling hours will be held at a later date at the convenience of the family.
Guestbook at FalardeauFH.com
Contributions in Jo’s memory can be made to the American Cancer Society.

title: Think your milk belongs in the fridge door? Experts say think again. Here's why
text:
You’re could be storing milk wrong — an expert explains why
The easiest place to reach is also one of the worst places to keep it.
You’re could be storing milk wrong — an expert explains why
The easiest place to reach is also one of the worst places to keep it.
Most refrigerator doors have a penthouse for butter, so it’s reasonable to assume the other shelves are meant for dairy. But you might want to think twice before you put your carton of milk away.
Related video above: Does the Sniff Test Work on All Foods?
We get it—fridge space is precious. And if efficiency is your only goal, storing milk in the door makes perfect sense. It’s not the ideal spot, however, if you want to keep your milk fresh for as long as possible. To explain why, we consulted Amy Hite, Project Management Director for Bottom Freezer at GE Appliances. Here’s what you need to know.
Fridge Temperatures Aren’t Consistent
A refrigerator keeps things cold, but the temperature isn’t exactly the same in every area. As a general rule of thumb, you can expect it to get colder the further back you go.
“The coolest areas of a refrigerator are typically toward the back of the fresh-food compartment and near the locations near the air vents (which are typically in the back),” Hite explains.
If the back of the fridge is the coldest zone, the door is the opposite. “The door tends to experience the greatest temperature fluctuations because it is exposed most directly and frequently to warmer room air when the refrigerator is opened,” Hite says.
Why You Shouldn’t Store Milk In The Fridge Door
Some foods spoil more easily than others. Butter, for instance, has so little moisture that it can last in the fridge for months. But compared to other dairy products, butter is an outlier.
Milk is much more vulnerable to spoilage. Its combination of moisture and nutrients makes it an inviting environment for bacteria, which can feed on lactose and produce lactic acid, giving spoiled milk its sour taste.
Pasteurization helps reduce harmful and spoilage-causing bacteria before milk reaches your fridge. But once you open the carton, keeping it consistently cold becomes especially important. Warmer temperatures allow bacteria to multiply more quickly—which makes the door a less-than-ideal place to store it.
“Foods that benefit from a more consistent, colder environment are generally best stored on the main refrigerator shelves rather than in the door,” Hite says. Keeping dairy products and raw meat and poultry near the back of the fridge can significantly extend their lifespans.
If you shouldn’t store milk in the door, what can you put there? “More temperature-tolerant items, such as many condiments, are well suited for door storage,” Hite says. Preserved foods like pickles and anchovies, as well as bottled and canned drinks, can handle those temperature fluctuations too.
Organizing your fridge by temperature zones may require breaking some habits, but the prolonged freshness of your food is worth it.

title: Some of the best learning takes place during recess
text:
Danielle Dalton, OTD, OTR/L, is an occupational therapist, an educator at the University of Southern Maine and the newly established Maine Say YES to RECESS chapter leader.
Growing up as a Mainer, recess meant making the most of whatever the weather gave us: snowball fights, building forts, making snow angels, sliding down a wet slide from the morning dew, splashing in mud puddles, playing four square and running around with friends until the bell rang.
We made up our own games, figured things out as we went, and didn’t need much more than a little time and freedom away from adults to play. Those simple recess moments are some of the childhood memories that have stayed with me.
As an occupational therapist and university educator, I now see those memories differently. I wasn’t simply taking a break from learning. I was learning.
I was learning how to negotiate when my friends and I couldn’t agree on a game. I was learning how to solve problems when something didn’t go as planned. I was learning how to take turns, communicate, navigate conflict, manage frustration and make decisions without an adult directing every step.
I was also moving, imagining, creating and connecting. That’s learning, too.
We sometimes talk about recess as though it happens between the important parts of the school day, as if learning happens in the classroom and recess is simply a break from it.
But what if we’ve been asking the wrong question? Instead of asking how much instructional time children can afford to lose for recess, perhaps we should ask: What are children learning while they play?
Think about an ordinary recess. A child figures out how to join a game already in progress. Two children disagree about the rules. Someone becomes frustrated when they lose. A group decides what to play next. A child takes a risk, makes a mistake and decides what to do next.
There is no worksheet or multiple-choice answer. They’re learning by doing.
We rightly care about whether children can read, write and solve math problems. Those skills matter tremendously. But so do the skills that allow children to navigate the world beyond a worksheet: communication, problem-solving, flexibility, self-regulation, collaboration and independence. These skills are foundational to how children participate in school, relationships and life.
As an occupational therapist, I think about the skills children need not only to complete a task but also to participate in life. Children don’t develop these skills only because we teach them about them. They develop them by doing.
The playground gives children a place to do exactly that.
The American Academy of Pediatrics 2026 policy statement recognizes recess as an important part of children’s physical, social, emotional and cognitive development, and identifies communication, negotiation, problem-solving and self-regulation among the skills supported through recess. It also emphasizes that recess and physical education serve different, complementary purposes.
Maine’s Department of Education similarly describes recess as time to move, play, problem-solve and socialize. Its wellness policy recommends 20 or more minutes of recess each day for elementary students, but that is a model policy, not a statewide minimum. Maine law protects recess from being withheld as a disciplinary consequence for students in grade 5 and below, but Maine does not currently establish a statewide minimum amount of daily recess.
This is part of what led me to become the Maine chapter leader for Say YES to RECESS. SYTR’s national mission is to ensure every child has access to at least 60 minutes of unstructured play each day. In Maine, our petition calls for two 30-minute recess periods, creating protected time for children to move, play, connect and learn through play.
This isn’t about choosing recess over academics. It is about recognizing that play is part of learning, and that some of the most important skills children develop cannot be taught solely through instruction.
When I think back to those Maine recesses, I don’t remember them as time we took away from learning. I remember them as learning. I remember them as childhood. And I believe Maine’s children deserve both.

title: A hungry chambermaid bit into an apple a century ago and helped solve a high-wire diamond heist
text:
A hungry chambermaid bit into an apple a century ago and helped solve a high-wire diamond heist
Suzanne Schiltz was hungry. Cleaning is exhausting business, especially as a hotel chambermaid in Paris — one of the most visited cities in the world, even in 1926. So when she saw an apple in the suitcase of two young men one December while neatening up their room, she took it. After a bite, Schiltz' teeth struck something so hard they almost shattered: the Grand Condé diamond. It was one of the rarest gemstones in France. And it was also missing.
Two months earlier, a couple of amateur thieves had robbed the historic castle, Château de Chantilly, 50 kilometers north of Paris. They had little more than a pair of tall ladders between them, but the extent of their burglary — more than 75 pieces of jewelry housed inside the castle's museum, valued at $3,000,000 at the time — led the police to believe the culprits were seasoned acrobatic masterminds, or at least double-crossing museum staff.
In fact, Leon Kauffer and Emile Souter were both demobilized French aviators in their early 20s, and well out of their depth. Despite their success in swiping the jewels, they failed to sell them. Before their arrest, Kauffer and Souter had only managed to make 30,000 francs (about $1,200 at the time) off the stolen loot. Their biggest mistake was stealing the Grand Condé, a 9.01-carat pink diamond so famous no jeweler would touch it for fear of incrimination.
"Every policeman across Europe was looking for it," said Mathieu Deldicque, chief heritage curator and director of the Musée Condé, in a phone call.
This October, the naturally pink diamond will go on display at the Château de Chantilly to commemorate the 100th anniversary of the theft. It's also the first time the piece has been shown at a major exhibition open to the public for a century, Deldicque said.
The jewel has been in the Condé family's possession since 1740. While its exact country of origin is still a mystery, with possible regions spanning from India to Borneo to Brazil, archival documents show it traveled to France where its first owner was Louis Henri de Bourbon, Prince of Condé — the prime minister between 1723 and 1726.
The gemstone was originally set in a medal of the Order of the Golden Fleece — the most important order of knighthood — and was later removed to be mounted on a ring. A written proclamation from the 18th century commanded that every eldest Condé son must have their turn inheriting the diamond.
"It was part of the symbolic heritage of this family," Deldicque said.
Although the curator declined to put a price on the diamond or its insurance cost, Deldicque did emphasize that "pink diamonds are the rarest and most expensive on the market." In 1983, a similar sized gemstone was valued between $500,000 and $600,000, while in 2010, a much larger pink diamond sold for $46 million. Neither have the historical provenance of the Condé diamond, however.
Its theft is still front of Deldicque's mind. Yes, it's been 100 years. But it's also been less than 12 months since another high-profile heist: the Louvre burglary in October 2025, where several priceless crown jewels were taken from the most famous museum in Paris. Many are still unrecovered.
"Lots of historical diamonds were stolen," he said of the Louvre theft. "We share great solidarity with our colleagues." That incident almost made Deldicque change his mind on his own showcase, which had already been planned. "I hesitated for many weeks to postpone or to cancel the exhibition," he said.
But they persevered, and instead did something that likely protected the pink diamond from resale the first time around. With the support of L'École, School of Jewelry Arts, the museum was able to enlist gemologists from France, Canada and Switzerland to conduct extensive studies and scientific analysis on the stone's chemical composition, rarity, clarity and density.
They hope this bank of publicly available information detailing the jewel's unique specificities makes it easily identifiable, and therefore, unsellable. Kind of like an "identity card," Deldicque said. "You can't do anything with it, because it's too popular," he said.
While staging a public exhibition of such a rare piece is undoubtedly a risk, Deldicque insists it's important to not be put off by the prospect of robbery — which seem to be mounting. Less than two weeks ago, a $4 million diamond necklace once owned by Egyptian royalty was taken in a smash-and-grab robbery in Vienna, Austria.
Beyond the Condé diamond's historical significance, gemstones themselves "are works of art, and works of nature," he said. "Diamonds are quite particular. You can't enjoy them through pictures, videos, photographs and so on. Their color, their light, their presence are actually so strong that you have to see them in real life." This pink diamond in particular, Deldicque says, even "has a bit of orange in it."

title: A replica Oval Office near the White House just got a new Trump makeover. Gold flourishes abound
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — It’s glitzier. And there’s way more gold.
The People’s House museum exhibit has overhauled its replica Oval Office for visitors to experience President Donald Trump’s second-term design choices.
Gleaming vases, golden-hued swirling onlays, two dozen portraits in heavy gilded frames and knickknacks crowding nearly every available surface: the same rococo flourishes that Trump has installed in the world’s most famous workspace have been recreated down to each wall appliqué in a museum just up Pennsylvania Avenue from the White House.
“As political as the Oval Office is, it really is also the office of the American people,” said Luke Boorady, managing director of The People’s House: A White House Experience. “And we want visitors who come here to feel more connected to this space.”
Public tours of the White House do not include the West Wing. So the White House Historical Association set about recreating the Oval Office, opening the exhibit in September 2024. It is the same size as the real one, and visitors often marvel at how small it feels.
A team of specialized designers has been making over the exhibit, visiting Trump’s Oval Office while the Republican president was away. Experts in North Carolina worked to recreate Trump’s many wall appliqués, while one from Indianapolis handled 3D scanning and printing of other specialized objects. California frame-makers did carving by hand for the gold frames of Trump’s chosen 24 portraits, and teams from Canada and Virginia worked on replicas of vases and other tabletop pieces, Boorady said.
There are also two mirrors and a copy of the Declaration of Independence, just like in Trump’s actual office.
The president has molded the White House in his own image
A real estate developer before he became a politician, Trump has revamped the White House to his extravagant tastes as part of his push to leave his mark on the nation’s capital while he is still in office.
When asked by Time magazine last week what he would miss most about the White House after he leaves, Trump said, “This beautiful room that nobody should be allowed to rip down. The Oval Office.” He said he had asked his chief of staff to make his altered office “a federal landmark.”
In addition to filling the Oval Office with bling, Trump paved over the lawn near the Rose Garden to build a patio space reminiscent of the one at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida. He installed a row of presidential portraits along the colonnade between the White House residence and the West Wing.
He erected towering flagpoles on the North and South lawns, renovated the Palm Room and the bathroom that is part of the famous Lincoln Bedroom and ordered restoration work of the North Portico’s front columns.
But Trump seems proudest of the $400 million ballroom that he is building after ordering that the East Wing be demolished. “It relaxes me, actually,” the president said about the ballroom project during an unrelated event last week.
Trump’s sense of ownership of the White House is now such that while recently defending his attempt to ban CNN, MS Now and Politico from its grounds, the president had a momentary slip of the tongue. “I don’t have to let them into my — into the people’s house,” he said.
A replica of Trump’s first term Oval Office gets a makeover
When the White House Historical Association first opened its Oval Office duplicate, it mirrored Democratic President Joe Biden’s design. After the 2024 election, the association updated the exhibit to match Trump’s first-term style.
Last week, a crew of 25 people worked from early Monday through late Friday to get the second-term transformation ready, making the finishing touches on Saturday.
Boorady said Biden was the first president to hang double layers of portraits over the Oval Office fireplace. Trump has expanded that all around the room, stacking the walls with portraits including those of George Washington, Andrew Jackson and Benjamin Franklin.
In the real Oval Office, the colors are made more brilliant by using gilded gold leaf. In the replica, crews used a paint solution. Boorady said they did not use gold leaf to protect against chipping or other wear-and-tear from visitors moving through the area.
Trump was once spotted using superglue to try to affix gold ornaments to the Oval Office fireplace, according to Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan in their book “Regime Change.”
But no superglue was needed in the replica office. Crews used laser levels and temporary adhesive to fix items to the walls, checking their work for accuracy against renderings of the actual office before nailing many adornments to the walls.
It’s not all new flair with Trump
There are many things in Trump’s Oval Office that have stood the test of time: a beige-patterned rug from the Ronald Reagan era, gold draperies from Bill Clinton’s tenure, and couches and chairs from the George W. Bush White House.
Of course there is a copy of the Resolute Desk. Visitors to the People’s House are allowed to sit in the chairs and behind the replicated desk, which Trump and most presidents have used since it was gifted to President Rutherford B. Hayes in 1880.
The White House Historical Association declined to say how much remaking the replica Oval Office cost. The organization, created in 1961 by first lady Jacqueline Kennedy, receives no government funding, and raises money through private donations and sales of retail merchandise.
Trump briefly stopped by its gift shop during an unannounced visit to the People’s House in August 2025. Asked whether Trump would come for a personal peek at his newly replicated workspace, Boorady replied, “I don’t know” before adding that he is “always welcome.”

title: Troy Jackson says he ‘feels great’ ahead of upcoming debates with Susan Collins
text:
Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson said he “feels great” ahead of his upcoming debates with Republican Sen. Susan Collins.
At the debates, Jackson wants to talk about Collins’ voting record and issues that aren’t being discussed in political ads, he said at a canvassing event Sunday in Bangor.
“Let’s actually get in front of people and talk about, you know, the issues that are affecting Mainers instead of running attack ads about people’s families,” Jackson said.
Jackson is scheduled to debate Collins four times in the next two weeks, in what will be a test for the candidate and the campaign he quickly built after becoming the Democratic nominee in July. It’s unclear what topics will be debated.
The Allagash native said he’s been preparing for the debates in the hours after the town halls and events he’s held. Although he didn’t say exactly what talking points or campaign issues he’s been studying, he said he expected his and Collins’ voting records to be compared.
“Your record is always something I felt very strongly about. It’s your record. So I am very excited to be up on the debate stage and talk about the things that I’ve done compared to the things that she’s done,” Jackson said.
When talking about Collins’ previous votes, Jackson pointed to a Bangor Daily News article showing the Republican senator votes with her party more than 90% of the time. Jackson did not say anything specific about his own record, except that he’s “proud of what I’ve fought for.”
Collins’ alleged involvement in a pay-to-play donation scheme involving defense contractor Navatek, which was reported by ProPublica last month, has seen Jackson and Collins throw statements at each other. Collins has denied the allegations.
When asked about Collins telling News Center Maine, “Shame on Chuck Schumer, shame on Troy Jackson for spreading these baseless lies,” during an event yesterday, Jackson said he didn’t know the article was being reported and doesn’t know what he’s “supposed to do about it.”
“Shame on me? Shame on her for being, you know, so corrupt. I didn’t do that. That’s on her,” Jackson said. “I don’t know what else to say about it, but I’m sure she is very concerned about it. It does look very damning, and people are going to remember November 3.”
The first debate between Collins and Jackson is at 7 p.m. Tuesday on CBS 13.

title: Maine’s rural maternity wards require a mindset shift
text:
The continuing closure of Maine’s rural maternity wards makes me wish there was someone I could grab by the collar and shake a little and go, “This is why we shouldn’t be treating healthcare as a consumer good instead of a public investment for a functional, healthy society!”
I would have to shake an awful lot of collars.
The reason rural hospitals keep closing down maternity wards is money. America doesn’t think of healthcare as a right, or a social investment. We think of it as a consumer good like any other, so if the market won’t support its presence, businesses stop offering it.
Healthcare providers need to make money in order to keep their doors open. Even nonprofits like MaineHealth, which don’t need to worry about a rate of return for investors expecting profit, need to at least break even to continue providing those services (and those suspiciously beefy executive salaries, of course).
Pretty much everyone agreed that having maternity care and birthing hospitals in rural areas is important for the health and safety of mothers and babies, as well as for the community in general.
As one of the protesters against the closure of Miles Hospital’s maternity ward in Damariscotta pointed out, “What happens if you can’t be born in a community, you can only die there?”
But what’s the solution? MaineHealth magics up more money? Maybe robs Peter to pay Paul and cuts services elsewhere in the system? The population of Lincoln County isn’t going to suddenly and immediately explode to the point where a fee-for-service birth center model is viable.
All three candidates for governor have said that rural maternity closures are something that they’re going to work on and stop from happening, but what’s their plan?
I mean, all Republicans know how to do when there’s a problem is cut taxes, which isn’t going to help in this situation. Democrats are probably more interested in directly helping by subsiding a hospital, but for how long? How much?
Our system isn’t set up for ongoing state subsidy through direct payments like that. Plus, there are a ton of competing budget commands and local moms don’t have a small army of well-paid lobbyists to prowl the halls of the State House. And then you’d get people complaining that they shouldn’t have to pay for maternity care if they can’t get pregnant.
I don’t think the reason we don’t have a universal healthcare system in America is the concept of “Ooh, government healthcare scary.” I know there are some people who think that way, but we already have examples of both government-run direct healthcare — the VA — and government- provided health insurance programs, in Medicare and Medicaid. Those programs could certainly use some improvement, but they are very much present and functional and the citizens who benefit are generally satisfied.
No, the reason we don’t have it is because Americans are obsessed with this idea of “deserving.” We don’t want “OUR” taxes paying for “THEIR” healthcare. Who “they” are changes from person to person, of course. (Meanwhile, the sad truth is your taxes are mostly going to Medicare, Social Security and defense contractors’ stock accounts.)
Think about roads, right? A long time ago American leaders all decided that in order for us to have a healthy, thriving society and economy, we needed roads connecting us, from dirt paths to superhighways. So we made it happen, and everyone contributes, and everyone can use the roads.
You don’t have a subscription to roads through your employer. You don’t get road access on a marketplace. You can still drive on them if you’re poor. They’re funded by our taxes (including, yes, tolls). People don’t get mad that other people they don’t like, or who have made choices they disapprove of, get to use the roads. (Well, other than the usual road rage.) And yes, I know that lots roads are terribly maintained; my family used to play “Buxton Slalom” with potholes in our hometown. This isn’t my most perfect metaphor.
The problem is not just electing politicians who are willing to put in the work to build us a universal healthcare system, although of course we have to do that too. We have to change our view of what healthcare is for. Is it for profit generation, or is it a social good?
If it’s a social good that we need for a functioning society, can we come to terms with the fact that, yes, “your” taxes may be paying for services that you don’t directly benefit from because our society as a whole would really benefit from having that health system.
Until then, rural facilities are just going to keep shutting down, no matter how important they are to their communities, no matter how many lives are at stake.

‘A hero’: 13-year-old killed shielding younger sister from gunfire at apartment complex
text:
SHREVEPORT, La. (KSLA/Gray News) - A 13-year-old Louisiana boy who was killed while shielding his younger sister from gunfire at an apartment complex’s basketball court is being hailed as a hero.
Sha’michal Russell, 13, was among three children shot last Monday on a basketball court at a Shreveport apartment complex after a shooter fired multiple rounds from a distance, according to Shreveport Police. He later died from his injuries at the hospital.
Jessica Haley, who serves as the Shreveport Police Department’s chaplain, is Sha’michal’s aunt. She says the 13-year-old was trying to protect his younger sister when the gunfire erupted.
“He was shielding his 3-year-old sister at the park to keep her from being hit by the bullets,” Haley said. “He is a hero, a loving heart. He is a hero. He shielded his own sister.”
Thanks to her brother, Sha’michal’s sister was not among the children injured in the shooting.
Family remembers Sha’michal as a playful boy who loved his sister
For his actions, Sha’michal will posthumously receive the Youth Heroism Award from the Youth Peace & Justice Foundation, also known as the Uvalde Foundation. The award recognizes young people nationwide who demonstrate exceptional courage, compassion and a willingness to help others in moments of crisis.
The 13-year-old will be the first teenager to receive the award posthumously.
Family members remember Sha’michal as a loving, playful boy who was quick to help neighbors, loved sports, made others laugh and cared deeply for his sister.
“Sha’michal’s family has told us about a boy who loved his little sister and tried to protect her,” said Daniel Chapin, founder and president of the foundation. “He was only 13 years old. He should still be here growing up with his family. We want to recognize the courage his family described and make sure people remember Sha’michal for the life he lived and the person he was.”
The foundation has launched an emergency fundraiser to assist Sha’michal’s family with funeral and memorial expenses. Additional funds may provide emergency support to the two surviving victims, ages 2 and 17, and their families once their needs are verified.
“We want the money raised for these families to actually get to these families,” Chapin said. “We’re going to take the time to verify who we need to work with and how the funds should be delivered, and then, we’ll get the assistance where it is needed.”
Police charge 19-year-old cousins in shooting
Shreveport Police say two cousins – Javion and Alonzo Abbott, both 19 – have been arrested and charged in connection with the shooting that killed Sha’michal.
Javion Abbott is charged with second-degree murder and two counts of attempted second-degree murder.
Alonzo Abbott is charged with one count of principal to second-degree murder and two counts of principal to attempted second-degree murder.
Police say the investigation is ongoing, and additional arrests are possible.

title: US Marine arrested for alleged murder of a woman on Okinawa, sparks outrage from Japan
text:
US Marine arrested for alleged murder of a woman on Okinawa, sparks outrage from Japan
Japanese police arrested a U.S. Marine in the alleged robbery and murder of a woman on Okinawa, officials said Sunday, the latest criminal case on the southern island where the heavy American troop presence has remained a sensitive issue.
Related video: What matters to veterans and military families ahead of the midterms?
The Okinawa prefectural police said they arrested a 20-year-old Marine stationed at the Futenma Air Station on suspicion of killing a 39-year-old local woman at a hotel in Naha, Okinawa's capital city, and taking her wallet and backpack in the early hours of Saturday.
Kyodo News agency, citing the police, reported the woman's body was found in her hotel room and she appeared to have been strangled to death.
Police said security camera footage showed the man believed to be the suspect entering the hotel with the victim and coming out alone. An officer arrested the suspect after spotting him walking alone on a street in Naha’s entertainment district late Saturday, Kyodo said.
“The case deals a major shock and adds fear to the Okinawans who have already been forced to live next to U.S. bases,” newly elected Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja told reporters. “It is absolutely unforgivable and we are outraged.”
“I must say, discipline and troop education are not working at all,” said Koja, referring to the U.S. military’s measures taken in response to past criminal cases.
Some 50,000 U.S. troops are deployed in Japan under a bilateral security pact, about half of them on Okinawa, whose strategic role is seen as increasingly important for the Japan-U.S. military alliance amid growing tensions with China. Japan's southwestern shift in its military focus centers heavily on Okinawa and its nearby islands.
Okinawans have long complained about noise, pollution and crime related to U.S. bases, with crimes involving U.S. service members on Okinawa complicating ties between Japan’s central government and the Okinawa administration. The latest case comes as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s cabinet pushes to further fortify its Japanese military presence on Okinawa and work more closely with the U.S. military.
“The occurrence of the heinous crime is extremely regrettable,” Takaichi said in her message on X. She said her government has strongly protested to the U.S. side and demanded maximum cooperation with the Japanese authorities in the investigation, as well as tougher discipline for U.S. service members and preventive measures.
Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi summoned U.S. Ambassador to Japan George Glass to his office and conveyed “outrage," the ministry said in a statement.
Glass, on X, expressed condolences to the victim's family, adding that the United States is cooperating with the Japanese national and local governments.
The U.S. Marine Corps said in a statement the suspect is assigned to the III Marine Expeditionary Force on Okinawa and that it is fully cooperating with Japanese authorities. “The Marine Corps takes these allegations very seriously and expects every Marine to adhere to the highest standards of behavior."
Futenma base, located in a densely populated area in central Okinawa, has been a sore spot for many Okinawans for decades, who demanded its relocation. Despite protests, the central government greenlit construction to relocate the base to Henoko on Okinawa’s eastern coast, though the project has faced massive delays.
A high-profile 1995 rape of a 12-year-old girl by three U.S. service members sparked massive protests against the heavy U.S. troop presence on Okinawa. The number of arrests related to U.S. service members and their families exceeded 100 last year, according to prefectural police. Repeated occurrences of sexual crimes and some of their delayed disclosures have also sparked outrage on Okinawa in recent years.

title: Week Ahead in Washington: October 4
text:

title: Patriots stun Buffalo with late game heroics
text:
ORCHARD PARK, N.Y. — Drake Maye threw three touchdown passes, including Efton Chism’s one-handed catch with 1:50 remaining, and the New England Patriots defeated the Buffalo Bills 29-26 on Sunday.
Romeo Doubs had touchdown catches of 2 and 14 yards, and Rhamondre Stevenson scored on a 1-yard run.
Though Maye’s turnover troubles continued with an interception and a lost fumble in the first half, the third-year starter was sharp in the final minutes after New England fell behind 26-21.
Maye’s 23-yard TD pass to Chism came on third-and-5, with the receiver bringing in the ball with his right hand and maintaining control in the end zone. Maye then hit Stevenson for the 2-point conversion.
Despite having a minute left and the ball at their 40, Josh Allen turned overly aggressive. On second-and-6, he spun out of Dre’Mont Jones’ sack attempt, stepped up in the pocket and went deep only to have his underthrown pass intended for Josh Palmer intercepted by Craig Woodson.
Taking over at the Patriots 19, Maye put the finishing touches on the win by rolling to his right and lobbing a 12-yard pass to Hunter Henry in allowing the Patriots to run out the clock.
The Patriots improved to 2-2 and for once put aside questions about a sputtering and turnover-prone offense.
The Bills, meantime, dropped to 3-1 in Buffalo’s first loss at its new Highmark Stadium, and first under new coach Joe Brady.
Maye finished 22 of 37 for 269 yards in overcoming the criticism he’s faced in opening the season by combining for six interceptions and a lost fumble in his first three starts. The lost fumble, recovered by the Buffalo at its 30, was on Maye, who lost the ball as Bills tackle Ed Oliver shoved an offensive lineman into him.
The interception, however, was on Doubs, who made the catch and in the process spun around and lost control of the ball, which sailed into the hands of cornerback Dee Alford.
The Bills had their sloppy moments, too, a week after committing five turnovers in a 24-16 win over the Los Angeles Chargers.
Receiver Khalil Shakir lost a fumble, in addition to Allen’s interception — his third of the season. Allen finished 23 of 33 for 253 yards, including a 34-yard go-ahead touchdown to Keon Coleman with 4:27 remaining. The touchdown put Buffalo up 26-21, but the 2-point conversion attempt failed when Palmer never looked for Allen’s pass directed his way.
Allen also scored on a 2-yard run, while James Cook scored on an 8-yard run.
The Bills were limited to 340 total yards and 19 first downs, both season lows, and resembled nothing like the high-powered unit that opened the season combining for 855 yards and 77 points.
The outing was a breakthrough for the Patriots’ slumbering offense, which posted season highs with 405 yards and 26 first downs. New England’s defense also rallied in containing the Bills despite missing its top cornerback Christian Gonzalez and starting defensive tackle Christian Barmore because of shoulder injuries.
ALLEN MILESTONES
Allen’s 2-yard touchdown run to tie the game at 14 with one minute left in the first half was his 88th career from scrimmage (rushing/receiving) to break the team record held by Hall of Famers Thurman Thomas and Andre Reed. It was also Allen’s 86th TD rushing, moving him into a tie with Priest Holmes for 16th place on the NFL’s career list.
INJURIES
Patriots: WR Mack Hollins hurt his calf.
Bills: WR DJ Moore did not return after hurting his shoulder attempting to make a diving catch in the second quarter. DT Ed Oliver left in the third quarter with a knee injury. And a secondary already missing Christian Benford (toe), lost Dee Alford to an ankle injury in the second half.
UP NEXT
Patriots: host the Las Vegas on Sunday.
Bills: at the Los Angeles Rams on “Monday Night Football” on Oct. 12

title: Obituary: Barbara (Gulian) Sawyer
text:
FALMOUTH – Barbara Gulian Sawyer, 93, died Sept. 18, 2026.
Barbara lived her life with optimism and grace. She lived a vital life right up to the end with her last adventure at The Cliff House just three weeks before her death. If it was a sunny day, it might be a trip to Kettle Cove to sit by the Rugosa’s with Italians; she loved it most because the parking was free and to watch the lobsters being hauled in. She loved a day at Scarborough Beach to dig her heals in with a great book, a spring ski day at Sugarloaf with lunch on the deck, a day aboard the Grand Banks with her husband Tom, Judy and Louie or cruising up the coast with John Robinson and gang.
Barbara was endlessly fascinated by life. Another history book, a gorgeous art book, another great cookbook or a historical novel. As a child, she was a slow reader, but pushed herself with her books and newspapers. She became a competitive swimmer in high school; she once said it was the one thing she excelled in. She built rock walls at the Gilsland Farm House where she and Tom lived most of their life. There she tended her many gardens well into her later 80s. Not to mention chasing the ground hogs away from her gardens! A strong lady.
Barbara and Tom had many adventures in the world. She loved researching the next adventure and planning the itinerary. And she especially loved creating travelogs of each adventure with photos and ephemera from the trips. Her children’s biggest worry is what to do with all these volumes! Judy and Barb recently made a collage from one of the books that reduced the volume by a smidgen. Just 55 volumes left.
She planned a ski trip for her kids. The thrill of skiing at Zermatt and later down to the challenging Chamonix’s Valley Blanche. We said, just don’t look down, Mom! A bit scary, but there was always the smell of lunch midway down. Barbara and Tom were there for the early days of skiing at Sugarloaf Mountain before the lifts; hiking in and skiing down the one trail, Winters Way.
Barbara was born in Newark, N.J. Her family moved to Buxton, Maine and later to Beacon Street in Portland.
Barbara is survived by her children, Judy Lake (Carson) of Pawlet, Vt., and Andrew (Tisha) of Falmouth; and her adoring grandsons Duncan, Morgan, Alden and Jack. I say “adoring” because they all were so sweet with their Gram. They doted on her often, meeting her in Portsmouth, N.H. for her favorite meal, breakfast.
She is the last child of the Gulian family. She was preceded by Pat Gulian, Judy Switzer, Bob Gulian and Marylou. Her parents were Dorothy Young and Grasse Gulian of Falmouth. Grasse’s family immigrated to the U.S. from Armenia in 1906; they saw tragedies building at that time.
Barb was a favorite Cub Scout leader, a member of the Falmouth Planning Commission, a board member of The Maine Audubon, volunteer at Katherine Morrill Day Nursery, The Woman’s Exchange, The United Way and helped bring the Volvo Tennis Tournament to Portland.
The family is grateful for her wonderful caregivers led by Zoe and prior by Ester. They meant the world to Barbara and were always up for her big adventures of lunch out, the breakfasts out or a trip to the farmers market or a movie. The caregivers directive— fun and getting Mom out of the house! We are also thankful for the end of life care at Maine Medical Center as well as a very short stint with Andwell Hospice. All she wanted was to get home to her sunroom to die as she wished. A lovely life was had.
Please plant a purple flower in memory of Mom, and try to make the world a kinder place.
There will be a Celebration of Life in the spring.
Please visit http://www.jonesrichandbarnes.com to leave condolences for the Sawyer family and share a memory of Barbara.
