title: Sarah McQuaid continues her marathon year of touring with autumn USA & UK runs
Some of the best learning takes place during recess
text:
Danielle Dalton, OTD, OTR/L, is an occupational therapist, an educator at the University of Southern Maine and the newly established Maine Say YES to RECESS chapter leader.
Growing up as a Mainer, recess meant making the most of whatever the weather gave us: snowball fights, building forts, making snow angels, sliding down a wet slide from the morning dew, splashing in mud puddles, playing four square and running around with friends until the bell rang.
We made up our own games, figured things out as we went, and didn’t need much more than a little time and freedom away from adults to play. Those simple recess moments are some of the childhood memories that have stayed with me.
As an occupational therapist and university educator, I now see those memories differently. I wasn’t simply taking a break from learning. I was learning.
I was learning how to negotiate when my friends and I couldn’t agree on a game. I was learning how to solve problems when something didn’t go as planned. I was learning how to take turns, communicate, navigate conflict, manage frustration and make decisions without an adult directing every step.
I was also moving, imagining, creating and connecting. That’s learning, too.
We sometimes talk about recess as though it happens between the important parts of the school day, as if learning happens in the classroom and recess is simply a break from it.
But what if we’ve been asking the wrong question? Instead of asking how much instructional time children can afford to lose for recess, perhaps we should ask: What are children learning while they play?
Think about an ordinary recess. A child figures out how to join a game already in progress. Two children disagree about the rules. Someone becomes frustrated when they lose. A group decides what to play next. A child takes a risk, makes a mistake and decides what to do next.
There is no worksheet or multiple-choice answer. They’re learning by doing.
We rightly care about whether children can read, write and solve math problems. Those skills matter tremendously. But so do the skills that allow children to navigate the world beyond a worksheet: communication, problem-solving, flexibility, self-regulation, collaboration and independence. These skills are foundational to how children participate in school, relationships and life.
As an occupational therapist, I think about the skills children need not only to complete a task but also to participate in life. Children don’t develop these skills only because we teach them about them. They develop them by doing.
The playground gives children a place to do exactly that.
The American Academy of Pediatrics 2026 policy statement recognizes recess as an important part of children’s physical, social, emotional and cognitive development, and identifies communication, negotiation, problem-solving and self-regulation among the skills supported through recess. It also emphasizes that recess and physical education serve different, complementary purposes.
Maine’s Department of Education similarly describes recess as time to move, play, problem-solve and socialize. Its wellness policy recommends 20 or more minutes of recess each day for elementary students, but that is a model policy, not a statewide minimum. Maine law protects recess from being withheld as a disciplinary consequence for students in grade 5 and below, but Maine does not currently establish a statewide minimum amount of daily recess.
This is part of what led me to become the Maine chapter leader for Say YES to RECESS. SYTR’s national mission is to ensure every child has access to at least 60 minutes of unstructured play each day. In Maine, our petition calls for two 30-minute recess periods, creating protected time for children to move, play, connect and learn through play.
This isn’t about choosing recess over academics. It is about recognizing that play is part of learning, and that some of the most important skills children develop cannot be taught solely through instruction.
When I think back to those Maine recesses, I don’t remember them as time we took away from learning. I remember them as learning. I remember them as childhood. And I believe Maine’s children deserve both.

title: Ellsworth Fire Department battles house fire on Christian Ridge Road
text:
ELLSWORTH, Maine (WABI) - The Ellsworth Fire Department responded to a house fire on Christian Ridge Road Friday afternoon.
Firefighters arrived just after 1 p.m. to heavy smoke coming from the home and fire in the attic and second floor.
The fire burned in two separate attic spaces, making it challenging to control. Ellsworth Fire said no fire hydrants were in the area, forcing crews to use tankers.
A partial roof collapse and ceiling collapse occurred before the fire was declared under control about four hours later.
The Ellsworth fire chief said Christian Ridge Road was closed while crews worked.
No injuries were reported. The family is being assisted by the American Red Cross.
The fire marshal’s office is investigating the cause of the fire.

title: 2 dead, 35 injured in homecoming party mass shooting in Georgia
text:
VIENNA, Ga. (WALB/Gray News) - Two people are dead and 35 people have been injured in a mass shooting at a homecoming party in Georgia, according to officials.
According to the Georgia Bureau of Investigation, the shooting happened Sunday around 1:25 a.m. in Vienna, Georgia, during a homecoming block party where deputies were monitoring a crowd of more than 1,000 people.
Dooly County Coroner Brett Walls identified the deceased victims as JaQuevion Jackson, 21, and Macaleb Jackson, 23.
The victims’ bodies will be given to the Georgia Bureau of Investigation for autopsies.
Dooly County Sheriff Craig Peavy said shots were fired at at least 50 people in at least two locations about a block apart. At least 25 people were shot and taken to the hospital, and as many as 35 people may have been injured.
The Georgia Bureau of Investigation is assisting local authorities with the investigation.
An impromptu community prayer vigil was organized Sunday morning in response to the shooting. Around 100 people gathered at the courthouse in Vienna, Georgia, to pray for the victims and their families.

title: Obituary: Robert H. B. Cox
text:
CHESTERVILLE – Robert H. B. Cox, 95, of Chesterville, passed at home with family by his side on Sept. 28, 2026.
Robert was born on March 1, 1931, in Portland, to Herbert H. Cox and Gladys M. (Bishop) Cox. He attended several schools in Maine and Florida. He joined the U.S. Air Force in 1948 and retired in 1969. Upon retirement, he and his family moved back to Maine and settled down in Chesterville.
Robert was employed by Franklin Memorial Hospital as their credit manager from 1970 to 1977. He also worked as constable and fence viewer for the town of Chesterville from 1971 to 1994. In 1977, he was appointed as a deputy by Sheriff Kenneth French to the Franklin County Sheriffs Office; he served for 40 years on the force.
On June 6, 1954, Robert married Mabel B. Lane in Augusta, Maine, and together they shared 72 wonderful years. They raised two children, Laurence Cox of Florida and Darlene Pacheco of Maine.
Robert was a 50-plus years member of the Farmington Elks Lodge # 2430 and a brother for 50-plus years of the Wilton Masonic Lodge # 156 A.F & A.M. He was also a member of the Farmington American Legion Post # 28.
He enjoyed snowmobiling, traveling and spending time with his family.
Robert is survived by his wife, Mabel Cox; children, Larry Cox and wife Michelle, and Darlene Pacheco and life partner Ted; his five grandchildren; nine great-grandchildren; and one great-great-grandchild.
He was preceded in death by his parents, Herbert and Gladys Cox; and one brother, Herbert Cox Jr.
A funeral service with an Elks Lodge presentation honoring Robert will be held Saturday, Oct. 3, at 4 p.m. with refreshments to follow, located at Dan & Scott’s Cremation & Funeral Service, 488 Farmington Falls Rd., Farmington.
A private burial will take place at a later date at the Maine Veteran’s Memorial Cemetery located in Augusta.
The family wishes to thank the wonderful caregivers from Visiting Angels and Gentevia Hospice for their compassion and excellent care.
Arrangements are under the care of Dan & Scott’s Cremation & Funeral Services, 488 Farmington Falls Rd., Farmington, ME 04938, where memories, photos and condolences may be shared at http://www.dsfuneral.com.
In lieu of flowers, memorial donations may be made to the local food pantry and the local heating assistance program.

title: Obituary: Cynthia Ann Chapman
text:
PORTLAND – Cynthia Ann Chapman “Cindy” passed away peacefully at Seaside Health Care in Portland, Maine, on Thursday, Aug. 20, 2026. She was born March 2, 1952 in Bangor; she was the daughter of Franklin and Madelyn (Binnette) Chapman.
Cindy grew up in Old Town. As a teenager she moved to Pittsfield with her family and graduated from Nokomis High School. Shortly after graduation she moved to Portland, where she lived independently for over 50 years. Cindy loved living in Portland. She knew all the bus routes and all the bus drivers and they knew her. Cindy always had jokes and friendly banter ready for everyone she met; she enjoyed making people laugh and she really loved to laugh. Cindy’s favorite place in Portland was the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception where she was a loyal member of the parish; she had a deep devotion to the Blessed Virgin Mary.
Cindy loved her family completely and as her family grew she enthusiastically welcomed each new brother-in-law, sister-in-law, niece, and nephew. She always remembered every birthday, anniversary, and holiday with cards and little gifts. Cards were her trademark; she chose them with great care to make sure they were absolutely perfect for each person and every occasion. Cindy really loved holidays, especially spending Christmas with different family members and the 4th of July at Cold Stream.
Cindy is survived by her five siblings and their families, Mary (Chapman) and Donald Fletcher, their daughter Chaney (Fletcher) and Mark Wahl (children Mark Jr, Bradley, and Cameron) and son Christopher and Alexis (Ramos) Fletcher (children Carter, Alivia, and Cooper); Ralph and Althea (Lyons) Chapman, their son Thomas and Marta (Leon) Chapman and daughter Madelyn (Chapman) and Travis Choy; Alice Chapman and Rajan Gupta, their son Neel and Aliena (Krausert) Gupta (daughter Gabriella Mae) and son Nevin Gupta; Christine (Chapman) and Christopher Urban, their daughter Catherine (Urban) and Andrew DeGrado (daughter Marilyn) and son John and Annie (Parks) Urban (daughters Jane and Sybil); Kenneth and Beth (Blair) Chapman, their sons Alexander and William.
Cindy was very much loved and she will be greatly missed.

title: US Marine arrested for alleged murder of a woman on Okinawa
text:
TOKYO (AP) — Japanese police arrested a U.S. Marine accused of robbing and killing a woman on Okinawa, officials said Sunday, in the latest criminal case involving U.S. military personnel on the southern island where the heavy American troop presence is a sensitive issue.
The Okinawa prefectural police said they arrested a 20-year-old Marine stationed at the Futenma Air Station on suspicion of killing a 39-year-old local woman at a hotel in Naha, Okinawa’s capital city, and taking her wallet and backpack early Saturday.
Kyodo News agency, citing the police, reported the woman’s body was found in her hotel room and she appeared to have been strangled.
Police said security camera footage showed a man believed to be the suspect entering the hotel with the woman and leaving alone. An officer arrested the suspect after spotting him walking alone on a street in Okinawa City’s entertainment district late Saturday, Kyodo said.
“The case deals a major shock and adds fear to the Okinawans who have already been forced to live next to U.S. bases,” newly elected Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja told reporters. “It is absolutely unforgivable and we are outraged.”
“I must say, discipline and troop education are not working at all,” said Koja, referring to the U.S. military’s measures taken in response to past criminal cases.
Some 50,000 U.S. troops are deployed in Japan under a bilateral security pact, about half of them on Okinawa, whose strategic role is seen as increasingly important for the Japan-U.S. military alliance amid growing tensions with China. Japan’s southwestern shift in its military focus centers heavily on Okinawa and its nearby islands.
Okinawans have long complained about noise, pollution and crime related to U.S. bases, with crimes involving U.S. service members on Okinawa complicating ties between Japan’s central government and the Okinawa administration. The latest case comes as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s cabinet pushes to further fortify its Japanese military presence on Okinawa and work more closely with the U.S. military.
“The occurrence of the heinous crime is extremely regrettable,” Takaichi said in her message on X. She said her government has strongly protested to the U.S. side and demanded maximum cooperation with the Japanese authorities in the investigation, as well as tougher discipline for U.S. service members and preventive measures.
Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi summoned U.S. Ambassador to Japan George Glass to his office and conveyed “outrage,” the ministry said in a statement.
Glass, on X, expressed condolences to the victim’s family, adding that the United States is cooperating with the Japanese national and local governments.
The U.S. Marine Corps said in a statement the suspect is assigned to the III Marine Expeditionary Force on Okinawa and that it is fully cooperating with Japanese authorities. “The Marine Corps takes these allegations very seriously and expects every Marine to adhere to the highest standards of behavior.”
Futenma base, located in a densely populated area in central Okinawa, has been a sore spot for many Okinawans for decades, who demanded its relocation. Despite protests, the central government greenlit construction to relocate the base to Henoko on Okinawa’s eastern coast, though the project has faced massive delays.
The rape of a 12-year-old girl by three U.S. service members in 1995 sparked massive protests against the heavy U.S. troop presence on Okinawa. The number of arrests related to U.S. service members and their families exceeded 100 last year, according to prefectural police. Repeated occurrence of sexual crimes and some of their delayed disclosures have also sparked outrage on Okinawa in recent years.
___
This story corrects the location where the suspect was spotted after the alleged crime to Okinawa City, not Naha.

title: US Air Force removes all bombers from British air base targeted by a suspected terror attack
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. Air Force has brought home its bombers stationed at a U.S.-run military air base in England used to strike Iran following an investigation into a planned terror attack at the RAF Fairford base.
The bombers were redeployed back to their home bases in the United States, according to a Pentagon official who was not authorized to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke Sunday on condition of anonymity.
Aviation watchers such as the Military Air Tracking Alliance have observed dozens of B-52 and B-1 bombers operating out of RAF Fairford since the opening days of the Iran war. Observers noticed a host of B-1 bombers fly out of the base on Sunday.
The move comes as President Donald Trump weighs options for his war on Iran — including new strikes — despite his initial promises to Americans that the campaign would last a matter of weeks.
“We have decisions that I’ll make about Iran. Iran’s been decimated. So the only question is — it’ll either be the easy way, or the hard way,” Trump told reporters on Saturday as he left the White House for a rally in Ohio.
A dual British-Iranian national was arrested in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terror attack, following a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September. In total, six people have been taken into custody and then released on bail during the investigation.
British authorities have linked the incident to Tehran. Iran has denied involvement. It has previously said it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.
U.K. officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arson and other attacks in Britain and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the U.K. if conflicts in the Middle East continue.
RAF Fairford, located 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.
The U.S. military still maintains a sizable presence in the Middle East. On Thursday, a U.S. official said the recently deployed USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier, as well as the USS Malkin Island amphibious readiness group — a group of ships that together carry over 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines — are heading for the region. The official said the move could result in three carriers in the region as early as the end of October.

AP writer Melissa Goldin contributed from New York.

title: 7-year-old girl stabbed to death while walking along sidewalk in broad daylight
text:
CHICAGO (WLS) - Police in Chicago say a 7-year-old girl was walking along a neighborhood sidewalk when she was stabbed to death in broad daylight. Witnesses to the attack chased down the suspect and held her until officers arrived.
Chicago Police say a 7-year-old girl was walking along a sidewalk in the city’s Chatham neighborhood when a woman approached her just before noon Saturday. Investigators say the woman stabbed the girl multiple times in the back with a sharp object.
The victim was taken to the hospital, where she was pronounced dead. The Cook County Medical Examiner’s Office has identified her as Edimari Hernandez Chacon.
Bystanders who witnessed the attack chased down the suspect and held her until officers arrived. She is now in police custody, and charges are pending.
Authorities have not said whether the stabbing was a random attack or if the suspect knew the 7-year-old. They are still trying to determine a motive.
Residents expressed outrage and grief following the attack.
“I just don’t know what this world is coming to ... for a 7-year-old like that to be getting stabbed,” resident Denesta Freeman said. “I never thought it would come to this point. I never did. These kids nowadays are not getting to live their life.”
Alderwoman Michelle Harris of the 8th Ward released a statement following the attack:
“I am deeply saddened by the senseless stabbing of a 7 year old child in our neighborhood. My heart goes out to her family, friends, and everyone who is affected by this horrific incident. No child should ever have to experience violence or fear while simply walking down the sidewalk.
“I also want to recognize and thank the bystanders who quickly intervened—helping to detain the suspect and get assistance on the way. Their quick actions may have prevented further harm.
“I urge anyone with information to contact the Chicago Police Department. Our community must come together to support the victim and hold the perpetrator accountable.”

title: What to know about the investigation into Cornell University gang rape allegations
text:
(AP) - An intense, public outcry over a woman’s account of being gang-raped at a Cornell University fraternity house prompted New York’s governor this week to angrily yank control of the investigation away from the local prosecutor who didn’t initially see what happened as a crime.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has said Cornell police omitted key information that could have affected his decision whether or not to pursue criminal charges.
Now, the task of unraveling the case will fall to the state’s attorney general, Letitia James, who was appointed as a special prosecutor.
James, a Democrat best known for tangling with President Donald Trump, suggested at a news conference Friday that her investigation wouldn’t be rushed. She described it as a months-long process, with no predetermined outcome.
Here’s what we know and don’t know about the woman’s allegations and the investigations that followed:
A lawsuit shone a fresh light on the woman’s allegations
The woman sued Cornell and seven former students last month, alleging she was given ketamine and became completely incapacitated while members of the Chi Phi fraternity sexually assaulted her at their campus residence in October 2024.
She reported the alleged assault to campus police about three weeks later, giving investigators a detailed account over two days. She also spoke with Cornell’s disciplinary investigators.
But Van Houten quickly declined to pursue charges or further investigation after reviewing a police summary of her interview.
After the victim filed her civil suit, Van Houten said it contained allegations he had never seen. He contended Cornell’s police had withheld key information, including a transcript of the woman’s interview where she explicitly said she was “100% confident” she was raped.
Van Houten said the materials suggested she had consented to some sex with multiple men, hadn’t been forced into other acts, and was intoxicated, but not to the point of helplessness.
Under New York law, being too drunk or high to consent to sex isn’t necessarily enough to support a rape charge. The law distinguishes that from being physically helpless or incapacitated by drugs administered without consent.
Van Houten later reopened the investigation. “Seeking justice sometimes requires us to reconsider or reopen cases when we are provided with additional evidence,” he said.
The school’s investigation produced conflicting accounts
Only a fraction of the evidence collected by the school has become public, but the portions that have provided a fuller — though disputed — timeline of events, as well as a glimpse at how the men responded to being accused.
According to the records, the woman had been invited to the fraternity by a member for whom she had long held strong romantic feelings. Cornell’s disciplinary panel found that she initially consented to sex with that man and one of his friends, though she later alleged in her lawsuit that she had been pressured into taking drugs and alcohol and was too intoxicated to consent.
Later, other men started coming into the room, some drawn by a message one of the fraternity brothers sent to a Snapchat group at 1:42 a.m. using a vulgar term to advertise that a woman’s body was freely available.
The woman told investigators that her intoxication had rendered her partly defenseless. She said some of the men inhaled drugs off her unclothed body.
The records also show that she acknowledged that her memory of the night was spotty, due to her extreme inebriation, and had verbally acquiesced to some acts she later felt were sexual abuse.
Some of the accused men disputed her account when speaking to investigators, or said that the drug use and sexual activity were consensual.
Cornell hasn’t detailed the results of its investigation, but said it resulted in some students being expelled. The records show it also cleared at least some of the men of sexual assault allegations.
New York’s governor was outraged by the police investigation
Hochul said she appointed James because she had lost faith in Van Houten’s handling of the case. She said Van Houten should have asked Cornell for more information and interviewed the woman before closing it.
“This woman, this young woman, had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable,” she said. “And then at every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her.”
Van Houten said he supports James’ appointment but maintains that New York law didn’t allow him to prosecute based solely on the woman’s allegations that she was too incapacitated to consent.
The case sparks calls for change
At a Cornell Student Assembly meeting Thursday, students and other members of the university community spent more than 2 1/2 hours discussing the handling of sexual assault allegations. Some expressed fear, anger, and grief — while others shared their own experiences of sexual violence on campus.
Among them was Jane Wang, who said she had reported being sexually assaulted at Cornell a year earlier.
When she filed her Title IX case in the midst of “mental, physical and emotional recovery from the assault,” she said, “I was also met with an abundance of paperwork, very little instruction on how to navigate it and no follow-up from our Title IX office of an outcome.”
The presidents of every fraternity in Cornell’s Interfraternity Council voted unanimously to cancel social events this weekend in response to the allegations, according to The Cornell Daily Sun. Twenty student organizations are also planning a protest Monday to voice support for a promised independent review of Cornell’s handling of the case and advocate changes to its sexual assault policies, the newspaper reported.
In a video message Saturday, Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff pledged greater transparency amid the mounting outrage about how the school handled the case. He called the gang rape allegations “deeply disturbing” and said the case would weigh on the university for years to come.
The case has also renewed scrutiny of a New York sexual assault law that makes it more difficult to prosecute cases involving people too intoxicated to consent. New York is one of 19 states with such laws.
Hochul said Friday that she supports changing the law.

title: 1 dead, 2 injured after downtown Las Vegas shooting
text:
LAS VEGAS (FOX5/Gray News) — One person is dead, and two others are injured after a shooting during First Friday in downtown Las Vegas Friday night.
According to a Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department press release, officers were in the area of South Main Street and West Charleston Boulevard at approximately 10:17 p.m. on Oct. 2 when they heard shots being fired.
Officers ran into a crowd and located two people suffering from apparent gunshot wounds. Additional officers located a third victim. All three were transported to a nearby hospital, where one person was pronounced deceased.
In an overnight briefing, LVMPD homicide Lt. Robert Price said the two other victims have non-life-threatening injuries.
Detectives determined a physical altercation occurred between several individuals. At some point, an unknown male produced a firearm and began shooting, striking multiple people, police said. The suspect fled prior to officers arriving.
The First Friday Foundation said it is heartbroken, grateful for Metro’s swift response, and will provide a response on future events before planning or announcing any future events.
“Very unfortunately, we are heartbroken to confirm the incident during tonight’s event involving a shooting/gunfire and a reported 3 injuries in the vicinity of the event in its last minutes. We are grateful for Las Vegas Metro’s swift response to the situation, and are devastated by the impact of this tragic event for everyone who was affected. As we navigate waiting for all the details so we can fully understand and process what happened, please know we are committed to doing everything we can in identifying the most thorough and appropriate response possible which we will provide before the planning or announcement of any future events. In the meantime, please support the community’s local artists, vendors, musicians, and attendees during this difficult time.”
The Arts District Neighborhood Association said it is deeply saddened and that they will work to help make First Friday safer moving forward.
Mayor Pro Tem Olivia Diaz expressed her sympathy with the victims and attendees from the First Friday shooting.
The LVMPD Homicide Section is leading the investigation. The identification of the decedent, as well as the cause and manner of death, will be released by the Clark County Coroner’s Office.

title: Christa Pike has not regained consciousness since failed execution, lawyer says
text:
Christa Pike has not regained consciousness since failed execution, lawyer says
Christa Pike has remained unconscious and on a ventilator at a hospital in the four days since her failed execution in Tennessee, and her prognosis might not be known for days more, one of her lawyers said Sunday.
Related video: Media witnesses recall what happened during Christa Pike’s failed execution
Little has been released about Pike's condition since Wednesday night's execution attempt. She has since remained hospitalized under guard as doctors try to get the massive dose of the barbiturate pentobarbital out of her system.
When asked whether she ever regained consciousness after the execution attempt, Assistant Federal Defender Stephen Ferrell, Pike's lawyer, said on CNN's "State of the Union": "Not that I am aware of."
Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in a jealous rage in 1995. She became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row.
Tennessee prison officials gave Pike two doses of the lethal injection drug on Wednesday night. The pentobarbital didn't kill her, but her lawyers said her arms were burned and blistered from the caustic drugs.
Pike gave someone her medical power of attorney and that person is protecting her privacy, Ferrell said.
"I'm not sure what all they may have told that person," Ferrell said.
Pike's attorneys have not identified who is making Pike's medical decisions.
A spokeswoman for Pike's defense team said in a statement early Sunday that "we appreciate all respect for Christa's rightful privacy."

title: Weather Discussion 10/4/26
‘Gone silent’: Rumford church replaces old pipe organ with digital model
text:
RUMFORD — Until about a half century ago, most large churches featured a pipe organ — a large musical instrument that produces sound by pushing air through rows of metal or wooden pipes.
Now, many of those churches, like St. Athanasius & St. John Church in Rumford, are modernizing, opting to digitize their instruments as parts for the aging pipe organs become increasingly hard to find and difficult to repair.
On Palm Sunday in late March this year, the church received a new Rodgers digital organ, and so far it’s living up to expectations.
“This new digital Rodgers console does everything the pipes do, and so much more,” St. Athanasius organist Nick Puiia said. “Most people could not tell the difference if I played the pipes or I played this. Not knowing what it was, I probably could not tell the difference.”
The old Estey pipe organ at the 126 Maine Ave. church was installed in 1927. Puiia said it’s been rebuilt a few times over the past years, but two years ago, it had a catastrophic failure.
“The control system behind it, all the electronics, just went fried,” he said. “The pipe organ was in need of a new rebuild anyway, and it was controlled by a 40-year-old Rodgers console, which also had some electronic voices that filled out the pipe sounds.”
Puiia said they looked at many different options to repair the old half pipe, half electronic organ, but the cost would have been “astronomical.”
“In addition to having to replace the console because the 1987 Rodgers console, in order to run the pipes, we had to have a special chip made,” he said. “And it was written in binary code by a gentleman from MIT, and it was just for that instrument, and we were on the spare.”
Puiia said he first played the old organ in 1991, and he’s been playing regularly here since 1994.
He said St. Athanasius’ pipe organ was built for the church to be filled with 1,100 people.
“It was very, very loud. We have 125, 150 people at mass,” Puiia said. “It was always too loud. On the pipe, you can’t control how loud it is. With the new organ, we have not heard a complaint that it’s too loud.”
The previous two or three years with the analog organ, Puiia said, “It was fighting me. Things weren’t working. I had to figure out what worked. What worked one day didn’t work the next. Now having everything work like it should is a treat.”
As churches modernize, he said, the old pipe organs are hardly ever used, “even if they still exist.”
“They’ve gone silent over the years,” Puiia said.
TOO EXPENSIVE
Puiia said one of the biggest factors in switching to the digital organ was cost.
“We had the money for the digital organ,” he said, which cost $98,000. “We didn’t have the money to repair the pipe organ,” Puiia said. “What we replaced was the console that controlled the pipe organ.”
Puiia said the pipes are in really good shape, but everything underneath it is all cracked, and the wind lines needed to be redone, a process that hasn’t happened since the 1970s or ’80s.
Additionally, finding someone who knows how to repair this type of organ is also difficult.
“The way this organ was built, it was not built to be fixed,” he said. “…They were built for your average country church that didn’t have a lot of money. They were just a working-class organ. They weren’t built as concert instruments, or with the future in mind.”
Repairing the pipe organ is “on the way, way back burner because it’s a half-million dollar-plus project. Some of the quotes were over a million dollars to get the pipe organ up and running in this church,” he said.
With the new digital organ, Puiia said fixing the pipe organ is “the last thing we need to think about.”
The church, he said, needs new floors and also needs to be painted.
“There’s other priorities,” he said.
Puiia added, “Now that we have a 100 percent working instrument that does everything we need, the pipe organ is the last thing we need to think about.”
The Rev. Aaron Damboise, pastor of Parish of the Holy Savior, which includes St. Athanasius & St. John and Our Lady of the Snows in Bethel, said having the new digital organ is a two-part blessing.
“The organ is extremely important in the amount of worship because it’s one of the instruments that’s been used for centuries to help raise the heart and mind,” he said.
Damboise said having Puiia play helps elevate the music program.
“Being able to play the organ is becoming a skill that’s not being taken up by a lot of younger people,” Damboise said. “We’ve got some younger people in our congregation, so we’re hoping that by having them hear this that they’ll be interested in this instrument.”
Damboise said the money to replace the old organ was set aside for the church, but it needed to be done.
“In the end, we thought we’d have time to think about raising money, but we didn’t end up having that,” he said.
Damboise said the church has a congregation of about 400 people.
OLD VERSUS NEW
Puiia said the new organ includes four musical styles — American, British, French cathedral and North German baroque.
“It’s just different styles. This can pretty much play every type of organ music ever written, the way the composer wanted it to sound,” he said. “This instrument has some non-organ sounds in it, as well as a full piano. That technology wasn’t there 40 years ago. There’s so much in this.”
The new organ is very user friendly, Puiia said.
“It also has the same layout as our former one, so pretty much everything is where it was,” he said. “This was pretty much the replacement model for the other one.”
Puiia noted another difference with the new organ is that he can record music that could be played if he isn’t there. “Then someone downstairs could play it with their app on their phone,” he said.
The old organ was about double the size, and inside was row after row of components, capacitors and resistors. Inside the new organ was a small compartment about the size of an I-Pad, Puiia added.
The old organ received maintenance twice a year, but as time went on, it became more difficult to find someone to do the work because other churches weren’t maintaining their organs.
“There was a time when our tuner would come and he’d stop here and then go to the Green Church in Mexico to tune their organ. As time went on, as their funds dwindled, the Mexico church stopped using them, so what was $700 became $2,500 for that service twice a year,” said Puiia.
There’s really no maintenance to the new organ, he said, which they searched for for three and a half to four years.
Puiia said the analog organ went to the landfill.
“It was just old electronics. There was no longer parts available for it,” he said. “It was the equivalent of a 1970s TV.”
DEDICATION
St. Athanasius will hold a dedication of the new Rodgers digital organ on Sunday, Oct. 11.
The day will begin at 9:30 a.m. with a special mass with a blessing of the organ by Fr. Aaron Damboise. After mass, there will be an open house in the choir loft to look at the organ and experience it first hand.
At 2 p.m. a recital will be held featuring Scott Vaillancourt, music director at St. Peter and Paul Basilica in Lewiston, with music from all periods.
Puiia noted that years ago, Vaillancourt delivered a recital using the old organ, “so he’ll be recreating some of the programming he did on that one (with the new organ).”
On Dec. 27, the Sunday after Christmas, Puiia said the church will be having a Festival of Lessons and Carols, a non-denominational service that will include people from many churches throughout the area.
“We’ll be creating a giant choir, and they’ll be singing a variety of Christmas pieces and some readings,” he said. “That will be another part of the introductory year of the organ.”
He added that if it goes well, it may become an annual event in this church.
Another big event will soon be in the planning stages.
Damboise said the church will celebrate the 100th anniversary of the building on Christmas Day 2027.
In 1905, a group of Franco Americans came together and purchased the land to build a Catholic church. Construction began in 1906 and finished for Christmas midnight mass in 1927. It was built on the basement church of St. John Baptiste and served the French-speaking parishioners until 1970 when the parishes of St. Athanasius and St. John merged.

Maine broadcasting legend honored at Bangor Historical Society
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The Bangor Historical Society for Liberty & Legacy held its annual awards night tonight to celebrate those who have left a lasting impact on our community.
George Hale was one of the award honorees.
“I came to Bangor 70 years ago. I guess they think I’m walking history now. I’m honored that they recognized the years I put in and the things that I’ve done. You don’t do these things for awards, you do it because that’s the thing to do,” said Hale.
Hale is a Maine broadcasting legend and WABI alum.
He received the Judge John E. Godfrey Eye Witness to History award.
The William Stone engraving of the Declaration of Independence was also at the event tonight, in celebration of America’s 250 birthday.

title: Obituary: William D. McCalmon
text:
YARMOUTH – William D. McCalmon, 84, passed away peacefully at his home in Yarmouth on Sept. 20, 2026. Bill was born in Portland, Maine on Oct. 18, 1941, the son of the late Irving and Lorraine (Daniels) McCalmon.
Bill grew up in Portland, living on Munjoy Hill and Peaks Island. A fixture at the Portland Boys Club, he discovered his lifelong love of swimming, which flourished throughout his years at Portland High School. Alongside his brother, Irv, he dominated the Maine swimming scene and beyond, earning the nickname “The Mighty Macs” for their remarkable accomplishments. As captain of the Portland High School swim team, Bill set multiple school and meet records, won four Maine State individual titles, a New England high school title and went on to compete for the University of Connecticut. A 2024 inductee into the Maine Swimming Hall of Fame, Bill took great pride in his athletic accomplishments.
After college, Bill served as a medic in the Army National Reserves before embarking on a career in education and coaching. His kind heart and genuine love of children drew him to special education. After earning his master’s degree, he became principal of PREP, a school for children with special needs, and later served as Director of Special Education for the City of Portland. His dedication to children and their families left a lasting mark on the community.
In 1971, Bill met the love of his life, Mary Jane, at the Old Port Tavern. They married in 1973 and raised two children, Ryan and Sarah, with immense love and pride. His greatest joy was his family, especially his six grandchildren, who affectionately knew him as “Grumpy.”
A lifelong learner and true renaissance man, Bill eventually transitioned into the business world, working in sales, investments, and stock brokerage. His final and perhaps most beloved chapter was spent running the Long Island Store in Casco Bay for 20 years. There, Bill became a cherished island fixture, holding court daily with friends, family, and visitors, sharing stories, laughter, and his unmistakable gift for connecting with people. During those years, he rediscovered his passion for painting, transforming the store into an impromptu art gallery. His paintings found their way into the homes and hearts of countless visitors, many of whom still treasure his work.
Most know Bill as a tremendous golfer, always willing to play a round and give you some tips. He also loved fishing, painting, scuba diving, running, “old man poker”, reading biographies, and watching baseball. He especially cherished the many years he spent golfing and fishing with dear friends, most notably his lifelong friend, Harvey Wheeler.
Bill’s greatest passion was his family, and his personal motto, “I’m ALL IN,” said everything about the way he lived. He showed up for as many games, practices, track meets, concerts, graduations, birthdays, holidays, and vacations as he possibly could. His greatest gifts were his time and presence – a joke to lift your spirits, a story to make you laugh, a hug when you needed one, or simply an attentive ear. He was his family’s biggest cheerleader and most devoted fan, right through his final weeks. His love, humor, generosity, and unwavering presence will be deeply missed and forever cherished.
Bill was predeceased by his sister, Elizabeth Tracy.
He is survived by his beloved wife of 53 years, Mary Jane (Jacobs) McCalmon; his children, Ryan McCalmon and his wife Sarah Dodwell, and Sarah (McCalmon) Olivares and her husband Eric Olivares; his six grandchildren, Benjamin, Aaron, Nora, Asher, Camden, and William; his siblings, Irv McCalmon, Marie Guimont, and Jane Doyle; and many beloved extended family members.
A celebration of Bill’s life will be held Wednesday, Nov. 4, at Ocean Gateway in Portland. Guests are welcome to arrive at 3 p.m., remembrances will begin at 3:30 p.m., followed by a reception until 6 p.m.
In lieu of flowers, donations in Bill’s memory may be made to Barbara Bush Children’s Hospital through its website.

title: New Hampshire man arrested in connection with fatal hit-and-run incident in Wells
Hearts of Pine overcome 3-goal deficit to earn draw
text:
Diego Gonzalez’s penalty kick right before the final whistle kept the Portland Hearts of Pine’s slim playoff hopes alive.
The Hearts of Pine nearly scored on a stoppage-time corner kick, but after the ball was deflected, Diogo Barbosa was fouled in the box in the 97th minute. That gave Gonzalez a penalty kick, which he buried in the back of the net to secure a 3-3 draw with Spokane Velocity FC in a USL1 soccer match Saturday in Spokane.
Hearts of Pine (7-12-10) now have 31 points, putting them eight behind Fort Wayne FC for the eighth and final postseason spot.
Heading into halftime, the Hearts looked headed for their 13th defeat of the season. Spokane scored three goals in a 10-minute spurt at the end of the opening half. Nil Vinyals netted the first goal and set up scores by Neco Brett and Andre Lewis.
Portland played much better in the second half and got on the scoreboard in the 64th minute whenFelipe Rodriguez Gentile scored off an assist from Matteo Kidd. The Hearts of Pine cut their deficit to 3-2 on a goal by Aboubacar Camara.
The Hearts of Pine, ranked 13th in the league, next host fourth-ranked Athletic Club Boise, which has already clinched a playoff berth, Saturday at 5 p.m. at Fitzpatrick Stadium in Portland.

title: Obituary: Margaret “Maggie” (Mahon) Perkins
text:
GARDINER – Margaret “Maggie” Mahon Perkins, 83, of Gardiner, Maine, a beacon of warmth and generosity, passed away peacefully on Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026.
Born on March 16, 1943, in the heart of Treenagh, Ireland, Maggie’s life was a testament to her unwavering kindness and dedication to others. She was a cherished soul whose presence enriched the lives of all who had the privilege of knowing her.
While visiting family in England, Maggie met her future husband, Raymond, during his service in the Air Force. In 1960, Maggie traveled to Gardiner, Maine to marry Ray and begin her new life in America. Maggie and Ray moved into Ray’s family home on Central Street where they raised their two daughters and lived for the remainder of their lives.
For much of her life, Maggie worked in the restaurant industry as a server and manager and later became co-owner of the Kennebec Wharf in Hallowell with her husband, Ray. A few years later the two established R&M Catering and created wonderful food for many weddings, lobster bakes and meetings throughout central Maine. Both ventures filled her passion for hospitality and her genuine care for people.
Maggie was a natural people person, a best friend to many, and her greatest joy was found in hosting family gatherings, where card games, laughter and love filled her home. Her defining characteristic was her constant consideration for others; she was always looking out and caring for people. Above all, Maggie was deeply devoted to her daughters, Susanne and Carolyn, as well as her grandchildren and great-grandchildren. Their boundless love and care for her reflected the very best of her own generous spirit—a legacy of love they will carry in their hearts forever.
Maggie was preceded in death by her parents, Thomas and Mary Mahon; her husband of 62 years, Raymond Perkins; her beloved sister, Bridie Doherty; and her son-in-law, Christopher Condon.
She is survived by her two daughters, Susanne Mansir and Carolyn Condon and her partner Tieche Shelton III; three grandchildren, Robert Condon and his wife, Katie, Kelsie Sue Condon, and Richard Mansir and his wife Gina LoMonaco; three great-grandchildren, Richard “Ricky” Mansir, Christopher Condon and Reid Condon.
Maggie’s family would like to convey very special thanks to the staff of MaineGeneral Hospice for their kind and compassionate care allowing her to spend her final days at home surrounded by family and dear friends.
A private family service will be held at a later date.
Condolences, memories, and photos may be shared with the family on the obituary page of the Staples Funeral Home website, http://www.staplesfuneralhome.com

title: 2 shot dead and dozens injured at neighborhood block party shooting in southern Georgia
text:
VIENNA, Georgia (AP) — Two people were shot to death in a hail of gunfire and nearly three dozen others were injured at a homecoming weekend block party early Sunday morning in southern Georgia, according to state law enforcement officials.
More than 1,000 people were gathered at the site, and more than 50 shots were fired in at least two locations about a block apart in Vienna, Dooly County Sheriff Craig Peavy told WMAZ-TV.
Peavy said people were “going every direction” and that, even while officers were on the scene, more gunfire erupted about a block away.
“We don’t know if it’s coming at us or someone else,” he said. “You just have to keep doing what you’re doing and hope you don’t get hit by gunfire.”
The incident took place over homecoming weekend for Dooly County High School.
The shooting was not at a school-sponsored event, said Sherrod Willaford, superintendent of the Dooly County School System.
“We recognize that its impact may reach many of our students, families, and staff,” he said in a statement. Schools will open Monday, he said, but additional safety measures have been put in place. He did not specify what they are.
Dooly County Sheriff’s Office deputies were on patrol at a neighborhood block party around 1:25 a.m. Sunday in Vienna when shots were fired, the Georgia Bureau of Investigation said in a statement.
Vienna is about 130 miles (about 210 kilometers) south of Atlanta and about a 50-mile (80-kilometer) drive south on the Interstate 75 corridor from the central Georgia city of Macon, where authorities say 12 teens were wounded by gunfire during a confrontation between people at a birthday party last week at a city park.
Deputies found two people dead at the scene and multiple others who had been shot, officials said. Police did not specify how many of the 35 injured had been shot or provide any details about the injuries or their severity. The victims were taken to several hospitals for treatment, the GBI said.
Dooly County Coroner Brett Walls said the two men, ages 20 and 23, were pronounced dead at the scene with fatal gunshot wounds. He said multiple other people were also shot, calling the scene “horrific.”
Walls told the Atlanta Journal-Constitution that multiple people were struck by bullets and roughly a dozen others were hurt while trying to flee.
“This doesn’t — it’s not supposed to — happen in a small town like that. It’s something you hear on the news in bigger cities,” Walls told the newspaper, adding hospitals were flooded with the injured. “And even in bigger cities, you don’t hear that kind of a number.”
Authorities have not said whether any suspects are in custody or being sought. No motive has been given for the shooting.
Vienna Mayor Eddie Daniels said the shooting was about a block from his house and he “saw a lot of blue lights.” Daniels said he hadn’t spoken with law enforcement officials yet and had no details about what had happened.
Daniels said the city hadn’t issued any kind of permit for the block party and he didn’t know if it was a homecoming party.
Georgia Bureau of Investigation spokesperson Lydia Bullard declined to answer questions about the shooting, saying it was an ongoing investigation.
___

title: Why are more young adults having strokes now than 30 years ago?
text:
More young adults having strokes now than 30 years ago
Strokes are often thought of as a condition affecting older adults, but new national data show strokes among younger adults have doubled over the past 30 years.
That trend has doctors searching for answers while urging younger people not to ignore warning signs or skip routine medical care.
Why researchers are concerned
Dr. Michelle Leppert, a vascular neurologist at Tufts Medical Center in Boston, said researchers still do not fully understand what is driving the increase.
Some experts point to a rise in certain risk factors, such as high blood pressure, diabetes and high cholesterol, but Leppert said it can't be the only explanation. Otherwise, she would expect to see a similar increase in heart attacks among young adults -- and there isn't one.
Leppert also noted that strokes are occurring more often in women under 45 than in men, highlighting the need for more research.
Know the warning signs
Leppert emphasized the American Stroke Association’s BE FAST mnemonic for recognizing stroke symptoms:
- Balance problems
- Eye or vision changes
- Face drooping
- Arm weakness
- Speech difficulties
- Time to call for emergency care
“The faster you can get in, the better chance we have of reversing these symptoms,” she said.
She said younger adults should not ignore sudden headaches or any new neurological symptoms.
Reducing your risk
Leppert’s advice for young adults is straightforward: don’t skip your annual wellness visits. Even healthy people in their 20s, 30s and 40s may have risk factors that can be identified during routine checkups.
She also said young women who experience migraines with aura should talk with their health care provider about birth control options that do not contain any estrogen.

title: Obituary: Rita S. Fortin
text:
BENTON – Rita S. Fortin, 84, of Benton, Maine, passed away at her home on Sept. 28, 2026, following a brief but courageous battle with metastatic breast cancer. She left this world bathed in the love of her family.
Rita was born on March 24, 1942, the seventh of 10 children of Noel and Rose Bolduc. She graduated high school from Bloomfield Academy in Skowhegan and went on to graduate from Augusta General Hospital’s radiology technology program.
In 1962, she married the love of her life, Gerald “Jerry” Fortin, with whom she raised her five children on their family farm in Benton. As her family grew, Rita stepped away from her career as a radiation technologist and embraced her roles as a full-time mother and farm wife. Rita resumed her career 20 years later when her youngest child was in junior high. She worked as an x-ray technician and mammography technologist at Inland Hospital in Waterville and later at Sebasticook Hospital in Pittsfield until her retirement in 2010.
Rita was a vivacious woman who brought her full self to everything she did. She was a fully involved and present mother who, together with Jerry, created a loving, fun and hard-working family life on the farm. She was known for wearing bright colors, fun socks, and holiday attire on every opportunity. Having taken up quilting with her sisters in the late 1980s, Rita and her sisters met every week for over 25 years to sew together. She made a point of making a hand-made quilt for each of her children and grandchildren and she also made a crocheted Afghan blanket for each of her great-grandchildren. Highly scheduled and ever on the go, she once left her own birthday party to attend a funeral of a community member.
Rita lived her life in service to others with enthusiasm, laughter and joy. She showed up for people in every conceivable way – usually with homemade food. Aside from the countless individual ways she supported family and friends throughout her life, Rita was also an active member of the Immaculate Heart of Mary Catholic Church in Fairfield, where she taught catechism to Catholic children for 15 years and for over 20 years, she taught Rites of Christian Initiation to adults wanting to become Catholic. She also served on the Parish Council and served as a lector and Eucharist Minister for many years. Rita was an active member of Victor Grange of Fairfield Center for over 50 years; she participated in the Grange “Senior Circle,” cooking and serving meals to the elderly well into her 80s; she was a member of Clinton Day Group of Cooperative Extension for over 50 years, serving as president for many of her last several years; a member of Somerset County Cooperative Extension, and she volunteered at the Fairfield Food Panty twice a month for the past 10 years.
Until her death, Rita remained entrenched in the community that she loved so dearly. It was a great joy to watch her perform plays over the years through her 70s and 80s, both with Victor Grange and as a member of the Recycled Shakespeare Troupe in Fairfield, of which she was an original member. She experienced great joy participating in a weekly sewing group over the past 10 years, and in more recent years she took up painting lessons with her friend and cribbage tournament partner, Jean Savage. Despite constantly being pulled in multiple directions, Rita never failed to make time for those she loved. When she gave a gift, she gave it with love and when she gave you her attention, she gave you every bit of it.
Rita leaves behind her five children, Judy Fortin of Benton and the child of her heart, Jackie; Joan Fortin and her husband, Chet Randall, of Portland and their children Michael and Lainey Randall; Andy Fortin and his partner, Sandy Irving, of Benton and his children Anthony Fortin and wife, Malley, Timothy Fortin and wife, Stephanie, Nakita Gangloff and husband Charles, and Gary Wilber; Jan Bancroft and her husband, Ryan, of New Orleans, La. and their children, Sarah, Rachel, and Matthew Bancroft; and Allan Fortin and his wife, Pamela, of Fairfield, and their children Madelyn McKenzie and her husband, Brody, and Jackson Fortin and his fiancé, Victoria Dubay; and great-grandchildren, Samuel and Harrison McKenzie, Henry Fortin, and Alexandria and Charles Gangloff.
She is also survived by a large extended family, including her brother, Raymond Bolduc and his wife, Peg, of Auburn, N.H.; and an array of cherished nieces and nephews along with their spouses.
Rita was predeceased by her beloved husband of 56 years, Gerald Fortin; her parents, Noel and Rose Bolduc; eight of her siblings; and eight of her nieces and nephews.

A reception will follow immediately after the mass. A private committal will take place at a later time.

title: Colder night tonight but more sun tomorrow, rain chances increase Monday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Comfortable highs tomorrow after some chilly lows but overall a really spectacular fall weekend for the entire region. More turbulent weather arrives Monday into the workweek with rain possible and gusty winds following it but enjoy this weekend while you can because fall colors are in full bloom and the temps will be very comfortable and sunshine will dominate.
Tonight: Frosty to freeze conditions especially to the north.
Temps will drop into the 30s for most tonight and some cold spots way up north may see a few 20s on the thermometer. While growing season has ended if you do have any plants left out now is the time to bring them in.
Sunday: Very similar day with a colder start
The spots that see frost on Sunday morning will likely rebound quickly as the sun comes out quickly Sunday morning. Few clouds if any will be visible on Sunday across the state. As I mentioned, this is the weekend to get out and see the leaves or enjoy a fall festival or football game! Highs mainly in the low 60s with light winds.
Sunday night: Clouds arrive ahead of next system
It will cloud up and stay relatively warm on Sunday night ahead of our next system which will arrive on Monday. Winds will also pick up out of the SW at 10-15 mph overnight.
Monday and beyond: Rain possible on Monday followed by gusty winds.
Rain may arrive in the early on Monday but there is still a good amount of uncertainty in terms of when and how much rain we will get on Monday across the region as a cold front moves through. What is looking quite likely however is Tuesday is looking quite breezy and will knock a large number of leaves off the trees and being some colder temps as well.
Tonight: Quite chilly with lows in the 30s and low 40s. Winds light.
Tomorrow: Another sun filled day. Highs near 60. Winds NW at 5-10 mph
Sunday night: Not as cold and clouds arrive. Lows near 50. Winds SW at 10-15 mph
Monday: Showers arrive with general cloudiness. Highs near 60. Winds SW at 10-15 mph.
Monday night: Cooling off again, with some showers sticking around. Breezy. Lows in the 30s with winds W at 15-20 mph

title: US Air Force pulls all bombers from key British air base targeted by a suspected terror attack
text:
US Air Force pulls all bombers from UK air base targeted by a suspected terror attack
The U.S. Air Force has brought home its bombers stationed at a U.S.-run military air base in England used to strike Iran following an investigation into a planned terror attack at the RAF Fairford base.
The bombers were redeployed back to their home bases in the United States, according to a Pentagon official who was not authorized to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke Sunday on condition of anonymity.
Related previous coverage in the player above: Trump criticizes UK for releasing suspects in alleged terror plot targeting base used by US
Aviation watchers such as the Military Air Tracking Alliance have observed dozens of B-52 and B-1 bombers operating out of RAF Fairford since the opening days of the Iran war. Observers noticed a host of B-1 bombers fly out of the base on Sunday.
The move comes as President Donald Trump weighs options for his war on Iran — including new strikes — despite his initial promises to Americans that the campaign would last a matter of weeks.
“We have decisions that I’ll make about Iran. Iran’s been decimated. So the only question is — it’ll either be the easy way, or the hard way,” Trump told reporters on Saturday as he left the White House for a rally in Ohio.
A dual British-Iranian national was arrested in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terror attack, following a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September. In total, six people have been taken into custody and then released on bail during the investigation.
British authorities have linked the incident to Tehran. Iran has denied involvement. It has previously said it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.
U.K. officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arson and other attacks in Britain and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the U.K. if conflicts in the Middle East continue.
RAF Fairford, located 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.
The U.S. military still maintains a sizable presence in the Middle East. On Thursday, a U.S. official said the recently deployed USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier, as well as the USS Malkin Island amphibious readiness group — a group of ships that together carry over 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines — are heading for the region. The official said the move could result in three carriers in the region as early as the end of October.

title: Maine Marathon winners soak in atmosphere, experience
text:
PORTLAND — Dylan Stoltzfus made a heart shape with his hands as he made his way to the finish line.
It was evident how much winning the 35th annual Maine Community Bank Maine Marathon meant.
“I spent a really long time with an injury in college,” said Stoltzfus, 24, a Portland resident. “I thought I would never run again, never race again. This is the first big race I’ve ever won. It feels like years in the wilderness and this is like coming out.”
Stoltzfus finished with a time of 2 hours, 23 minutes, 59 seconds, easily out-distancing runnerup Steven Fritzsche of Kennebunk (2:31.12). Will Faden of Somerville, Massachusetts (2:32.02) placed third.
Betsy Burke, 42, of Rye, New York finished first in the women’s field with a time of 2:54.08.
This was her second time running the race.
“I was really surprised,” Burke said. “It was fun. I had people to run with and felt pretty good until about (mile) 21 and then just tried to turn my brain off.”
Burke’s husband and his family are from Blue Hill, so she visits Maine often.
“I felt really good in the hills, like (miles) 12 to 18, then started feeling much worse,” Burke said, laughing. “But I felt good for a while and was like, ‘this is great,’ and then I knew I could just get to the end.”
Alyssa Carreau of Old Lyme, Connecticut (2:55.39) and Linnea Maynard of Portland (2:57.32) followed in second and third places, respectively.
On the half marathon side, winners JP Flavin and Megan O’Neil broke new ground.
As teammates who train out of Rochester, Michigan, not only was this the pair’s first time in Maine, but they earned course records in the men’s and women’s half marathon races.
“Oh my gosh, it’s gorgeous,” O’Neil said said of Maine. “I’m from Michigan. All my friends are super jealous I got to go to Maine in October. … Beautiful day for running, perfect temperature, not too windy.”
O’Neil, 30, finished in 1:14.34. Her time was 32 seconds faster than Cliodhna O’Malley’s record-setting run last year.
Flavin, 28, finished with a time of 1:03.00, beating previous record holder Colin Cernik’s 2025 time by 1:39.
“I’m in the middle of preparing for (the) New York City Marathon, so it’s kind of more of a workout, but it was fun,” Flavin said. “It was (a) good group of guys to work with for 10 miles and I was going to pick it up the last 5K and got rolling down those hills. The crowd was awesome, running past everyone was so much fun, so it was a blast.”
Next to finish were two Massachusetts runners — Cameron Dickson from Jamaica Plain (1:03.30) in second place and Ned Farrington of Cohasset (1:03.48) in third.
Heather Gallant of Wayne (1:15.38) and Isabel Seay of Hanover, New Hampshire (1:16.28) joined O’Neil on the podium in second and third place, respectively.

title: Despair over future fuels political anxiety for college students on the cusp of adulthood
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
EAST LANSING, Mich. (AP) — Frankie Llerandi, 21, has been unable to land a single internship in his three years at Michigan State University.
He will graduate in the spring with an economics degree and an interest in data analytics, but true adulthood seems maddeningly far away. Most of his cousins have not been able to buy a house or start a family deep into their 30s.
Kira Saiti, a 19-year-old sophomore, is more upset about the broader world than her own future. Every time she looks at her phone she sees images of violence and horror, both in the Middle East and closer to home.
“It’s kind of hard to look at that and say, ‘This world is a great place,’” she said.
Julian Bautista, 20, saw his chosen profession of environmental work decimated by Trump administration cuts, pushing the junior to decide he will leave the United States to find work in the Netherlands when he graduates. He considers what remains his home country for the next 18 months to be a failure of democracy led by what he sees as corrupt politicians.
“Throughout my life, we’ve either stagnated or declined, we haven’t improved,” Bautista said.
For many of their classmates on campus and elsewhere around the country, the present looks bleak and the future uncertain at best. Their anxiety is fueling a restlessness with a national political system that they worry is no longer capable of improving their lives or no longer interested in helping.
Two years ago, grim economic vibes helped Donald Trump win a far larger share of young voters than is typical for a Republican — 47%, according to AP VoteCast, an extensive survey of the electorate. Now, anxiety about artificial intelligence and the Iran war has been added to the mix, powering a wave of disruptive candidates on the opposite end of the political spectrum who have been embraced by college students.
Llerandi, Saiti and Bautista all support a slate of progressive, antiestablishment Democratic candidates in Michigan who are pledging to shake up the status quo. Among them are Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official running for U.S. Senate, and Will Lawrence, a liberal activist trying to unseat Tom Barrett, the Republican congressman who represents the swing district that includes the university.
The future looks bleak for many students
Anxieties about the job market, homeownership and adulthood are widespread across the campus, even among those who are not deeply involved in politics.
“It’s just something to laugh at, but, you know, I really do want a house when I’m older,” said Praveen Amunugama, a 21-year-old biochemistry major who plans to go to graduate school in hopes the job market improves over the next two years.
His friends feel the same way.
“They want to be able to afford things, raise a good family,” he said.
Despite the economic angst among young people, at first blush the picture does not look that bad for them. The unemployment rate for those age 22 to 27 is 7.2%, higher than the broader rate of 4.1% but lower than some other moments of economic calm.
A 2024 study found members of the younger generation known as Generation Z are poised to be wealthier than millennials, who themselves are wealthier than the prior generation despite the persistent sense of economic doom that accompanied their entry into the job market during the Great Recession.
Kevin Corinth, the economist who co-authored that study, said he understands Gen Z angst, given modern uncertainties, especially the prospect of AI reshaping various industries and data showing younger people are taking longer to leave home and start families.
“For previous generations, if you took certain paths you were likely to succeed, to do better than your parents,” said Corinth, who is at the American Enterprise Institute, a center-right think tank. For young people now, he acknowledged, that path is not as clear.
Kathryn Edwards, a Texas-based economist, noted that unemployment among recent college graduates is at 5.6%, higher than at most other times in recent history other than the Great Recession. Combined with historically high housing prices and rising costs for essentials such as food and healthcare, that is a challenging environment for young people.
“It’s pretty bad for them,” Edwards said, adding that young people are picking up on broader warning signs in the economy. “So many aspects of our current economy, I think young people have gotten right.”
They are also fully exposed to the new form of job hunting: AI-powered, digital and done almost exclusively online, where it is hard to discern real job openings from fake ones.
“Think about the amount they get spammed and scammed, and there are tons of fake jobs out there,” said Marla McGraw, assistant dean of career management in Michigan State’s business school. “They’re always coming in here going, ‘Is this real?’”
She spends a lot of time trying to buck up disenchanted students.
“Our message right now is the job market is tough, but you’re tougher,” McGraw said.
Students say political leaders are falling short
Young Americans’ optimism about the job market has plummeted since 2024 and the gap between their view of the economy and those of their elders is greater than almost anywhere in the world, according to a Gallup survey earlier this year.
They are less likely to be engaged in politics and less likely to think it is important to vote, an Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll found. They also are less likely to be concerned about political violence.
That dissolution of beliefs in traditional political values worries Karlee VanAntwerp.
The 21-year-old Michigan State senior is also head of the local chapter of Turning Point, the group for young conservatives whose founder, Charlie Kirk, was assassinated last year. VanAntwerp has been horrified to see Kirk’s killing repeatedly, and sometimes menacingly, mocked online.
“Gen Z tends to be more extreme with their views,” VanAntwerp said. “It makes it hard to work with people of different political beliefs, because even if you’re in the middle, they assume you’re crazy.”
VanAntwerp sees that feeding into the despair many of her generation feel about real change ever happening.
“One administration does a bunch of stuff, another administration comes in and wipes it all out,” said VanAntwerp, who is also working for Barrett’s campaign. “It feels like we always go in circles. That contributes to the political temperature being so high, because people feel nothing changes.”
Her politics are the polar opposite of many liberal students who gathered to hear Lawrence, Barrett’s Democratic challenger, talk in a classroom one recent evening, but there was a similar desire for dramatic change. Lawrence sympathized with the glum feelings of early adulthood and urged the students not to succumb to despair.
“When I was a little younger I wanted to drop out of society, and it was organizing that gave me a path in life,” Lawrence said.
After the candidate left, however, Bautista still sounded on the verge of despair. He talked about how online influencers he trusts deride Democrats such as Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York as “mini-mes” because, Bautista contended, they are just watered-down versions of Trump.
“Our leaders are representing us less,” Bautista said. “People are desperate for big stuff.”

title: Obituary: Ralph Warren Lewis
text:
BRUNSWICK – Ralph Warren Lewis, 93, passed away peacefully in his sleep on Sept. 14, 2026, in Topsham, Maine.
Born in Concordia, Kan., to Arthur and Sylvia Lewis. He loved growing up in Concordia. In high school, he was a class officer, Eagle Scout with a Gold Palm and school photographer.
Ralph loved music, singing bass in barbershop quartets and church choirs throughout his life. He also had a lifelong passion for photography.
In 1952, Ralph married his high school sweetheart, Shirley Scovell. They shared 67 years together until her passing in 2019.
Ralph joined the U.S. Navy in 1953 as a naval photographer. During his remarkable 27-year career, he rose from E-3 to chief petty officer and ultimately retired as a lieutenant commander. His service took him around the world, including Operation Deep Freeze in Antarctica.
After retiring, Ralph remained active with the National Association of Naval Photographers and began a second career with Apple computers, eventually founding Mac-Care.
Ralph also loved mystery novels, woodworking, traveling, his church, his shipmates, and a good sea story.
He is survived by his sister, Evelyn Springstead; children Kathy Smith, Lynn Koenig (Dave), Bryan Lewis (Tess), and Ken Lewis (Reba); and many nieces and nephews.
Ralph loved his family, his faith, and life. His family takes comfort knowing he and Shirley are together again.
Fair winds and following seas, Ralph. We’ve got the watch.

title: Don’t let Maine’s candidates take the off ramp on transportation
text:
Here’s a question you should ask people running for office: How will we get there?
Gas, diesel and vehicles are quickly rising in price. In a Gorman Foundation report, 30% of Mainers don’t drive and that number may rise as the affordability of driving come into play. So, it is campaign season and candidates are running for town, state and national offices.
At your door or at any meeting where candidates are available ask them this: What are your thoughts on transportation? How will we manage as our budget for transportation outstrips our income; isn’t support for public transportation necessary?
Please ask these questions while the candidates are running; they need to think long and deeply about how to best serve their constituents. Drivers and non-drivers need thoughtful policies.
Steve Hoad
Windsor

title: Search suspended for 6 people on missing medical flight from Bermuda to Boston
text:
(AP) - Authorities on Sunday suspended the search off the Massachusetts coast for six people on an air ambulance that disappeared during a flight from Bermuda to Boston.
The U.S. Coast Guard said authorities searched more than 4,400 miles (7,081 kilometers) over a span of 66 hours for the four Canadians and two people from Bermuda who were on board.
“Suspending a search is not an easy decision,” Rear Adm. Matthew Lake, commander of the Coast Guard’s northeast district, said in a statement. “We express our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones affected by the tragedy and our gratitude for our partner agencies who helped support search efforts.”
The Federal Aviation Administration contacted the Coast Guard at 2 a.m. Saturday that it had lost contact with the Gulfstream G100 carrying six people over the Atlantic Ocean. Searchers later Saturday found a “debris field” off the coast of Nantucket, Lake had said at a news conference on Sunday.
Coast Guard crews along with the New York National Guard’s Air Rescue Wing and Massachusetts authorities searched a vast area using fixed-wing aircraft, helicopters, boats and cutters.
The depth of the water around the debris field was 80 to 90 feet (about 24 to 27 meters).
The Canadian-registered air ambulance jet had four crew members and two passengers aboard when it departed Bermuda’s L.F. Wade International Airport for the nighttime flight to Massachusetts, according to a statement from the Bermuda airport’s operator, Skyport.
Air traffic audio indicates that the plane may have been “coming in blind” when a storm loomed ahead shortly before it vanished.
The pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the jet approached the coast, according to air traffic control audio posted by LiveATC.net. “Roger, you said you’re coming in blind. Is that what you said?” a controller can be heard asking the pilot.
That makes Mary Schiavo, who is a former Inspector General of the Transportation Department, think the plane may have lost its navigational instruments just as a storm moved across its path on radar. The plane also descended sharply from its cruising altitude of around 24,000 feet to around 10,000 feet, according to preliminary data from flight tracking site FlightRadar24.
“Something bad happened with this big drop, and they flew into this big storm. It’s a terrible place to have a loss of your instruments and be flying blind,” said Schiavo, who is an aviation attorney. “It’s very easy to get disoriented and not know if you’re turning, climbing, descending, etc.”
___
AP Transportation Writer Josh Funk, Associated Press writer Amy Taxin and Associated Press reporter Laura Turbay in Little Rock, Arkansas, a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative, contributed to this report.
