title: Maine Marathon held in Portland sees record number of runners
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Marathon held in Portland sees record number of runners
Over 5,500 runners signed up to run in the Maine Marathon on Sunday in Portland, an all-time high in the history of the race.
The winner in the women's division was Betsy Burke, who finished with a time of 2:54:08. The Rye, New York, native said she didn't come into Sunday morning expecting the win.
"I know the bike came up to me sometime in the teens and said something, and I was like 'What?' He said 'You're in the lead.' That's weird," recalled Burke.
Burke said that she had won races in the past, but it has been a while, and the training leading up to this year's race had a bit of a speed bump.
"I ran a lot less," said Burke. "I had foot surgery in January. So I do a lot of it on the Peloton now, but, you know, I still work hard."
The male winner was Dylan Stoltzfus, who came in at 2:23:59, a personal record, according to Stoltzfus.
For him, this year was a revenge tale. In last year's race, Stoltzfus came in fifth, and he was determined to get a better result in this year's race.
"Anyone who knows me knows I haven't shut up about this for like two months," answered Stoltzfus. "You never know who's going to show up. Just nightmares of someone who I have no chance against, but traditionally 2:25ish gets it done."
When he crossed the finish line, he was met by cheers and roars, some coming from those closest to him, including his roommates and his girlfriend.
"She puts up with so much. She makes me feel like a superhero," commented Stoltzfus. "Getting back to see her was all I could think about for the last five miles."
"He has spent the last year running," recalled his roommate Cole. "Even when he was watching a movie in the living room, he's on the foam roller just stretching out. Just saying 'I'm going to win the marathon, I'm going to win it.'"
According to race organizers, the marathon has a financial impact on the city of $3 million. They said that 54% of the runners come from out of state not only to run the course, but also to explore the city and state.
"When I first took over, we worked on our brand and our purpose, and we decided to be a destination race," stated Race Director Bob Dunfey. "And so we market throughout the country and the world."
According to Dunfey, the race also brought in an estimated $700,000 to $900,000 for around 100 charities, including the marathon's beneficiaries and individual nonprofits chosen by the runners.

title: How Maine’s schools need to be approaching AI
text:
Joseph Hennessey, MSEd, is an educator who has served in classroom and building-level leadership roles, most recently in central Maine. He was the 2018 Piscataquis County Teacher of the Year, the 2019 Maine Teacher of the Year, the 2020 National University Teacher of the Year for Maine and is currently an American Service Fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School of Government.
Toward the end of the last school year, I sat with a middle school teacher and her student in the classroom to address misuse of AI on an important assignment. Were Google and Gemini (Google’s AI assistant) really different forms of sources? How much “assistance” from AI qualified as too much, at this developmental level, in this content area, at this juncture in history?
Our district’s acceptable use policy had been provisionally updated, but we had not yet had time to share the changes with students. The teacher did not want to penalize the student unfairly; the student did not want to receive an “incomplete” for the assignment; and I did not want to establish a precedent that would be difficult to maintain.
In the end, we used this meeting as an educational opportunity for the student, and the teacher and I revised plans to deliver even more digital literacy to all middle school students in the coming year — this was a positive result in the face of complex circumstances.
***
Public education has been grappling with the AI issue for several years. As Kate Meyer and Nicole Davis reminded me in their recent book “EduProtocol Field Guide: AI Literacy Edition,” however, we are only limited in our use of AI by the constraints of our imaginations.
There are many reasons one could be optimistic about AI’s application in public schools, but students’ and schools’ relationships to this emerging technology are still very unclear, as evidenced in my anecdote above.
What’s undeniable, though, is that artificial intelligence affects the environment much more than it should. Schools should thus treat AI as what it is: a very expensive, very precious commodity that is not to be misused, squandered or discarded. Casual use of AI in education at this stage is careless use of AI that we can ill afford.
In 2024, the Berkeley Lab projected that AI “hyperscale” data centers would consume 98% of all water used by the sector by 2028. New Yorker contributor Steven Witt noted in his 2025 article that each new AI data center built in the United States is expected to use one gigawatt of electricity per year, which is more than the entire annual energy use of Philadelphia.
According to Noman Bashir of MIT and his colleagues, the global electricity consumption of data centers is expected to reach 800 terawatt hours in 2026, which is more than three times the annual energy use of California.
And while this is a small portion of the overall environmental demands of the United States and globe (according to CBS News, more water is needed to produce one hamburger than to conduct hundreds of AI queries), it is very important to consider. AI and its natural resource usage is part of a critical context concerning energy behaviors. And if there are popular movements to limit red meat consumption (i.e., Meatless Mondays addressing the hamburger problem), a similar standard should be applied to AI in general and in education in particular.
Schools already teach about natural resource conservation and climate change. AI must be a distinct part of that discourse precisely because we do not know how large it will be. When the student described above had used AI so frequently and inefficiently to complete a single assignment, they likely had not considered their environmental impact as much as their desire to produce excellent work.
Our colleagues and communities expect that schools will embrace AI in a manner that is net productive and equips our students with the knowledge and skills to confront a rapidly evolving society. These are large tasks along an uncertain path. In response, we should tread conscientiously on that path, not fearfully.
In accordance with the federal and various worthy state-level AI frameworks on offer, three questions guide my use:
- Am I producing something concrete that will make sense to others and mean something to others?
- Am I producing something durable that will stand the test of time rather than become immediately irrelevant?
- Am I producing something reusable that can be taken offline and into the real world with necessarily needing more AI?
If the AI task satisfies those criteria for me, then the product will satisfy the different human forward frameworks. For students, this means putting in the real work of learning, whether AI is used in the beginning, middle or end stages of a task. No machine or algorithm should be doing the thinking for you.
For teachers, this means generating the core materials (lesson plans, supplemental handouts, differentiated readings), and then using your own professional judgment to create replicable learning experiences for students. Teachers are still the experts; AI is a tool.
For administrators, this means crafting queries carefully the first time and working with colleagues to polish the message. Use efficient prompting to get it right the first time and do the important refining work offline.
And for all of us in public education, this means not demanding pristine, symmetrical perfection from student work. We should be far more interested in work that looks like a young person made it with an authentic combination of time, effort and risk-taking. Let’s let children express themselves through their assignments, even if it involves occasional smudges, curved lines or wrinkled edges.
***
The student whom I met with in that classroom in June had dutifully participated in class, had worked with their peers every day and had wanted to do exceptionally well when they turned to Gemini.
Yet what they learned in that unit overall is of far more importance to me than whether or not the end product sounded like it was written by a generic college student. That polish was worth far less, pedagogically, to their teacher or our school than what it cost to produce environmentally.
AI will become more efficient, and scale will help, but good habits should be developed now. As educators, we must model more effectively as the technology and its potential emerges. Let’s use AI more conscientiously to preserve cognition and the environment at the same time.

title: On cusp of merger, 'Digger bombs for Warner Bros., 'Verity' takes No. 1 at box office
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — On the cusp of the studio’s merger with Paramount, Warner Bros.’ “Digger” flopped in its opening weekend, handing Tom Cruise one of the worst debuts of his career and serving as a bitter final note for Warner Bros. as a standalone studio.
No. 1 in North American theaters instead went to Amazon MGM’s “Verity,” extending the streak for Colleen Hoover adaptations at the box office. It debuted with $32.6 million. The film, directed by Michael Showalter, stars Dakota Johnson as a writer hired to ghostwrite a book series by an incapacitated author (Anne Hathaway).
But all eyes were on how “Digger,” one of the year’s biggest gambles, would perform. Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s critically panned satire grossed a paltry $8 million domestically. Cruise is typically a big draw overseas, but international sales, $12 million from 74 markets, were also weak.
After reviews so bad that Warner Bros. opted to run “decide for yourself” ads, estimates for “Digger” had been revised down over the past week.
It’s a painfully rough start for a movie that cost at least $125 million to make. Reports have pegged the production budget closer to $150 million. The marketing spend is estimated at another $100 million.
“Digger” had been positioned as a potential awards-season heavyweight, dated almost exactly the same as Warner Bros.’ “One Battle After Another” was last year. “Digger” is a similarly politically charged release that handed a large budget to a top filmmaker working from an original story.
But this big swing by Warner Bros. Motion Picture Group co-chairs Michael De Luca and Pam Abdy won’t pay off as well as “One Battle After Another.” It grossed $213.2 million worldwide and, more importantly, won best picture at the Academy Awards.
‘Digger’ flops at a moment of Hollywood transformation
The disappointing opening comes just as Paramount Skydance is closing its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. After U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín on Wednesday approved the $110 billion deal, Paramount said it would close the merger on Tuesday.
In a flush year for Hollywood, Warner Bros. has failed to get one film to $100 million domestically, though its December release, “Dune: Part III,” will easily cross that. De Luca and Abdy are expected to depart Warner Bros. this week. Mass layoffs are anticipated to follow.
“‘Digger’ collapsed this weekend and the new management of the combined Paramount and Warner Bros., David Ellison and Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg, will soon decide what kind of movies they want from WB,” wrote David A. Gross, a film consultant who publishes a newsletter on box office figures. “Paramount does not have a recent history of making big, auteur-driven films like this — that strategy appears to be over and out.”
Critics (51% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes) slammed “Digger” as a strained climate change farce, though Cruise’s over-the-top performance was received more warmly. Audiences agreed, giving it a “C+” CinemaScore.
Cruise has spent most of the last decade starring in “Mission: Impossible” movies and “Top Gun: Maverick,” both franchises that have allowed him to remain a top action hero into his 60s. The 64-year-old’s last major box-office disappointment was 2017’s “The Mummy,” which grossed $409.2 million worldwide on a $195 million budget.
To help sell “Digger,” Cruise pulled out all the stops. He even granted his first lengthy magazine interview in years.
‘Avengers: Endgame’ retakes all-time crown
Last weekend’s top film, “Avengers Endgame: Encore,” slid to seventh place with $4.4 million domestically and $14.4 million overseas. But the Marvel re-release’s second week allowed “Endgame” to just nudge ahead of “Avatar” to reclaim the title of highest grossing film ever, not accounting for inflation. The two films have traded spots in recent years with re-releases. “Endgame” now tallies $2.9255 billion, while “Avatar” has $2.9237 billion.
The rest of the top-sellers in cinemas over the weekend were holdovers: Zach Cregger’s video game adaptation “Resident Evil” for Sony Pictures; Lance Oppenheim’s A24 drama “Primetime,” with Robert Pattinson as “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen; and Paramount’s “Heart of the Beast,” starring Brad Pitt as a retired veteran who treks through the Alaskan wilderness with his combat dog after a plane crash.
In its third week, “Resident Evil” came in second with $12.5 million. “Heart of the Beast” followed with $11 million. And “Primetime” collected $8 million in its second weekend.
Top 10 movies by domestic box office
With final domestic figures being released Monday, this list factors in the estimated ticket sales for Friday through Sunday at U.S. and Canadian theaters, according to Rentrak:
1. “Verity,” $32.6 million.
2. “Resident Evil,” $12.5 million.
3. “Heart of the Beast,” $11 million.
4. “Primetime,” $8 million.
5. “Digger,” $8 million.
6. “Forgotten Island,” $7.2 million.
7. “Avengers: Endgame: Encore,” $4.4 million.
8. “Drishyam: The Conclusion,” $2.7 million.
9. “Practical Magic 2,” $2.7 million.
10. “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” $2.5 million.

title: Western Maine’s beloved oversized load, and a flawless plan to get us off gasoline
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Color me in shades of gloom
If you’re having trouble accepting that summer is really over and that The Bleak Times are upon us, then gentlemen and womenfolk, I give you Monday, Sept. 28. This was a day so dark and dismal, I believe a new shade of gray was created just for the occasion. It was cold outside and it was rainy, but mostly it was that grim shade of gray that really brought forth the full power of seasonal depression. If asked to describe it, I’d say that Monday was the color inside a coffin just before the lid is closed, locking us inside infernal darkness forevermore. This color, Burial Gray, will be offered in the next release of Crayola crayons. Have fun with it!
Oversized load
Much ballyhoooed this week was the shipment of a massive boiler being transported from Jay to South Portland. The regions through which the load was traveling stopped just short of throwing parades to welcome the giant heap. Everyday Joes created expansive maps to reveal the load’s travels through the area, with predicted arrival times and reported sightings of the doohickey. I expect by the time this is done, someone will have named the big heap the way they name hurricanes and snowstorms in these times. Songs may be written about the load and sung in taverns across the land.
Oh, by the way, since the earlier portion of this rant, I’ve named the load “Newman” after Paul Newman and his excellent work in the movie “The Blob.”
The Mangler
This would have been a fine name for our beloved Oversize Load of Western Maine, too, since it bears at least a passing resemblance to the Stephen King story about a giant piece of laundry equipment that tears up its moorings and rumbles off to terrorize villagers. I dunno though, I feel like Paul Newman’s feelings might be hurt if I were to change the name at this juncture.
Gassed
Last week we talked about the fun of standing around a grocery store meat counter and listening to shoppers grumble about the price of meat. If you think that’s fun, open your ears the next time you’re putting gas in your car. New swear words are being invented every day at the gas pumps as the prices continue to reach eye-popping levels. I tell you, if we could find a way to run our cars and trucks on rage alone, we’d never need another drop of gas. Of course, that would put us in good moods and the rage would be gone, so … My plan still needs some work.
Mark LaFlamme is an award-winning Sun Journal reporter and columnist. He’s covered the nighttime police beat since 1994, which is just grand because he doesn’t like getting out of bed before noon. He is the author of eight published novels and rides a dual sport motorcycle everywhere he goes. Unless it’s winter, in which case he just sulks a lot.

title: Don’t let Maine’s candidates take the off ramp on transportation
text:
Here’s a question you should ask people running for office: How will we get there?
Gas, diesel and vehicles are quickly rising in price. In a Gorman Foundation report, 30% of Mainers don’t drive and that number may rise as the affordability of driving come into play. So, it is campaign season and candidates are running for town, state and national offices.
At your door or at any meeting where candidates are available ask them this: What are your thoughts on transportation? How will we manage as our budget for transportation outstrips our income; isn’t support for public transportation necessary?
Please ask these questions while the candidates are running; they need to think long and deeply about how to best serve their constituents. Drivers and non-drivers need thoughtful policies.
Steve Hoad
Windsor

title: Teen accused of mixing toxic chemicals in cafeteria faces attempted murder, terrorism charges
text:
PORTLAND, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - A 15-year-old Oregon high school student accused of mixing toxic chemicals in the school cafeteria is facing attempted murder and terrorism charges.
Portland Police say a Benson Polytechnic High School student brought common household chemicals from home and mixed them in the school cafeteria on Sept. 8 before passing out due to inhaling the toxic gases. Investigators identified the mix as hydrogen sulfide and hydrogen cyanide.
The 15-year-old appeared in court Friday afternoon, facing a first-degree domestic terrorism charge in connection with the incident. Later Friday, the Multnomah County District Attorney’s Office also announced 12 counts of attempted murder.
Teen allegedly linked to violent extremist group ‘764′
Multnomah County Deputy District Attorney Eric Zimmerman said at least seven students and staff needed medical care after the Sept. 8 incident, and more than 100 people were checked at the school that day. He said investigators believe more people could have been harmed.
“It was really confusing. For one second, I’m in class, and I’m eating the school breakfast then next, I’m out on Buckman getting evacuated,” said Benson junior Eva Branstetter.
Zimmerman said surveillance video shows the suspect arriving in gloves and dark clothing and pouring chemicals from a white jug. A search of his home turned up many dangerous chemicals and reactive substances, including materials that can be used in thermite-type mixtures, along with social media posts about making acetone peroxide.
Prosecutors also pointed to social media posts referencing a “kill/death ratio,” along with language about self-harm and wanting to cause death to himself and others.
Benson Vice Principal Joe Metassik said the teen had been a responsible student before but said the impact on students has been “terror,” and it has been hard to get kids to return to school.
Zimmerman said the FBI is reviewing seized papers, hard drives and computers found Friday morning, including what he described as extensive references to “764,” a violent extremist group. He said the review is ongoing.
The state asked that the teen be held at the Donald E. Long county detention center until investigators better understand the full scope and asked that he be taken into custody right away.
Teen needs mental health treatment, defense attorney says
Defense attorney Norah Van Dusen acknowledged the seriousness of the allegations and submitted letters from the teenager’s personal psychiatrist and a psychiatrist at the Perry Center. Both recommend continued psychiatric care.
Van Dusen said the Perry Center is locked and secure with no access to the outside world or social media. She quoted from one letter: “Failure to provide this level of mental health support currently is estimated to come at high risk.”
She said the teen remains at high risk of suicide, has a serious depression diagnosis and is cooperating with treatment but has a long road ahead.
Van Dusen said the teen has strong family support, with his father present in court and visiting daily at the Perry Center. She said he appeared voluntarily, has made no effort to run, has no prior court history and has a stable placement at the Perry Center. She asked that he be released to his father to return to the Perry Center to continue treatment his doctors described as medically necessary.
The teen’s father said the current placement at the Perry Center is best, noting his son is only one week into a program that normally lasts six to eight weeks.
Some parents said they just want whatever gets the 15-year-old the help he needs.
“To me, I just feel like he needs the help, and a program would be better,” said Benson parent Loressa Williams.
“I hope he gets help, and I think that’s the most important thing and he doesn’t hurt himself or others in the future,” said Benson parent Ryan Branstetter.
The judge followed the recommendation from the Juvenile Department and ordered the teen released to his father, with the expectation he return immediately to the Perry Center. Conditions include attending all future hearings, not running away and not leaving the program. The judge set another hearing in about six weeks, after treatment, to decide future custody status.
Prosecutors immediately asked the judge to reconsider. A re-hearing is scheduled for Tuesday afternoon with a circuit court judge.

text:

It was a full Saturday of high school soccer across Aroostook County and beyond, with Katahdin putting together a huge day on both sides of the field, two games requiring double overtime, and several other County teams picking up key wins.

title: Search ongoing for missing medical flight from Bermuda to Boston as crews plan to scour ocean floor
text:
A search continued Sunday off the Massachusetts coast for an air ambulance carrying six people that disappeared during a flight from Bermuda to Boston as authorities planned to comb the seabed floor, the U.S. Coast Guard said.
The Federal Aviation Administration contacted the Coast Guard at 2 a.m. Saturday that it had lost contact with the Gulfstream G100 carrying four Canadians and two Bermudian nationals over the Atlantic Ocean. Searchers later Saturday found a “debris field” off the coast of Nantucket, Coast Guard Northeast District Rear Adm. Matt Lake said at a news conference Sunday.
Coast Guard crews along with the New York National Guard’s Air Rescue Wing and Massachusetts authorities have since searched an area encompassing 2,840 square miles (7,356 square kilometers) using fixed-wing aircraft, helicopters, boats and cutters.
“This is a large and demanding search area,” Lake said.
The depth of the water around the debris field was 80 to 90 feet (about 24 to 27 meters). The Coast Guard was in the process of deploying sonar to search the seabed floor, he said.
The Coast Guard has been updating the next of kin of those aboard the Canadian-registered air ambulance jet with the progress of the search, Lake said.
Weather has not been a factor in the search efforts, said Coast Guard Capt. John McTamney, chief of response for the northeast district.
“We’ll continue to search and saturate the area until we’re at the point where we are confident that if there were any survivors remaining on the surface of the water, we would have found them,” McTamney said.
The plane had four crew members and two passengers aboard when it departed Bermuda’s L.F. Wade International Airport for the nighttime flight to Massachusetts, according to a statement from the Bermuda airport’s operator, Skyport.
Air traffic audio indicates that the plane may have been “coming in blind” when a storm loomed ahead shortly before it vanished.
The pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the jet approached the coast, according to air traffic control audio posted by LiveATC.net. “Roger, you said you’re coming in blind. Is that what you said?” a controller can be heard asking the pilot.
That makes Mary Schiavo, who is a former Inspector General of the Transportation Department, think the plane may have lost its navigational instruments just as a storm moved across its path on radar. The plane also descended sharply from its cruising altitude of around 24,000 feet to around 10,000 feet, according to preliminary data from flight tracking site FlightRadar24.
“Something bad happened with this big drop, and they flew into this big storm. It’s a terrible place to have a loss of your instruments and be flying blind,” said Schiavo, who is an aviation attorney. “It’s very easy to get disoriented and not know if you’re turning, climbing, descending, etc.”
Transport Canada was closely monitoring and working with authorities on search and rescue efforts, the country’s Minister of Transport Steven MacKinnon said on the social platform X.
___
AP Transportation Writer Josh Funk and Associated Press reporter Laura Turbay in Little Rock, Arkansas, a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative, contributed to this report. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: We must hold our leaders accountable for their voting records
text:
There is a lot of sad-sacking going around the Republican campaigns this season. The “woe is me” and “I do not support the consequences of what I voted for” cries can be heard from east to west. And I have nary an iota of sympathy for the whiners.
Not only do adults understand that there are always consequences for one’s actions, but these guys and gals had a blueprint to read from that made it clear President Donald Trump is incapable of not antagonizing important groups of voters, particularly their own constituents, whom they chose to ignore for most of the last 22 months.
Why did Trump et al. lose in 2020? Because he managed to anger one voting bloc after another until there were just too many ticked off voters for him to win.
What is baffling is that seasoned politicians in Washington, D.C., seem incapable of seeing what happened publicly, over and over again, for months during the last year of his first term. And now they want to claim that they were fooled by his banter?
Failing to appreciate the long-term consequences of an action or a vote is not a reasonable excuse for their choices. They must all be held accountable by the voters.
Jenifer Duryea
Limington

title: Sen. Susan Collins responds to Gov. Janet Mills' calls to approve increased LIHEAP funding
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Sen. Susan Collins responds to Gov. Janet Mills' calls to approve increased LIHEAP funding
Sen. Collins says Maine needs alternative options for home heating.
Sen. Susan Collins responds to Gov. Janet Mills' calls to approve increased LIHEAP funding
Sen. Collins says Maine needs alternative options for home heating.
Sen. Susan Collins is supporting Gov. Janet Mills' calls to Congress to approve increased LIHEAP funding.
On Friday, Mills sent a letter to Maine's Congressional Delegation saying current funding is not keeping up with heating oil costs and did not factor in the price increase caused by the war in Iran.
The DOER said Maine consumes more residential heating oil per capita than any other state and significantly more per capita than the five other states in New England. Approximately 50% of all Maine households rely on fuel oil as their primary heat source, although that has declined steadily from a mark of 70% in 2010, according to the DOER. Last year, Maine households received more than $42 million in LIHEAP funding last year.
Sen. Collins has asked the federal government to release the maximum amount of funding for LIHEAP. The Trump administration has proposed zeroing out funding for the program, but Collins has continued her push to increase it. The Senate appropriations committee has pushed to continue funding at more than $4 million this year.
Sen. Collins says Maine needs alternative options for home heating. "I have always thought that we should build a pipeline to bring Shale Gas from Pennsylvania into Maine. Natural gas is cleaner than home heating oil, it is cleaner, and it is a good supplement," she said.
Gov. Mills has urged Mainers who need assistance to apply for the program. Applications opened in August and will stay open until funding is exhausted.

title: Death Notice: Jac Adam Clapp
Squishy toys recalled over potential hazards for children. Here’s how to get a refund
text:
(Gray News) - About 37,000 popular squishy toys sold nationwide were recalled because they potentially pose a deadly hazard to children, according to the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission.
The water beads inside the recalled squishy toys expand larger than permitted by the mandatory safety standard for toys. If a water bead is ingested, it can pose a choking or obstruction hazard inside a child’s body, which can cause severe discomfort, vomiting, dehydration or death.
The recalled squishy toys are dumpling and crazy squib ball toys.
The recalled squishy dumplings are model 3655 and come in multiple translucent colors containing glitter and water beads. The toys have a cartoon face and are packaged in a tan plastic container shaped like a bamboo steamer. “SQUISHY DUMPLING” is printed on the front of the removable package label. There are no markings on the product, other than the cartoon face.
The recalled crazy squib balls are model 3984 and come in multiple translucent colors containing glitter and water beads. The toys are individually wrapped in a white netting. “CRAZY SQUIB BALL” and “Squeeze it! Throw it!” are printed on the front of the package labeling.
Anyone with the recalled squishy toys should stop using them immediately and contact ABC Trading for a full refund.
The recalled toys were sold at ABC Trading stores in Los Angeles and other stores nationwide from April through June 2026 for between 41 cents and $1.25.

title: Death Notice: Margaret “Maggie” (Mahon) Perkins
Death Notice: Susan “Suz” Elizabeth Lamb
Death Notice: Marlene M. O’Leary
Christa Pike’s lawyer says she has not regained consciousness since her failed Tennessee execution
text:
(AP) - Christa Pike has remained unconscious and on a ventilator at a hospital in the four days since her failed execution in Tennessee, and her prognosis might not be known for days more, one of her lawyers said Sunday.
Little has been released about Pike’s condition since Wednesday night’s execution attempt. She has since remained hospitalized under guard as doctors try to get the massive dose of the barbiturate pentobarbital out of her system.
When asked whether she ever regained consciousness after the execution attempt, Assistant Federal Defender Stephen Ferrell, Pike’s lawyer, said on CNN’s “State of the Union”: “Not that I am aware of.”
Lawyer says Pike’s medical decisions are being decided by someone else
Tennessee prison officials gave Pike two doses of the lethal injection drug on Wednesday night. The pentobarbital didn’t kill her, but her lawyers said her arms were burned and blistered from the caustic drugs.
Pike gave someone her medical power of attorney and that person is protecting her privacy, Ferrell said.
“I’m not sure what all they may have told that person,” Ferrell said.
Pike’s attorneys have not identified who is making Pike’s medical decisions. They said they may not know for several more days whether or not she can recover.
“We don’t know right now, and we may never know what sort of torture she endured during that process, where her consciousness was, what physical pain there was — what mental torture she went through,” Ferrell said.
A spokeswoman for Pike’s defense team said in a statement early Sunday that “we appreciate all respect for Christa’s rightful privacy.”
Pike’s lawyer says Tennessee needs to be more open about executions
Pike’s execution was delayed for more than eight hours Wednesday as the U.S. Supreme Court considered, and ultimately overturned, a federal appeals court ruling to halt her lethal injection so judges could thoroughly review whether the jury that sentenced her to death should have considered sexual abuse she said she suffered as a child.
Her attorneys asked a court Friday to order Tennessee prison officials to preserve any written records, communication, images or video from the execution.
Tennessee, like many other states with capital punishment, keeps many details about executions secret from the people involved to details about how the drugs are manufactured or obtained or any tests done on their quality.
“The state of Tennessee has got to start telling its people exactly what it is doing so that in the democratic process, the people of Tennessee can decide if that’s what they want to be done in their name,” Ferrell told CNN.
Tennessee has struggled with executions before
This was the second time this year Tennessee has not been able to execute a prisoner who was seemingly moments away from death. In May, Tennessee stopped the execution of Tony Carruthers after staff placed an IV into his right arm but couldn’t get a secondary IV line.
Commissioner of the Tennessee Department of Correction Frank Strada announced Saturday he was resigning.
Gov. Bill Lee has ordered an independent investigation into the state’s capital punishment system conducted by former U.S. Attorney Ed Stanton. He also reviewed Tennessee’s execution procedures after Lee called off a different execution in 2022 and found the state did not comply with its own lethal injection process.
Prison officials and the Tennessee Attorney General’s Office have said little since Pike was taken to the hospital.
Future of Pike’s death penalty case is unclear
It is unclear what will happen in her death penalty case. Pike’s lawyers have asked the governor to commute her punishment to a life sentence.
“If she recovers, she may not fully recover. And there may be issues about her competence,” Ferrell said.

title: The choice is simple in Maine’s Senate race
text:
This paper has printed several letters that explain why the authors are voting for Susan Collins or Troy Jackson. It is interesting to hear the different perspectives, but when it really comes down to it, this is not about who has more energy or who has done more for the state. It comes down to the fact that our Republican-controlled Congress has done nothing to rein Donald Trump in.
They are allowing him to degrade free speech, massively cash in on the presidency, sell pardons, illegally deport and detain (and kill) innocent people and lie about election fraud. Most strikingly they are allowing him to waste taxpayer dollars on a needless war, ballrooms and arches and on and on.
In my view, Collins (who also no longer appears to have the power of the purse strings in Washington, D.C.) has consistently voted in a way that has allowed Trump’s agenda to move forward. The proof is there for anyone to see. Collins only votes against her party when they do not need her vote for an issue to pass. When they need her, she is right there for them.
A vote for Collins is a clear vote for Trump’s agenda. If people disapprove of what Trump is doing to this country, then they should not be voting for Collins, period. Jackson will call out Trump’s nonsense, something Collins has not been willing to do.
Margaret Duhamel
Woolwich

title: Don’t let Maine’s candidates take the off ramp on transportation
text:
Here’s a question you should ask people running for office: How will we get there?
Gas, diesel and vehicles are quickly rising in price. In a Gorman Foundation report, 30% of Mainers don’t drive and that number may rise as the affordability of driving come into play. So, it is campaign season and candidates are running for town, state and national offices.
At your door or at any meeting where candidates are available ask them this: What are your thoughts on transportation? How will we manage as our budget for transportation outstrips our income; isn’t support for public transportation necessary?
Please ask these questions while the candidates are running; they need to think long and deeply about how to best serve their constituents. Drivers and non-drivers need thoughtful policies.
Steve Hoad
Windsor

title: Quality of life in Maine is high — why do people say it’s getting worse?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The ground was still frozen eight years ago when Maggie Hoffman’s husband came to Bangor for a job interview. They left a charmed and vibrant life in New York, just outside the city, and eventually landed in Hampden, an 18th-century town of 8,000 in Penobscot County with few sidewalks.
In some ways, life is good — the way it should be.
Hoffman marvels at the Cooper’s hawks and the red foxes and the bald eagles circling above the ever-nourishing Penobscot River.
“Look, I got to learn how to pee in the woods when I came to Maine,” she said.
The Maine Trust for Local News partnered with the Siena Research Institute to survey 824 residents and take a snapshot of life in Maine. Although three out of four respondents described an overall positive quality of life, only 20% said life in the Pine Tree State is getting better or much better.
And 38% said life is getting worse or much worse — that’s more than double the share of people nationally who said things are getting worse in their communities, according to polling Siena conducted last year.
Mainers are more likely to feel safe and secure in their home than the average American. The state’s outdoor spaces, as Hoffman noted, as well as its schools (particularly higher education) and sense of community scored highly.
But they say healthcare is hard to find, housing costs are high and the likelihood a young person will get a job with opportunity for advancement is low. All of that contributes to the disproportionately high number of people feeling that things are getting worse.
“I haven’t seen anybody really doing anything toward fixing any of those problems,” said Justin Crockett, who grew up in Franklin County and is worried about the high cost of living and the scourge of drug addiction.
It’s not surprising to Bill Nemitz, a retired journalist who for decades wrote a column for the Portland Press Herald/Maine Sunday Telegram, that Mainers are simultaneously fond about the place they live and yet pessimistic about its future.
“Maine has always had a really strong self identity of — the slogan says it all — ‘the way life should be.’ And I think Mainers have always taken pride in that,” Nemitz said.
It’s a state with a tempered resistance to change.
With the deluge of thousands of new-comers who have moved to Maine since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, change can feel inevitable.
And, Nemitz added, it’s difficult to look at the contours and trend lines of the world “and not feel a tinge of pessimism.”
“The fact that Mainers feel that way more strongly, perhaps, than other people in the country might be reflective of the fact that they value what they have so dearly,” he said.
It’s not all pine trees and soaring raptors for the Hoffmans either.
Their 38-year-old son, Jake, lives at home and has developmental and intellectual disabilities. He is a rock music aficionado and a dog whisperer, his mom said, but requires a high level of support. Finding caretakers who can help meet Jake’s needs is increasingly difficult. Maggie blames the high cost of living and childcare, and the lack of affordable housing.
“I believe that our scarcest resource are human beings, and that we’re really forgetting what we need to do to keep Maine alive,” she said. “What are we, 1.4 million people in this vastness of beautiful forestry and great waters, and people can’t live here?”
JUMPING TO HELP OUT
When his neighbor fell and broke her arm, Joel Katz brought over a healthy portion of potato leek soup.
That’s the way their community on the Blue Hill peninsula in Hancock County works, he said.
As Katz, 74, considers what he loves about living in Maine, his neighbors come to mind first. “The people we live around are just outstanding,” he said.
Down East, 52% of those polled said that quality of life, lifestyle and sense of community was the No. 1 best thing about their life in Maine, and 46% said the same statewide.
Katz moved to Maine full time when he retired a decade ago from a career leading performing arts centers, but has lived on and off in the state for 41 years. He was the first executive director of UMaine’s Center for the Arts, now known as the Collins Center for the Arts.
In the last decade, Katz and his wife have taken up some typical pastimes of the retired: they garden, for both flowers and food; on Mondays, he’s part of a team of that delivers soup to about a hundred residents of the peninsula; and on Thursdays he volunteers at the Tree of Life Food Pantry.
He’s found a community in Penobscot unlike anything he’s ever seen before.
The way life should be, for a long time, evoked the way in which life in Maine was different from other places, said Bill Green, the retired TV reporter who hosted “Bill Green’s Maine,” a program about Maine’s outdoors.
Mainers’ sense of community identity becomes “really the glue that binds this state together through thick and thin,” added Nemitz, the former columnist.
“Day to day, you can go to Hannaford, you can go to the hardware store, and, like, people really are nice to each other, and that’s something to celebrate,” said Hoffman, of Hampden.
Patricia Smith, a Lewiston resident, raised her son in Buxton and always appreciated the little things, like how neighbors check on each other during storms and power outages, or her landlord hiring the 8th grader down the block to mow the lawn.
“What we need is that type of community support,” Smith, 63, said.
NO SMALL PRICE: MAINE’S RISING COST OF LIVING
Katz is fortunate, he recognizes, to have stable housing and a reliable way to feed himself.
But with the costs soaring, he and his wife have opted to forgo some luxuries of retirement: a trip to Europe is off the table right now; the couple is waiting on a plan to add a second utility room to their 1,000-square-foot home; and they’ve put off adding solar panels to the house since the tax credits dried up.
“We don’t think it’s wise to spend our reserves,” Katz said. “We plan to live a little longer and we don’t know what’s going to happen, quite frankly.”
More than any other issue, Mainers surveyed said affordability was the worst thing about living here.
At the food pantry and thrift shop where he and his wife volunteer, there’s been a sharp increase in the number of people walking through the door.
“The rich have been doing very well, and the poor even worse,” Katz said.
Down East, the rising cost of fuel and bait has slimmed profit margins in Washington County’s $100-million commercial fishing industry, said Charles Rudelitch, executive director of the Sunrise County Economic Council.
Diminished services, the dearth of emergency medical care and specialists chief among them, makes the rural county a hard sell for those looking to settle long term. The median home price in Washington County has more than doubled in the last decade, while wages have only risen 54%. That said, it’s still one of the more affordable places to live in the state.
But what it giveth in housing, it taketh away in jobs, said Sean Thomas, who moved to Calais four years ago from Brockton, Massachusetts.
“It’s taken me a long time to get established in having enough work,” he said. “I was under-employed for a long, long time.”
Thomas was among those who said things were getting somewhat worse. He also quite likes living in Maine.
“Calais reminds me of when I was a kid,” he said, adding, “It’s a bit like stepping back in time.”
In Maine, 32% of those polled said a young person in their community was likely to find a job with opportunity for advancement and 27% said it was unlikely, while 39% said it was a tossup. Down East, a third of respondents thought it was unlikely.
Now, Thomas works as a janitor cleaning a supermarket and office buildings a few nights per week. He got another part-time job, but it meant his Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits were cut “down to nothing.”
At 57, starting over in a small town, it’s hard to see how he might move up, professionally speaking.
The Woodland Pulp Mill, in Baileyville, is Washington County’s largest employer and is considered the county’s economic anchor. It’s the kind of place where employees can work for decades.
But those large-scale economic development projects are few and far between these days, Rudelitch said, given that political opposition can threaten a project and scare off investors. It’s hard to find the community consensus needed to swallow the downsides of something like that — the blows it could strike to quality of life and the environment, for example.
Rudelitch can envision a world in which rural Maine resembles something of its past: a place with economic opportunity where people want to move to start a family.
“But it’s hard to really imagine how that would actually happen right now,” he said.
NATURE: ‘THE GREATEST THING EVER’
Justin Crockett’s ancestors landed in Kittery in the mid-1600s and they never left.
“Every grandfather I ever had from that time until present day lived and died in the state of Maine,” he said.
Now 44 with two teenage kids of his own, Crockett isn’t sure he wants his grandchildren to grow up in Maine.
He was raised in a small town in Franklin County and now lives in central Maine. Crockett left 25 years ago to join the Air Force and returned in 2022, stunned by what he described as the state’s 180-degree turn for the worse.
Four childhood friends have died from drug overdoses, including one last winter. The sawmills buzzing in his hometown when he left are all gone and the quality of public education has dropped precipitously.
“How much worse is this drug problem going to get? How much worse is the housing crisis going to get?” Crockett said.
He, along with Smith, the Lewiston resident, were among the small minority of poll respondents who felt that crime and public safety were major problems in Maine, and it contributed to their perception that things were getting much worse.
It’s when he’s alone in the woods, hunting and watching the seasons change, that Crockett is reminded of why he loves Maine.
He and Hoffman, the New York transplant, are unlikely to agree on much, at least politically. But on this, they, and many others, stand on common ground.
Some 69% of respondents said the quality of the environment was better than in other places they’ve lived or know. Nature and the environment was the second-most popular pick (22%) when respondents were asked about the best thing in their community.
“If you want to go out and grasp the goodness of Maine, you can still do it,” said Green, the retired local TV personality.
Maine has vast forest lands and craggy coastlines, and ample opportunity to play and hunt and even make a living.
“It’s just the greatest thing ever, being out in nature,” Hoffman said.
Mainers say it’s a large part of what makes life here the way it should be.
And because Maine is a place where your neighbors will bring you soup.
Reuben M. Schafir is a Report for America corps member who writes about Indigenous and rural communities for the Portland Press Herald.

title: Replica Oval Office near White House given Trump makeover: New additions for viewers
text:
Replica Oval Office near White House given Trump makeover: New additions for viewers
It's glitzier. And there's way more gold.
The People's House museum exhibit has overhauled its replica Oval Office for visitors to experience President Donald Trump's second-term design choices.
Related video: Supreme Court allows ballroom project to continue for now
Gleaming vases, golden-hued swirling onlays, two dozen portraits in heavy gilded frames and knickknacks crowding nearly every available surface: the same rococo flourishes that Trump has installed in the world's most famous workspace have been recreated down to each wall appliqué in a museum just up Pennsylvania Avenue from the White House.
"As political as the Oval Office is, it really is also the office of the American people," said Luke Boorady, managing director of The People's House: A White House Experience. "And we want visitors who come here to feel more connected to this space."
Public tours of the White House do not include the West Wing. So the White House Historical Association set about recreating the Oval Office, opening the exhibit in September 2024. It is the same size as the real one, and visitors often marvel at how small it feels.
A team of specialized designers has been making over the exhibit, visiting Trump's Oval Office while the Republican president was away. Experts in North Carolina worked to recreate Trump's many wall appliqués, while one from Indianapolis handled 3D scanning and printing of other specialized objects. California frame-makers did carving by hand for the gold frames of Trump's chosen 24 portraits, and teams from Canada and Virginia worked on replicas of vases and other tabletop pieces, Boorady said.
There are also two mirrors and a copy of the Declaration of Independence, just like in Trump's actual office.
A real estate developer before he became a politician, Trump has revamped the White House to his extravagant tastes as part of his push to leave his mark on the nation's capital while he is still in office.
When asked by Time magazine last week what he would miss most about the White House after he leaves, Trump said, "This beautiful room that nobody should be allowed to rip down. The Oval Office." He said he had asked his chief of staff to make his altered office "a federal landmark."
In addition to filling the Oval Office with bling, Trump paved over the lawn near the Rose Garden to build a patio space reminiscent of the one at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida. He installed a row of presidential portraits along the colonnade between the White House residence and the West Wing.
He erected towering flagpoles on the North and South lawns, renovated the Palm Room and the bathroom that is part of the famous Lincoln Bedroom and ordered restoration work of the North Portico's front columns.
But Trump seems proudest of the $400 million ballroom that he is building after ordering that the East Wing be demolished. "It relaxes me, actually," the president said about the ballroom project during an unrelated event last week.
Trump's sense of ownership of the White House is now such that while recently defending his attempt to ban CNN, MS Now and Politico from its grounds, the president had a momentary slip of the tongue. "I don't have to let them into my — into the people's house," he said.
When the White House Historical Association first opened its Oval Office duplicate, it mirrored Democratic President Joe Biden's design. After the 2024 election, the association updated the exhibit to match Trump's first-term style.
Last week, a crew of 25 people worked from early Monday through late Friday to get the second-term transformation ready, making the finishing touches on Saturday.
Boorady said Biden was the first president to hang double layers of portraits over the Oval Office fireplace. Trump has expanded that all around the room, stacking the walls with portraits including those of George Washington, Andrew Jackson and Benjamin Franklin.
In the real Oval Office, the colors are made more brilliant by using gilded gold leaf. In the replica, crews used a paint solution. Boorady said they did not use gold leaf to protect against chipping or other wear-and-tear from visitors moving through the area.
Trump was once spotted using superglue to try to affix gold ornaments to the Oval Office fireplace, according to Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan in their book "Regime Change."
But no superglue was needed in the replica office. Crews used laser levels and temporary adhesive to fix items to the walls, checking their work for accuracy against renderings of the actual office before nailing many adornments to the walls.
There are many things in Trump's Oval Office that have stood the test of time: a beige-patterned rug from the Ronald Reagan era, gold draperies from Bill Clinton's tenure, and couches and chairs from the George W. Bush White House.
Of course there is a copy of the Resolute Desk. Visitors to the People's House are allowed to sit in the chairs and behind the replicated desk, which Trump and most presidents have used since it was gifted to President Rutherford B. Hayes in 1880.
The White House Historical Association declined to say how much remaking the replica Oval Office cost. The organization, created in 1961 by first lady Jacqueline Kennedy, receives no government funding, and raises money through private donations and sales of retail merchandise.
Trump briefly stopped by its gift shop during an unannounced visit to the People's House in August 2025. Asked whether Trump would come for a personal peek at his newly replicated workspace, Boorady replied, "I don't know" before adding that he is "always welcome."

title: We must hold our leaders accountable for their voting records
text:
There is a lot of sad-sacking going around the Republican campaigns this season. The “woe is me” and “I do not support the consequences of what I voted for” cries can be heard from east to west. And I have nary an iota of sympathy for the whiners.
Not only do adults understand that there are always consequences for one’s actions, but these guys and gals had a blueprint to read from that made it clear President Donald Trump is incapable of not antagonizing important groups of voters, particularly their own constituents, whom they chose to ignore for most of the last 22 months.
Why did Trump et al. lose in 2020? Because he managed to anger one voting bloc after another until there were just too many ticked off voters for him to win.
What is baffling is that seasoned politicians in Washington, D.C., seem incapable of seeing what happened publicly, over and over again, for months during the last year of his first term. And now they want to claim that they were fooled by his banter?
Failing to appreciate the long-term consequences of an action or a vote is not a reasonable excuse for their choices. They must all be held accountable by the voters.
Jenifer Duryea
Limington

title: Death Notice: Monique Juliette Nadeau
‘Avengers: Endgame’ Is Once Again the Highest-Grossing Movie Ever
text:
‘Avengers: Endgame’ Is Once Again the Highest-Grossing Movie in History
Avengers: Endgame’s encore in theaters has made it the biggest film of all-time ... again.
After a second weekend in theaters, Avengers Endgame: Encore — a re-release of Marvel’s massive 2019 blockbuster ith some new post-credits footage and teases for the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday — has brought its worldwide box-office total to $2.925 billion. That makes it the #1 film on the all-time box office chart. The previous record holder was James Cameron’s Avatar, which has earned $2.923 billion worldwide.
Those two films have traded the top spot on that all-time chart back and forth since Endgame first debuted in theaters in 2019. Endgame passed Avatar seven years ago, but then Avatar had its own re-release (Avatar: Encore?) that coincided with the of Avatar: The Way of Water in 2022, earning enough in that re-release to reclaim the number one slot on that all-time chart.
READ MORE: The Single Best Scene in Avengers: Endgame
Both franchises are now controlled by Disney, so whichever of the two movies is #1, Disney remains the undisputed box-office champ.
Avengers is one of the most successful franchises in the history of movies. Every single one of its films has earned more than $1 billion worldwide; its lowest-grosisng entry, 2015’s Avengers: Age of Ultron, still earned over $1.39 billion at the box office.
The franchise’s next film, Avengers: Doomsday, opens in theaters on December 18. Will it have what it takes to top Endgame and Avatar? Based on the early trailers, I kind of doubt. it. But then, few experts predicted Avatar: The Way of Water would become nearly as massive as the first Avatar.
And Marvel’s movies have topped themselves over and over; just a few months ago Spider-Man: Brand New Day became the biggest film in history in the United States. So who’s to say Doomsday can’t make history for Marvel all over again?

title: Frozen berries sold at Walmart and Trader Joe’s recalled. Here’s what to know
text:
(Gray News) - Frozen berries sold at Walmart and Trader Joe’s have been recalled because they may be contaminated with E. coli, according to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.
Packages of Great Value brand frozen organic blueberries and frozen organic Triple Berry Blend have been recalled. They were sold in 10-ounce bags at Walmart stores in 30 states. Also recalled are packages of Trader Joe’s frozen organic Mixed Berry Blend.
The Great Value frozen blueberries have a UPC code of 7874211213 and lot codes of 6 019 01, 6 040 01 and 6 163 01. They also have best if used by dates of Jan. 19, 2028; Feb. 9, 2028; and June 12, 2028.
The Great Value Triple Berry Blend contains strawberries, blackberries and blueberries. These packages have a UPC code of 7874211226 and lot codes of 6 031 01 and 6 041 01. They have best if used by dates of Jan. 31, 2028, and Feb. 10, 2028.
The affected states are Alabama, Arkansas, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Nebraska, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia, West Virginia and Wisconsin as well as Puerto Rico.
The Trader Joe’s Mixed Berry Blend includes strawberries, blackberries, blueberries and raspberries. It was sold in 12-ounce packages at stores in 26 states. The recalled products have a UPC code of 00977654, a lot code of 6 051 01 and a best before date of Feb. 20, 2028.
The affected states are Alabama, Arkansas, Colorado, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia and Wisconsin as well as the District of Columbia.
Anyone who bought the recalled products should not eat them but instead throw them away or return them to the store for a full refund.
Those with questions may contact Comfrut through email at Info.foodsafety@comfrut.com or by calling 336-899-5612 on weekdays from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. Eastern.
This recall is related to a larger recall of frozen organic blueberries produced and sold by Frutas y Hortalizas del Sur S.A. of San Carlos, Chile. The FDA says a total of 17 people were infected with E. coli. between May and August 2026, including six who were hospitalized.
An E. coli infection can cause severe stomach cramps, diarrhea and vomiting. Some infections may result in a serious complication known as hemolytic uremic syndrome, particularly in young children, older adults and those with weakened immune systems.

title: 1 dead, 2 injured after downtown Las Vegas shooting
text:
LAS VEGAS (FOX5/Gray News) — One person is dead, and two others are injured after a shooting during First Friday in downtown Las Vegas Friday night.
According to a Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department press release, officers were in the area of South Main Street and West Charleston Boulevard at approximately 10:17 p.m. on Oct. 2 when they heard shots being fired.
Officers ran into a crowd and located two people suffering from apparent gunshot wounds. Additional officers located a third victim. All three were transported to a nearby hospital, where one person was pronounced deceased.
In an overnight briefing, LVMPD homicide Lt. Robert Price said the two other victims have non-life-threatening injuries.
Detectives determined a physical altercation occurred between several individuals. At some point, an unknown male produced a firearm and began shooting, striking multiple people, police said. The suspect fled prior to officers arriving.
The First Friday Foundation said it is heartbroken, grateful for Metro’s swift response, and will provide a response on future events before planning or announcing any future events.
“Very unfortunately, we are heartbroken to confirm the incident during tonight’s event involving a shooting/gunfire and a reported 3 injuries in the vicinity of the event in its last minutes. We are grateful for Las Vegas Metro’s swift response to the situation, and are devastated by the impact of this tragic event for everyone who was affected. As we navigate waiting for all the details so we can fully understand and process what happened, please know we are committed to doing everything we can in identifying the most thorough and appropriate response possible which we will provide before the planning or announcement of any future events. In the meantime, please support the community’s local artists, vendors, musicians, and attendees during this difficult time.”
The Arts District Neighborhood Association said it is deeply saddened and that they will work to help make First Friday safer moving forward.
Mayor Pro Tem Olivia Diaz expressed her sympathy with the victims and attendees from the First Friday shooting.
The LVMPD Homicide Section is leading the investigation. The identification of the decedent, as well as the cause and manner of death, will be released by the Clark County Coroner’s Office.

title: Obituary: Atwood Packard “Woody” Dunham Jr.
text:
FREEPORT – Atwood Packard “Woody” Dunham, Jr., a devoted educator, veteran, and loving family man, passed away peacefully, with his family at his side, at Horizons in Brunswick, Maine on Sept. 27, 2026, at the age of 95.
Born on March 10, 1931, in Brockton, Mass. to Atwood Packard Dunham, Sr. and Edna Foye Dunham, Woody lived a life defined by a sense of duty and purpose.
As a young man, immediately after graduating from Wesleyan University in 1953, he answered the call to serve his country by enlisting in the U.S. Air Force during the Korean War. During his military service in Korea, he discovered his lifelong calling. Recognizing the potential in his fellow airmen, Woody dedicated much time to tutoring them, helping them prepare for and pass career-enhancing examinations. He also taught mathematics to local Koreans working on base. This experience sparked a deep realization within him: education was not only a tool to uplift individuals, but it was also the very foundation of a strong, enduring society.
Following his honorable discharge, Woody returned to school to pursue his passion for learning, first at Boston University where he received his Masters of Education in 1958. He then began his teaching journey in Mount Kisco, N.Y., returning summers to Wesleyan University for the Graduate Liberal Studies Program in mathematics, graduating in 1967. It was during this chapter of his life that he met the absolute love of his life, Marilyn. They married and ultimately settled in Wellesley, Mass. where they raised their children and enjoyed a life rich with family, friends, work and civic responsibility. The two were married for over 60 years, exemplifying a beautiful devotion that truly defined the vow “until death do us part.”
Woody’s distinguished career as an educator spanned from the early 1960s until his retirement in 1993. After teaching in Mount Kisco, he found his long-term professional home at Newton North High School in Newton, Mass. There, he inspired students as a dedicated Math teacher and later expanded his impact on the school community as an Administrative Principal. He believed fiercely that America is an ongoing work in progress, and that a robust education system is critical to sustaining and strengthening our democracy.
Outside the classroom and office, Woody felt a deep connection to nature and the elements. He loved sailing, finding immense peace and freedom out on the ocean. When on land, he could often be found tending his garden in a ripped old tee shirt, more holes than shirt, with the Red Sox blasting from an old radio. Cultivating the soil reminded him of the “Victory Gardens” of his youth, serving as a quiet, lifelong symbol of his enduring patriotism, patience, and work ethic.
Woody and Marilyn moved to Freeport, full time upon his retirement, enjoying much time with family and friends, traveling, including multiple trips to Italy, and many activities and organizations as Friends of Bowdoin College where Woody audited every Italian class available and joined an Italian Group with whom he continued to meet through the last weeks of his life. Woody was also a member of the Old Stone Post Investment Club, the Harraseeket Yacht Club and the South Freeport Congregational Church.
Woody was preceded in death by his beloved wife, Marilyn; his parents; and his sisters Ann Dunham Woodward and Mary Dunham Scott.
He is survived by his children Margaret “Meg” (Gregory) and Jonathan “Jon” (Rebecca); and five grandchildren, who will strive to carry forward his ideals.
An interment and memorial service will be held at a later date. Further details will be shared by the family. Arrangements and guidance are under the direction of Stetson’s Funeral Home, 12 Federal St., Brunswick. Condolences, memories and photos may be shared with the family by visiting the Stetson’s Funeral Home website http://www.StetsonFuneralHome.com .
In lieu of flowers, the family kindly requests that you consider making a contribution to a charity of your choice that focuses on educating youth or strengthening democratic institutions, honoring Woody’s lifelong belief in the power of knowledge and civic duty.

title: A familiar figure, a new voice: Meryl Streep's Aslan stirs gender debate over Gerwig's ‘Narnia’
text:
The public hasn’t viewed a single frame yet from director Greta Gerwig’s movie adaptation from the classic children’s book series, “The Chronicles of Narnia,” but a casting decision is already generating outrage from many conservative Christian commentators.
They’re distressed by news that a female actor — the Oscar-winning Meryl Streep — will be voicing the role of Aslan the lion in “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew.” Aslan is considered a literary representation of Jesus Christ in the seven Narnia books by British Christian author C.S. Lewis, published in the 1950s. The books depict the lion as male, with a glorious mane.
Filmmakers routinely take license in adapting books — compressing timelines, combining characters and more. Gerwig herself is resetting “The Magician’s Nephew” from around 1900 to the 1950s.
The casting of Streep doesn’t necessarily mean that Aslan will be depicted as female. But to conservative Christian critics, even the possibility of portraying a divine Christ figure as anything but male goes beyond artistic license. They deem it an attack on their faith, noting that the Bible and ancient creeds speak of God the Father and Jesus as the Son of God.
“This is a well-known ploy of the enemies of God, to subvert and destroy symbols of Christianity in an effort to win a war of attrition for the heart of the culture,” wrote Seth Udinsky in a column for the Christian Post, an evangelical news website. He contended that Gerwig is turning Aslan “transgender,” citing a newly released photo from the movie’s promoters, depicting the lion with rainbow-tinted whiskers.
Similar comments, and rebuttals, appear in numerous replies to Netflix’s posting about the casting on Instagram.
Some Lewis scholars and aficionados are taking a wait-and-see approach. The Netflix production is scheduled for theatrical release in February.
Kat Coffin, a New York-based writer and scholar of Lewis, said she has questions about the casting decision but added: “I am far more disturbed by the people who are violently opposed and angry at the idea that the incarnation of God could be anything even hinted toward feminine.”
Gerwig wanted a ‘profound but not pretentious’ voice
Gerwig, in public statements, hasn’t addressed the gender question directly, but did say she saw Streep as one of the few actors who could meet her criteria for Aslan’s voice.
“I wanted someone who was profound but not pretentious, who had gravitas but not morose self-seriousness,” Gerwig said. “Someone who could communicate depth and pathos as well as joy and delight. I wanted someone who was older than 70, so there was a wisdom of experience, but who also had the capacity of fresh wonder, like a child. And also to be one of the greatest actors to ever do it.”
Gerwig said she first read “The Magician’s Nephew” as a child, falling in love with the story and its enchanted world.
Gerwig is known for bringing feminist interpretations to her acclaimed movies “Barbie” and “Little Women,” also based on intellectual properties that have long been popular with children.
Further raising hackles is a report in the movie magazine Empire that Gerwig took inspiration from the pop artist David Bowie, known for his gender ambiguity, in depicting the lion with different-colored eyes and “bold red-striped visage.”
“The Magician’s Nephew” — published in 1955, eight years before Lewis’ death — tells the story of two children, Digory and Polly, who are sent to parallel worlds by evil magic. They ultimately arrive in the newly created, fantastical land of Narnia, but they inadvertently bring with them the evil witch, Jadis. In this and subsequent Narnia books, Aslan leads his young followers in combating and defeating evil.
Critic says Gospel themes can’t be treated like ‘The Odyssey’
For Ted Baehr, having a woman portray Aslan is a direct challenge to Christian doctrine on the nature of God.
Baehr is founder and publisher of Movieguide, which advises Christian parents on what to watch.
“This movie could do very well, but the better it does, there’s a lot of Christians who will be concerned for their children and grandchildren,” said Baehr, who led a company that produced a 1979 animated television version of another Narnia book.
Baehr praised Gerwig’s directing skills but said she may not understand the issue’s importance to many Christians. While Lewis said his Narnia books are not allegories, they do closely parallel biblical stories and concepts. Baehr said they can’t be adapted as readily as the recent Christopher Nolan movie “The Odyssey” did with Greek myth.
“The Gospel is not a myth,” he said.
The criticisms reflect the deep bond that many Christians, particularly evangelicals, feel with Lewis, who promoted Christian teachings and themes through fiction and nonfiction.
Narnia has a broad reader base, with reported sales of 120 million books worldwide since the first volume’s publication 75 years ago this month. Its Christian readers feel a particular sense of ownership.
“I know a lot of people who are genuinely concerned, because the original stories mean so much to them,” said Christin Ditchfield Lazo, an author of books on Lewis.
The Narnia series has “had a profound impact on the lives of millions of people — especially people of faith, who love the spiritual truths in these stories and want them to be faithfully represented,” she said.
Ditchfield Lazo urged Christians to reserve judgment.
“There’s a huge difference between a woman voicing a male character and the director changing the gender of the character,” she said. “It could be problematic, but we won’t know until we see the film.”
She noted that men and women have often played or voiced each others’ roles, from Shakespearean drama to modern animations.
Lewis family statement supports Gerwig’s work
Many evangelicals did embrace the early 2000s movies based on the first three Narnia books, with actor Liam Neeson providing the deep, masculine voice of Aslan.
Coffin said that God has been portrayed with feminine characteristics in other literary works — including Narnia itself, where Aslan also appears as a lamb with a “sweet milky voice.”
“I would describe that as a feminine presentation,” Coffin said.
A statement from the family of Lewis’ late wife, Joy Davidman Gresham, praised Gerwig for her “sincere passion” for the Narnia works.
“We saw this enthusiasm during our visit to the set in London,” said the statement, provided by Netflix. “We are thrilled to be working with such a talented and accomplished director and production team, and are keen to continue working with them on future projects.”
The C.S. Lewis Co. — holders of Lewis intellectual property rights and producers on the film — stated: “It’s incredibly moving to see how deeply Greta Gerwig has embraced C.S. Lewis’ world, and infused ‘Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew’ with joy, heart, and genuine love for the story.”

title: Auburn’s school investment in music gets the band together at Edward Little
text:
Bill Buzza has taught music for 34 years, with 14 of those years at Edward Little High School in Auburn.
In his entire time teaching, Buzza has never had as many students in his concert band class than he has now. The elective class has 54 students, which is up more than 20 students from last year.
Additionally, the Pep Band, which performs for high school football games and pep rallies, has around 24 students, nearly 10 more students than usual.
Buzza credits it to the Auburn School Department’s support for music education.
“It’s been a big investment,” he said. “It shows the kids we value what they are doing and also, through the town supporting it with their tax dollars, it shows that it’s a priority,” he said.
Edward Little High School has a strong foundation in music and performing arts, Buzza said.
In 2024, the Donald M. Gay Performing Arts Center opened at Edward Little High School, and The National Association of Music Merchants has recognized The Auburn School Department as one of the best communities for music education over the last two years. It’s based on factors that include the department’s music budget, school facilities, and graduation requirements.
But before that, the program suffered around the time of the pandemic.
The department saw a drop off in students interested in band, likely because of the restraints in place, like having to wear a specific mask with a mouth hole to play wind instruments and having to teach, play and learn instruction over Zoom. The students lost interest, Buzza said.
The school department’s music teachers were asked what they could do to bring the passion back to students. At the time, Buzza was one of two band teachers in the district, with the other an elementary and middle school teacher who bounced around between schools.
So in 2022, they added a position for an elementary-level band teacher.
“We believe in the value of music education and the importance of investing in a strong music program for our students,” Superintendent Sue Dorris said. “The strength of Auburn’s program comes from our dedicated educators, our talented students, and the support of our families and community.
“It’s exciting to see that the shared commitment reflected in the growing number of students choosing to participate.”
Hiring an additional teacher has allowed the school department to have a band teacher at each school level and gives the teachers the chance to spend more time with students.
“We started seeing growth immediately,” Buzza said. “Now we are seeing it trickle through the high school.”
All concert band students perform yearly for the elementary schools, and Buzza found that the performance usually sparks student interest in joining the concert band once they enter high school.
At Edward Little High School and the middle school, concert band is an elective that students opt into. In the earlier grades, all elementary students have music class, but they can choose to play an instrument through band if they want.
Pep Band is another option for students in concert band at Edward Little High School.
Buzza is delighted to see the band’s growth. From a musical perspective, it sounds better.
He’s also happy to see students play instruments at a time where most are plugged into their phones. Playing an instrument connects students with their entire brain, he said, and helps them learn how to problem-solve and develop discipline through practice, and it gives them a sense of community.
“We are seeing enthusiasm in kids. Being unplugged is great,” Buzza said. “When we are plugged in, we are unplugged from other people. Now, we are seeing them interact and supporting each other and seeing them work on common goals.”

title: Suspect in fatal Wells hit-and-run facing charges
text:
An Atkinson, N.H., man was arrested Sunday morning and is facing charges in connection with a fatal hit-and-run on Route 1 in Wells that occurred in March, according to a news release from the Maine State Police.
