title: How Maine’s schools need to be approaching AI
text:
Joseph Hennessey, MSEd, is an educator who has served in classroom and building-level leadership roles, most recently in central Maine. He was the 2018 Piscataquis County Teacher of the Year, the 2019 Maine Teacher of the Year, the 2020 National University Teacher of the Year for Maine and is currently an American Service Fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School of Government.
Toward the end of the last school year, I sat with a middle school teacher and her student in the classroom to address misuse of AI on an important assignment. Were Google and Gemini (Google’s AI assistant) really different forms of sources? How much “assistance” from AI qualified as too much, at this developmental level, in this content area, at this juncture in history?
Our district’s acceptable use policy had been provisionally updated, but we had not yet had time to share the changes with students. The teacher did not want to penalize the student unfairly; the student did not want to receive an “incomplete” for the assignment; and I did not want to establish a precedent that would be difficult to maintain.
In the end, we used this meeting as an educational opportunity for the student, and the teacher and I revised plans to deliver even more digital literacy to all middle school students in the coming year — this was a positive result in the face of complex circumstances.
***
Public education has been grappling with the AI issue for several years. As Kate Meyer and Nicole Davis reminded me in their recent book “EduProtocol Field Guide: AI Literacy Edition,” however, we are only limited in our use of AI by the constraints of our imaginations.
There are many reasons one could be optimistic about AI’s application in public schools, but students’ and schools’ relationships to this emerging technology are still very unclear, as evidenced in my anecdote above.
What’s undeniable, though, is that artificial intelligence affects the environment much more than it should. Schools should thus treat AI as what it is: a very expensive, very precious commodity that is not to be misused, squandered or discarded. Casual use of AI in education at this stage is careless use of AI that we can ill afford.
In 2024, the Berkeley Lab projected that AI “hyperscale” data centers would consume 98% of all water used by the sector by 2028. New Yorker contributor Steven Witt noted in his 2025 article that each new AI data center built in the United States is expected to use one gigawatt of electricity per year, which is more than the entire annual energy use of Philadelphia.
According to Noman Bashir of MIT and his colleagues, the global electricity consumption of data centers is expected to reach 800 terawatt hours in 2026, which is more than three times the annual energy use of California.
And while this is a small portion of the overall environmental demands of the United States and globe (according to CBS News, more water is needed to produce one hamburger than to conduct hundreds of AI queries), it is very important to consider. AI and its natural resource usage is part of a critical context concerning energy behaviors. And if there are popular movements to limit red meat consumption (i.e., Meatless Mondays addressing the hamburger problem), a similar standard should be applied to AI in general and in education in particular.
Schools already teach about natural resource conservation and climate change. AI must be a distinct part of that discourse precisely because we do not know how large it will be. When the student described above had used AI so frequently and inefficiently to complete a single assignment, they likely had not considered their environmental impact as much as their desire to produce excellent work.
Our colleagues and communities expect that schools will embrace AI in a manner that is net productive and equips our students with the knowledge and skills to confront a rapidly evolving society. These are large tasks along an uncertain path. In response, we should tread conscientiously on that path, not fearfully.
In accordance with the federal and various worthy state-level AI frameworks on offer, three questions guide my use:
- Am I producing something concrete that will make sense to others and mean something to others?
- Am I producing something durable that will stand the test of time rather than become immediately irrelevant?
- Am I producing something reusable that can be taken offline and into the real world with necessarily needing more AI?
If the AI task satisfies those criteria for me, then the product will satisfy the different human forward frameworks. For students, this means putting in the real work of learning, whether AI is used in the beginning, middle or end stages of a task. No machine or algorithm should be doing the thinking for you.
For teachers, this means generating the core materials (lesson plans, supplemental handouts, differentiated readings), and then using your own professional judgment to create replicable learning experiences for students. Teachers are still the experts; AI is a tool.
For administrators, this means crafting queries carefully the first time and working with colleagues to polish the message. Use efficient prompting to get it right the first time and do the important refining work offline.
And for all of us in public education, this means not demanding pristine, symmetrical perfection from student work. We should be far more interested in work that looks like a young person made it with an authentic combination of time, effort and risk-taking. Let’s let children express themselves through their assignments, even if it involves occasional smudges, curved lines or wrinkled edges.
***
The student whom I met with in that classroom in June had dutifully participated in class, had worked with their peers every day and had wanted to do exceptionally well when they turned to Gemini.
Yet what they learned in that unit overall is of far more importance to me than whether or not the end product sounded like it was written by a generic college student. That polish was worth far less, pedagogically, to their teacher or our school than what it cost to produce environmentally.
AI will become more efficient, and scale will help, but good habits should be developed now. As educators, we must model more effectively as the technology and its potential emerges. Let’s use AI more conscientiously to preserve cognition and the environment at the same time.

title: Russian drone slams into bridge in Kyiv as Germany's chancellor visits
text:
Russian drone slams into bridge in Kyiv as Germany’s chancellor visits
A Russian drone slammed into a bridge in the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv on Sunday as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited the city in a display of support for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Related video: Thousands of US troops heading to the Mideast amid uncertainty about war's direction
Video footage showed the moment the city's North Bridge was struck, sparking a huge plume of fire and black smoke while cars were still traveling across. There have so far not been reports of casualties.
Russia has been escalating its campaign against Ukraine's capital, and it is the second time the North Bridge has been hit in as many days.
It comes as Merz visited Kyiv alongside his Minister for Economic Affairs and Energy, Katarina Reiche, despite warnings from Russia on Saturday that foreign visitors and dignitaries to the Ukrainian capital are not safe amid a Russian onslaught of attacks.
"Ukraine is facing decisive weeks ahead," Merz wrote on X Saturday. "Therefore, I have traveled to Kyiv today with the message: You can rely on us."

title: 'Got to help each other': Elderly Nebraska couple nearly drowns in basement flood
text:
'Thought we were going to drown': Elderly Nebraska couple battles flood in basement
An elderly West Omaha, Nebraska, couple shared the moments they nearly drowned when water burst into their basement.
Wednesday night, the couple was in the basement when they said water rushed through a window. The 80-year-olds were gripping onto each other, trying to hold on as they swam through the flood. The only thing stronger than the current was their will to live.
“It was like a Colorado River rapid,” Ken Jones said.
Caught in the current were Ken and Sharon Jones.
“I've got a black eye, and my hip is sore, like I was in a fight overnight,” Ken Jones said.
Around midnight Wednesday, Ken Jones got a notification about water in his basement.
While he scoped out the issue in the furnace room, his wife came to check on him when the water burst through the window.
“I thought we were going to drown,” he said.
Furniture and beloved belongings were pushed into piles. The slick mud was still wet two days later.
They said the water rose five feet that night.
“We couldn't stand up,” Ken Jones said. “As I was going under, I said, ‘Help! We’ve got to help — got to help each other!’”
As they were thrown across the room with the furniture, Ken fought to hold on to his wife but lost his grip.
“The one thought on my mind: I've got to find her,” Ken Jones said.
Eventually, they found the stairs and had to walk halfway up the flight to get out of the water, which he described as “a true blessing.”
Sharon Jones said she never had a doubt that they would make it out alive.
“I knew we were going to make it,” she said. “If anything, I could pull him out if I needed to, but I knew we were not going to die.”
They called the local fire department. They said crews arrived within 10 minutes and checked on them and all the neighbors along the street.
“They had to park out on 132nd Street because they couldn’t get into this street because the street was flooded,” Ken Jones said.
He said an assessment estimated there were $15,000 to $25,000 in damages, just to restore, not to rebuild.
Ken Jones said their insurance will not help cover any of the cost, but neighbors like Mary Yearling stepped up to help.
“We're hoping that if we pull together and try to clean things up, that we can make it a little bit easier for them to deal with this catastrophe,” Yearling, the neighborhood’s property manager, said.
Yearling arranged to have a dumpster brought to the Jones’ home so they could get rid of unrecoverable items.
“We’re going to try to see if we can find some of those things, and hopefully she’ll be able to salvage some of them,” Yearling said. “We’re here until it gets done.”
Yearling said around a dozen people have reached out to help and five neighbors have been helping since day one.
“We never have any problem with people stepping up and helping like we’ve had this last couple of days,” Yearling said.
Although the Jones’ basement is completely destroyed, what matters most to them is they’re alive.
“They're just things,” Ken Jones said. “We've got our life.”

title: Maine’s rural maternity wards require a mindset shift
text:
The continuing closure of Maine’s rural maternity wards makes me wish there was someone I could grab by the collar and shake a little and go, “This is why we shouldn’t be treating healthcare as a consumer good instead of a public investment for a functional, healthy society!”
I would have to shake an awful lot of collars.
The reason rural hospitals keep closing down maternity wards is money. America doesn’t think of healthcare as a right, or a social investment. We think of it as a consumer good like any other, so if the market won’t support its presence, businesses stop offering it.
Healthcare providers need to make money in order to keep their doors open. Even nonprofits like MaineHealth, which don’t need to worry about a rate of return for investors expecting profit, need to at least break even to continue providing those services (and those suspiciously beefy executive salaries, of course).
Pretty much everyone agreed that having maternity care and birthing hospitals in rural areas is important for the health and safety of mothers and babies, as well as for the community in general.
As one of the protesters against the closure of Miles Hospital’s maternity ward in Damariscotta pointed out, “What happens if you can’t be born in a community, you can only die there?”
But what’s the solution? MaineHealth magics up more money? Maybe robs Peter to pay Paul and cuts services elsewhere in the system? The population of Lincoln County isn’t going to suddenly and immediately explode to the point where a fee-for-service birth center model is viable.
All three candidates for governor have said that rural maternity closures are something that they’re going to work on and stop from happening, but what’s their plan?
I mean, all Republicans know how to do when there’s a problem is cut taxes, which isn’t going to help in this situation. Democrats are probably more interested in directly helping by subsiding a hospital, but for how long? How much?
Our system isn’t set up for ongoing state subsidy through direct payments like that. Plus, there are a ton of competing budget commands and local moms don’t have a small army of well-paid lobbyists to prowl the halls of the State House. And then you’d get people complaining that they shouldn’t have to pay for maternity care if they can’t get pregnant.
I don’t think the reason we don’t have a universal healthcare system in America is the concept of “Ooh, government healthcare scary.” I know there are some people who think that way, but we already have examples of both government-run direct healthcare — the VA — and government- provided health insurance programs, in Medicare and Medicaid. Those programs could certainly use some improvement, but they are very much present and functional and the citizens who benefit are generally satisfied.
No, the reason we don’t have it is because Americans are obsessed with this idea of “deserving.” We don’t want “OUR” taxes paying for “THEIR” healthcare. Who “they” are changes from person to person, of course. (Meanwhile, the sad truth is your taxes are mostly going to Medicare, Social Security and defense contractors’ stock accounts.)
Think about roads, right? A long time ago American leaders all decided that in order for us to have a healthy, thriving society and economy, we needed roads connecting us, from dirt paths to superhighways. So we made it happen, and everyone contributes, and everyone can use the roads.
You don’t have a subscription to roads through your employer. You don’t get road access on a marketplace. You can still drive on them if you’re poor. They’re funded by our taxes (including, yes, tolls). People don’t get mad that other people they don’t like, or who have made choices they disapprove of, get to use the roads. (Well, other than the usual road rage.) And yes, I know that lots roads are terribly maintained; my family used to play “Buxton Slalom” with potholes in our hometown. This isn’t my most perfect metaphor.
The problem is not just electing politicians who are willing to put in the work to build us a universal healthcare system, although of course we have to do that too. We have to change our view of what healthcare is for. Is it for profit generation, or is it a social good?
If it’s a social good that we need for a functioning society, can we come to terms with the fact that, yes, “your” taxes may be paying for services that you don’t directly benefit from because our society as a whole would really benefit from having that health system.
Until then, rural facilities are just going to keep shutting down, no matter how important they are to their communities, no matter how many lives are at stake.

title: 'It's a catalyst for culture and arts': 100-year-old grain silo gets mural upgrade
text:
'It's a catalyst for culture and arts': 100-year-old grain silo gets mural upgrade
Art has always been part of Montana, with community leaders in one area adding another, much larger canvas in hopes of growing its own arts and culture scene.
Glendive, Montana, officials said it may be hard for many to miss its GTA grain elevator, thanks to Bozeman artist Griffin Foster turning the more than 100-year-old structure into a massive mural.
Watch CNN video in the playfinder above
The mural was inspired by what Foster saw when he came to visit eastern Montana.
"He was invited to a branding, and he came back to that, and that really spoke to him. He actually even wrestled calves," Jaime Shanks, with the Eastern Plains Economic Development Corporation, said. "They pulled him in to help. So, it was a great experience for him. And he said when he came out this way he really just felt like this is classic Montana with all of the agriculture. And so, when he started thinking about that tower, he asked us different questions. But it really led him to his vision for the tower."
The project was funded through the Montana Department of Commerce's Tourism development grant.
The goal: to give people driving through eastern Montana a reason to get off the interstate and into communities like Glendive.
"We really felt if we were to develop a tourism asset that could get people off the interstate and into our community, and specifically into our downtown, that was a good area to focus," Shanks said.
But community leaders said the impact could go beyond tourism.
They see projects like this as a way to make arts and culture more visible in eastern Montana.
"I think it's a catalyst for culture and arts," Shanks continued. "We don't have a ton of that in eastern Montana, and we have a lot of opportunity for it."
Shanks hopes Glendive can one day have the same kind of arts presence found in other parts of the state.
For now, that vision is taking shape, one brushstroke at a time.
The mural is on pace to be done the by second or third week of October, weather permitting.

title: Trump names national intelligence director Jay Clayton to lead a new federal AI task force
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Sunday tapped Jay Clayton, his director of national intelligence, to lead a new government task force on artificial intelligence.
Trump is calling it the “Super Intelligence Force,” because he has tried to rebrand AI as “super intelligence.” The announcement comes after Trump hosted top executives of AI companies at the White House last week and said they had signed a voluntary accord that would effectively self-police the development of the technology.
The task force will coordinate the federal effort “to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans,” Trump in a post on social media Sunday.
The task force will reach out to consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers and AI companies, the Republican president said.
Others on the task force include the Federal Trade Commission’s chairman, Andrew Ferguson; Emil Michael, the Pentagon’s chief technology officer; and Scott Kupor, the director of the Office of Personnel Management.
The group will report to Trump and his chief of staff, Susie Wiles.

Think about roads, right? A long time ago American leaders all decided that in order for us to have a healthy, thriving society and economy, we needed roads connecting us, from dirt paths to superhighways. So we made it happen, and everyone contributes, and everyone can use the roads.
You don’t have a subscription to roads through your employer. You don’t get road access on a marketplace. You can still drive on them if you’re poor. They’re funded by our taxes (including, yes, tolls). People don’t get mad that other people they don’t like, or who have made choices they disapprove of, get to use the roads. (Well, other than the usual road rage.) And yes, I know that lots roads are terribly maintained; my family used to play “Buxton Slalom” with potholes in our hometown. This isn’t my most perfect metaphor.
The problem is not just electing politicians who are willing to put in the work to build us a universal healthcare system, although of course we have to do that too. We have to change our view of what healthcare is for. Is it for profit generation, or is it a social good?
If it’s a social good that we need for a functioning society, can we come to terms with the fact that, yes, “your” taxes may be paying for services that you don’t directly benefit from because our society as a whole would really benefit from having that health system.
Until then, rural facilities are just going to keep shutting down, no matter how important they are to their communities, no matter how many lives are at stake.

title: School custodian honored for kidney donation that helped save teacher’s brother
text:
School custodian honored for kidney donation that helped save teacher’s brother
A custodian at the Boston Arts Academy received special recognition for donating his kidney to help a teacher’s brother on National Custodian Day.
“This gift is truly worth more than gold, or any monetary money,” said Thomas Thermidor, a teacher at the academy.
Andrew Allen, a custodian at the school, donated his kidney to Thermidor’s brother after the two colleagues developed a close friendship after years of working together on the fifth floor.
Thermidor recalled the moment he learned he wasn’t a match for his brother, and Allen immediately stepped in to help.
“Instantly went to the website, the program, and signed up and started the process,” Thermidor said.
Allen said his faith inspired him to take action.
“I was completely convicted by the Holy Spirit to at least go get the blood test to see if I could be a match to at least start the donation process. And I did, and I was a match,” Allen said.
Although Allen wasn’t a direct match due to the age difference between him and Thermidor’s brother, he still chose to donate his kidney to someone else, which helped move Thermidor’s brother up the transplant list.
“He actually was like, 'Yes, I still want to donate to somebody else that way they can move up my brother on the transplant list,'” Thermidor said.
A little more than a year later, Thermidor’s brother received a new kidney, and both men have recovered from their surgeries.
The two families now share a lifelong bond.
“Just trying to love my neighbor and trying to be obedient. You know, if I call myself a Christian, I want to be Christian,” Allen said.
“Inspirations like Andrew don’t always happen, but I’m just grateful that he was able to for me and to help me get a second chance at life,” Thermidor said.

title: It took me 9 years to finally find this remote Maine trail
text:
Nine years ago, I traveled into Lobster Lake to tag the Lobster Mountain hike, but through a comedy of errors, and try as I might, bushwhacking hither and yon, I never did find the trailhead.
I was misled by a photo of the trail that was (and still is) posted at the Lobster put-in. It incorrectly depicted where the trail began. Had I checked the proper map stowed in my gear, I would’ve fared better, but nooooo. Ha.
So here I am, nine years later, back at Lobster Lake with unfinished business.
The surface of Lobster Stream is like glass as we slide the old red canoe into the water and paddle away. If there’s a current on this upstream stretch of flatwater that connects Lobster Lake to the West Branch of the Penobscot River, it’s hardly detectable. We stroke easily, quietly, as if not to disturb the peaceful surroundings. We scan the thick shoreline woods of spruce and fir for moose, the grassy banks for beaver, otter, perhaps a mink.
A delightful half an hour and two miles later, we arrive at the opening of Lobster Lake and begin the transect across. Our destination is the lone campsite at Ogden Point, a lovely spot I’ve called home several times in the past. The mid-September afternoon is beautifully blue and pleasantly warm with a light breeze enough to cool our sweaty paddling selves.
The multiple humps of Lobster Mountain appear first, and then, as we approach the middle of the lake’s northwest sector, the long, flat, high ridgeline of Big Spencer Mountain comes into focus just over Lobster’s northernmost peak. Soon enough, over our shoulders to the northeast, the magnificent mass of Katahdin comes into view. We allow the canoe to drift that way and stop and rest a spell to enjoy the fine scene.
As we approach Ogden Point, we notice a canoe on shore, and then a couple of tents, and then people milling about. The site is occupied. Darn. We wave and carry on down the shore of the large bay, intent now on finding an open camp spot somewhere along there.
As we reach the sandy crescent, two women we’d met at the put-in wave us over to the site adjacent to them. We happily beach the canoe and unload. Home!
Just into the woods is a picnic table with a ridgepole and a fire pit. A privy is a few hundred feet away out back. I find a nice piece of soft ground for my tent and begin pitching camp. My buddy discovers that his tent is still in the bed of his pickup, which just so happens to be parked at the park-and-ride in Bangor. Oh well. The forecast is for clear weather, thankfully, so without a worry, he throws down his mattress and bag and calls it good.
We take camp chairs and the little cooler to the beach and set up. Then, with feet up on the canoe, we crack a couple of cold beers and smile in a big way. Happy hour has commenced at this most beautiful spot on one of Maine’s most beautiful lakes. The sun is sinking fast as we drink in the scenery, consider dinner, ponder the building of a campfire (or not) and watch a loon floating and diving, floating and diving.
The sun finally disappears behind the dark margin of trees. We linger a little longer while the sky becomes a kaleidoscope of orange and pink, sky blue and navy. Dinner is a lazy man’s freeze-dried bag of something, and then it’s back to the beach for a nightcap and to watch more of the larger-than-life show that is Lobster Lake. We are way “out there” and we know it, can feel it. Darkness falls, and with that, our eyelids. Sleepy time.
Lobster Lake is situated in the wild, wooded country east of Moosehead Lake and south of the Golden Road. More than a hundred miles from the salty Gulf of Maine coast, the name lobster isn’t one you’d normally associate with the northern Maine woods. But owing to a fluke of topography, the lake just so happens to be shaped like a lobster claw. The large eastern side of the lake is actually named Big Claw (think crusher claw), while the smaller western side is called Little Claw (think pincer claw).
Lobster Lake and a portion of the namesake mountain are part of the Penobscot River Corridor and Seboomook Public Lands. Administered by Maine’s Bureau of Parks and Lands, the vast conservation unit encompasses 100 rugged miles of rivers, lakes and streams in the upper reaches of the Penobscot River watershed.
It takes some doing to get to Lobster Lake, but it’s worth the effort. Access is from the east at Millinocket via the Golden Road or from the south at Kokadjo by way of Sias Hill Road. Gravel road travel is slow and the possibility of a flat tire is real, so prepare accordingly.
Either way, to reach Lobster Lake you must pass through the Caribou Lake checkpoint, where day-use and camping fees are charged by North Maine Woods (cash or check only).
The put-in is on Lobster Trip Road right after it passes over Lobster Stream. There’s ample parking, a privy and an information kiosk. Lobster Lake sports 11 campsites, first-come, first-served, each with a picnic table, fire pit and privy. There are also two group campsites. The lake is renowned for its unusual sedimentary and igneous rock formations, long stretches of sandy beach with great swimming and extraordinary sunsets.
There’s another big draw to Lobster, especially for hikers like you and me. A two-mile trail leads from Jackson Cove to a lookout at roughly the 2,000-foot contour on Lobster Mountain. The hike is pretty unique in that it’s one of just three in the entire Maine Mountain Guide that are accessible only by water. Takes some doing, don’t you know.
A gray morning. Coffee and breakfast. Ranger Tammy motors over to check on us and our permits. She’s in charge of the lake and more along the river corridor. Nice work if you can get it. We’re legit, and we wave as she cruises away to meet and greet other campers. To be sure, she does confirm the Lobster Mountain trailhead location.
We get our act together, load the boat and are off like a herd of turtles, paddling toward Jackson Cove.
Lo and behold, a half-hour later, there’s the sign I’ve longed to see: “Lobster Mtn. 2 Miles.” We pull the boat in, trade flip-flops for boots and socks, shoulder our day packs and strike off up the trail.
The trail winds gradually over the northern slope, and in just over an hour, we’ve reached the main outlook and a nice bench. My GPS reads 1.5 miles; duly noted.
The view over Lobster Lake is grand: wild, forested country as far as the eye can see. We step down to look around the corner and are greeted with a huge look at mighty Katahdin and many of its high neighbors. A wonderful reward that’s been worth the wait. We hang for a while, enjoy snacks and water and then begin the descent.
A new side trail, passed on the climb, beckons. Three hundred feet to its end, we revel in the big view of Big Moose Mountain and Moosehead Lake and the line of sharp-faced peaks, from Norcross, Eagle, Little Kineo and Shaw mountains to the iconic Mount Kineo. An impressive array, for sure.
The return paddle is a quiet one. We are simply awed by this remote place. Nearing the entrance to Lobster Stream, we stop paddling and let the wind turn us around. We enjoy one last, long, amazing view.
I’m wistful as we right ourselves and proceed into the stream for the final segment of the journey. Short a trip as it was, it’s been a hell of an adventure. I sneak one more look back before we turn the corner, already planning to return.

title: Search suspended for 6 people on missing medical flight from Bermuda to Boston
text:
(AP) - Authorities on Sunday suspended the search off the Massachusetts coast for six people on an air ambulance that disappeared during a flight from Bermuda to Boston.
The U.S. Coast Guard said authorities searched more than 4,400 miles (7,081 kilometers) over a span of 66 hours for the four Canadians and two people from Bermuda who were on board.
“Suspending a search is not an easy decision,” Rear Adm. Matthew Lake, commander of the Coast Guard’s northeast district, said in a statement. “We express our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones affected by the tragedy and our gratitude for our partner agencies who helped support search efforts.”
The Federal Aviation Administration contacted the Coast Guard at 2 a.m. Saturday that it had lost contact with the Gulfstream G100 carrying six people over the Atlantic Ocean. Searchers later Saturday found a “debris field” off the coast of Nantucket, Lake had said at a news conference on Sunday.
Coast Guard crews along with the New York National Guard’s Air Rescue Wing and Massachusetts authorities searched a vast area using fixed-wing aircraft, helicopters, boats and cutters.
The depth of the water around the debris field was 80 to 90 feet (about 24 to 27 meters).
The Canadian-registered air ambulance jet had four crew members and two passengers aboard when it departed Bermuda’s L.F. Wade International Airport for the nighttime flight to Massachusetts, according to a statement from the Bermuda airport’s operator, Skyport.
Air traffic audio indicates that the plane may have been “coming in blind” when a storm loomed ahead shortly before it vanished.
The pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the jet approached the coast, according to air traffic control audio posted by LiveATC.net. “Roger, you said you’re coming in blind. Is that what you said?” a controller can be heard asking the pilot.
That makes Mary Schiavo, who is a former Inspector General of the Transportation Department, think the plane may have lost its navigational instruments just as a storm moved across its path on radar. The plane also descended sharply from its cruising altitude of around 24,000 feet to around 10,000 feet, according to preliminary data from flight tracking site FlightRadar24.
“Something bad happened with this big drop, and they flew into this big storm. It’s a terrible place to have a loss of your instruments and be flying blind,” said Schiavo, who is an aviation attorney. “It’s very easy to get disoriented and not know if you’re turning, climbing, descending, etc.”
___
AP Transportation Writer Josh Funk, Associated Press writer Amy Taxin and Associated Press reporter Laura Turbay in Little Rock, Arkansas, a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative, contributed to this report. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: Tavern relocation to Blue Hill latest move in restaurateur's career
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Less than a year after opening at a prominent Main Street location in Bucksport, Stowaways Town Tavern is moving to Blue Hill.
Owner Rob DeGennaro said he plans to reopen Stowaways on Main Street in Blue Hill around Indigenous Peoples Day.
Stowaways opened in the four-story building at 63 Main Street in Bucksport in October 2025. The building is locally famous as the home of Macleod’s Restaurant, which operated there for 45 years before closing in 2025.
It is unclear exactly why Stowaways is on the move. Interviews with DeGennaro and the building’s owner, George MacLeod, reveal a disputed narrative.
MacLeod said he offered DeGennaro a chance to buy the building, which includes five apartments with water views. Deadlines to close on the sale were set, and moved from April to June to August 15 at DeGennaro’s insistence, MacLeod said, but the deal never went through.
According to MacLeod, the restaurant owner stopped paying rent.
“They were not even in touch,” MacLeod said. “I heard nothing.”
DeGennaro said he agreed to a six-month lease and was working on a loan from the Small Business Administration to purchase the building. He accused his landlord of asking for additional money after his business took off and said he refused to accept his rent checks.
DeGennaro also claims the building itself needed hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of improvements. MacLeod, however, said several upgrades were already made to the building, including new windows and electrical upgrades. He said he was required to disclose the building’s condition up front.
What is clear, is that this isn’t the first time DeGennaro has opened a restaurant in an iconic downtown building for a short stint before moving elsewhere. Stowaways Town Tavern is only the restaurateur’s most recent venture.
DeGennaro bought the Whale’s Rib Tavern and Pilgrim’s Inn in Deer Isle Village in the early 2000s and sold it in 2005. Over the next two decades, he went on to open restaurants in Southwest Harbor and Southern Florida.
In Castine in 2021, he opened Otters Waterfront Eatery in the building of the famous restaurant, Dennett’s Wharf. Otters closed the following year.
In 2024, DeGennaro opened Crybabies at the longtime site of the Harbor Café in downtown Stonington, which then closed the next year.
These recent restaurants have similar marketing and art styles. They all featured a large, varied menu with generous “family style” portions at relatively moderate prices.
Now, Stowaways’ new location in Blue Hill is the former home of Sandy’s Cafe, which closed permanently in January of this year after seven years.

title: Foot and Paddle: Little Jackson
Environmental groups sue Trump administration over eased vehicle fuel economy rules
text:
Environmental groups sue Trump administration over eased vehicle fuel economy rules
A group of environmental organizations sued the Trump administration on Friday over its recent relaxation of key vehicle fuel economy rules, a decision that the group says will make vehicles less efficient, contribute to more pollution and increase gas consumption.
Related video: Trump touts G7 plan to release oil and diesel reserves to address high prices
On Monday, the Trump administration lowered Corporate Average Fuel Economy, or CAFE, standards that set out how far new vehicles need to travel on a gallon of gasoline. The announcement was made as the Trump administration negotiated with Iran over reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
About a fifth of the world's oil passes through the strait on a typical day, and the fight over its control has sent energy prices soaring across the globe.
The environmental groups filed the petition for review Friday in the U.S. Court of Appeals against Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Jonathan Morrison, the administrator of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, which sets the rules.
“We’re taking the Trump administration to court for this reckless rollback that prioritizes Big Oil and automaker profits over American families,” Katherine Garcia, director of Sierra Club’s Clean Transportation for All program, said in a statement. “It is unlawful for Trump to turn back the clock on fuel-efficient cars, forcing drivers to waste more money on gas and communities to breathe toxic air.”
The Center for Biological Diversity, the Conservation Law Foundation, the Environmental Defense Fund and Public Citizen, along with the Sierra Club, filed the suit.
The Transportation Department and NHTSA earlier this week lowered the standards to an industry fleetwide average of roughly 34.9 miles per gallon for passenger cars and light trucks in the 2031 model year, down from a projected 50.4 miles per gallon under rules set by the Biden administration.
The administration said the change would provide Americans more vehicle choice and encourage consumers to buy newer, safer vehicles. Experts say reducing fuel economy requirements in vehicles does not necessarily lower their cost, nor would it automatically translate to new vehicle sales.
Duffy said the new rule also cuts the “illegal mandate that forced automakers to produce more expensive electric vehicles that American families didn’t want.”
There has never been a mandate that manufacturers sell EVs or Americans buy them; the rules and other cleaner vehicle standards incentivized automakers to sell a mix of electric, hybrid electric and increasingly-efficient gasoline-powered vehicles.
When reached for comment, a DOT spokesperson referred to statements made by Duffy: "This administration understands the freedom of every American family starts with affordable cars. That’s why our new standards will make that dream more achievable by letting auto manufacturers produce the cars that fit families’ needs at a lower price.”
Auto companies and industry groups broadly welcomed Monday's change, saying the rules under the Biden administration were too stringent and did not benefit consumers.
But environmental organizations decried the changes.
“With gas prices at historic highs, Trump picked the worst possible time to roll back federal mileage standards,” David Pettit, an attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity’s Climate Law Institute, said in a statement. “Oil companies will profit from less efficient cars, but drivers will take a hit to their wallets and our kids will breathe dirtier air. We’ll all pay the price for more tailpipe pollutants spewing everywhere from playgrounds to wild places. We’re asking the courts to put a stop to this callous giveaway to Big Oil and Big Auto.”
Gas prices have hovered around $4.50 and diesel has hit unprecedented heights in recent weeks, according to AAA.
The DOT said Monday that the rule would cut yearly oil consumption in 2050 by about 1.3 billion barrels as compared with yearly oil consumption in 2024, but NHTSA had estimated the 2024 standards would have saved 14 billion gallons of gasoline from being burned by that year.
Fuel economy requirements have been in place since the 1970s energy crisis, and over time, have led to improved average efficiency in vehicles.
President Donald Trump has made a number of moves to undercut cleaner vehicles in the U.S. These include eliminating electric vehicle tax credits; scrapping vehicle emissions standards; repealing the fines for automakers who don’t meet mileage rules; and attempting to block the nation’s EV charging buildout.
___
Alexa St. John is an Associated Press climate reporter.

title: Here's how to find out if you're eligible for Trump's promised $90 Medicare payments
text:
Here's how to find out if you're eligible for Trump's promised $90 Medicare payments
The White House says most Medicare Part B enrollees are eligible for the one-time payments.
Here's how to find out if you're eligible for Trump's promised $90 Medicare payments
The White House says most Medicare Part B enrollees are eligible for the one-time payments.
The Trump administration is sending one-time payments to some seniors on Medicare. It's the latest example of the president promising payments to Americans in the lead-up to midterm elections.
The White House said that payments of $90 per person will help more than 20 million enrollees pay for their Medicare Part B premiums.
"October premiums will be offset with these additional funds, and seniors will be able to use that money for their health care needs," President Donald Trump said in a video message released on Saturday. "The payments will be going out within days. You'll get your money almost immediately."
A fact sheet released Friday notes that most eligible seniors will receive a direct deposit in early October. Others will receive a check at their mailing address registered with Medicare.
The Trump administration said it is tapping into the Medicare Improvement Fund to cover the cost, which has never been used in this way before.
Who's eligible?
The White House said most, but not all, Medicare Part B enrollees are eligible for the payments. Those who already receive premium assistance through Medicaid or pay an adjusted amount based on income do not qualify.
Seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage, a private plan offered as an alternative to traditional coverage, are not eligible either.
You can call 1-800-633-4227 to find out if you're eligible for the premium rebate. Call the Social Security Administration at 1-800-772-12 for a status update on your payment.
Other promised payments
In a separate announcement last month, the Trump administration pledged to send $500 rebate checks to roughly 1 million Affordable Care Act enrollees across 30 states.
Meanwhile, on the campaign trail, the president has repeatedly promised to send every American adult $5,000 if Republicans maintain control of Congress. The proposal, which could cost more than $1 trillion, would likely face hurdles on Capitol Hill, as Democrats and some Republicans have already spoken out against it.
Some Democrats have accused the president of trying to buy votes ahead of this fall's midterm elections, as one new AP-NORC Center poll finds that less than one-fifth of American adults approve of his handling of the cost of living.

title: The choice is simple in Maine’s Senate race
text:
This paper has printed several letters that explain why the authors are voting for Susan Collins or Troy Jackson. It is interesting to hear the different perspectives, but when it really comes down to it, this is not about who has more energy or who has done more for the state. It comes down to the fact that our Republican-controlled Congress has done nothing to rein Donald Trump in.
They are allowing him to degrade free speech, massively cash in on the presidency, sell pardons, illegally deport and detain (and kill) innocent people and lie about election fraud. Most strikingly they are allowing him to waste taxpayer dollars on a needless war, ballrooms and arches and on and on.
In my view, Collins (who also no longer appears to have the power of the purse strings in Washington, D.C.) has consistently voted in a way that has allowed Trump’s agenda to move forward. The proof is there for anyone to see. Collins only votes against her party when they do not need her vote for an issue to pass. When they need her, she is right there for them.
A vote for Collins is a clear vote for Trump’s agenda. If people disapprove of what Trump is doing to this country, then they should not be voting for Collins, period. Jackson will call out Trump’s nonsense, something Collins has not been willing to do.
Margaret Duhamel
Woolwich

title: US Coast Guard continues search for passengers of missing plane off Nantucket
text:
Search suspended for missing passengers on board Boston-bound medical plane, US Coast Guard says
The U.S Coast Guard has suspended their search for the six missing passengers who were on board a medical aircraft that went missing off the Massachusetts coast, as of Sunday evening.
A crew from the Massachusetts Environmental Police joined the search Sunday morning for six missing passengers who were on board a medical aircraft that went missing off the Massachusetts coast.
Related video: Search continued Sunday for missing passengers onboard Boston-bound medical plane
On Saturday, the U.S. Coast Guard located debris that was confirmed to be associated with the missing aircraft off Nantucket, officials confirmed to Boston sister station WCVB on Saturday.
The Coast Guard said it is difficult to identify the parts of the plane that were found amongst the debris field.
The Coast Guard confirmed Sunday that the ongoing operation is a search and rescue mission and has not yet turned into a recovery.
"If there were any survivors remaining on the surface of the water, we would have found them," said Coast Guard Captain John McTamney.
The Gulfstream G-100 aircraft departed L.F. Wade International Airport in Bermuda and was traveling to Boston's Logan International Airport.
The Coast Guard, along with support from the New York National Guard and Massachusetts authorities, has searched nearly 3,000 square miles over two and a half days.
McTamney said that the current weather has proved favorable from a search perspective.
"Winds at 15 to 20 knots or so. Three-foot seas. All assets on scene and in the air have been able to effectively search the area. Weather has not been a large factor," McTamney said.
A Massport spokesperson confirmed that the aircraft did not arrive at Logan Airport as scheduled.
The Bermuda government and the Coast Guard said that they have been in contact with the families of those on board.
“My thoughts are with everyone on board and their families during this deeply worrying time," said Premier David Burt. "We are praying that all six people will be found safe, and we thank the search and rescue crews for their continuing efforts.”
In a statement from Skyport, the company that manages Wade International Airport, a spokesperson said that the aircraft was a Canadian-registered air ambulance that left its airport for Boston at 12:41 a.m. on Saturday.
The company said there were four crew members and two passengers on board. The passengers were traveling to Boston for medical care.
Four Canadians and two Bermudians were on board at the time of the plane's disappearance.
"The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has advised that air traffic controllers subsequently lost contact with the aircraft off the coast of Nantucket Island, Massachusetts, and a search is currently underway," the spokesperson said. "Skyport has no further information to provide at this time."
The Federal Aviation Administration said it issued a search and rescue alert for the plane at 1:20 a.m.
The FAA notified the U.S. Coast Guard that it lost contact with the plane, which is registered to Canadian-based Latitude Air Ambulance. The company confirmed that the missing plane is among its fleet.
The Coast Guard's response includes crews from Air Station Cape Cod, a 47-foot motor lifeboat crew from Station Brant Point and the USCGC William Sparling -- a fast response cutter.
The search is about 13 nautical miles off the coast and extends from about 30 nautical miles wide and 20 nautical miles long, according to the Coast Guard.

title: An opinion section study in contrasts
text:
It was a delight to read William Smith’s elegant op-ed on the promise of trickle-up economics (Sept. 13), indistinguishable from democratic socialism, that made clear the differences between what we in this country have: extreme disparities in wealth and opportunity, and what we would enjoy with trickle-up economics. It is no surprise most of our politicians disparage democratic socialism; it is not in their interests.
On the other hand, the op-ed next door in the section, by Charles Todorich (“Western civilization is dying and Europeans don’t seem to care”), contained a number of mistaken assumptions and conclusions.
For example, Todorich says that a majority of Europeans are pessimistic about the future and believe life will be harder for their children. In the EU, 70% are pessimists; in the U.S., that figure is roughly 70-75%, not much different. It is interesting that in Denmark, with the highest taxes in the EU, only about a third of parents are pessimistic about their children’s economic future. After all, they do get something for the taxes they pay: universal healthcare, free university education, a highly developed social security and welfare system and a high degree of income equality.
Todorich, who seems to believe that the Crusades were a moral high point for European Christianity, expressed concerned about Muslim emigration to Europe, but seems ignorant of its cause: wars initiated by the Bush/Cheney administration in the Middle East destabilized the region and made life there unbearable; emigration to safety is the result. He also believes that concerns about global warming are simply mass hysteria. I could only shake my head in disbelief.
Jonathan Mitschele
New Gloucester

title: We must hold our leaders accountable for their voting records
text:
There is a lot of sad-sacking going around the Republican campaigns this season. The “woe is me” and “I do not support the consequences of what I voted for” cries can be heard from east to west. And I have nary an iota of sympathy for the whiners.
Not only do adults understand that there are always consequences for one’s actions, but these guys and gals had a blueprint to read from that made it clear President Donald Trump is incapable of not antagonizing important groups of voters, particularly their own constituents, whom they chose to ignore for most of the last 22 months.
Why did Trump et al. lose in 2020? Because he managed to anger one voting bloc after another until there were just too many ticked off voters for him to win.
What is baffling is that seasoned politicians in Washington, D.C., seem incapable of seeing what happened publicly, over and over again, for months during the last year of his first term. And now they want to claim that they were fooled by his banter?
Failing to appreciate the long-term consequences of an action or a vote is not a reasonable excuse for their choices. They must all be held accountable by the voters.
Jenifer Duryea
Limington

title: 'Jane Doe' solidarity posts flood social media after Cornell rape lawsuit
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — It was one woman, then another, and another, until a trickle became a flood.
Countless women, and some men, posting on social media that they were Jane Doe, in support of a young woman using that name to file a lawsuit against Cornell University and seven fraternity members she accuses of raping her.
For many, claiming the name came along with sharing personal accounts of being sexually abused and assaulted, joining the wave of solidarity that has surged since journalists at the college’s independent student newspaper reported on the lawsuit filing late last month.
The impetus for some of those claiming the name was a desire to offer the woman some protection in this digital age, in response to those wanting to identify her real name online. They hope the flood of “I am Jane Doe” posts will confuse online algorithms.
Another moment of reckoning
The posts have come in all formats — video, photo, text — across the landscape of social media platforms.
The outcry reminds many of the energy at the heights of the #MeToo movement, which exploded a decade ago. Back then women posted their stories of sexual harassment and assault in the wake of a high-profile Hollywood case using the hashtag phrase, which had been introduced in that context a decade earlier.
“These moments … are encouraging more women to speak up and tell their stories,” said Emma Davidson Tribbs, founding director of the National Women’s Defense League. “They are giving people a level of bravery and comfort to come forward and speak their truth. And they can be incredibly catalyzing for change.”
Change is what Wendy Lea Brewer wants to see, and that inspired her to post reels on Instagram with captions including “I am Jane Doe” and “It’s time to speak.”
Brewer, 48, a singer, has her own experience with sexual abuse and has spoken of it in her songwriting and performing. But she felt like she was “screaming into the void” and people were not paying attention.
Outraged after hearing about the Cornell case, she went online and found community in the Jane Doe posts.
“We are all right here feeling the same thing, and we have had enough,” Brewer said.
The Associated Press typically does not name victims of sexual abuse unless they publicly identify themselves.
The protection of the crowd
The use of pseudonyms like Jane Doe in lawsuits has grown in recent decades, said Diana Simon, a professor of law at the University of Arizona.
While the legal system is geared toward transparency, with the expectation that parties in a suit would be named, there can be situations that are highly private or sensitive “where it would be in the person’s best interest to remain anonymous,” she said.
But that does not mean someone’s real identity would not get out, especially if people search for it.
That’s why Kelsey Combe made her “I am Jane Doe” post. The idea was that numerous similar posts could provide a form of online protection to the Cornell plaintiff if her name were to be revealed, by making it harder to determine its authenticity.
“It was to confuse the AI models and stand in solidarity with her,” said Combe, a photographer in the Midwest.
She decided to do so after seeing a reel from a content creator who posts as “women_inamerica,” talking about how important it was. It had already generated responses from many women by the time Combe posted anything.
The attempt to sow confusion worked in a way Combe was not expecting, though: She later saw that AI had linked her as the actual Jane Doe, saying it was Combe that sued Cornell. She was able to get it removed, but not without getting a taste of what public critique can be like.
“It was an interesting situation, because the second that I sounded the alarm about it … a lot of people were replying, ‘Well, you asked for this. You participated in this. What did you think was going to happen?’ And I was like, ‘Well, look at that,’” Combe said.
It only emphasizes what the solidarity efforts are trying to show, that there are larger systemic issues to be addressed rather than just individual cases, she said.
“It’s standing in solidarity with her, but it’s also acknowledging that to an extent we are Jane Doe, I think the majority of us, because … we have our own experiences with sexual assault,” Combe added.
“So we are all Jane Doe until nobody is.”

title: 2 dead, 35 injured in homecoming party mass shooting in Georgia
text:
VIENNA, Ga. (WALB/Gray News) - Two people are dead and 35 people have been injured in a mass shooting at a homecoming party in Georgia, according to officials.
According to the Georgia Bureau of Investigation, the shooting happened Sunday around 1:25 a.m. in Vienna, Georgia, during a homecoming block party where deputies were monitoring a crowd of more than 1,000 people.
Dooly County Coroner Brett Walls identified the deceased victims as JaQuevion Jackson, 21, and Macaleb Jackson, 23.
The victims’ bodies will be given to the Georgia Bureau of Investigation for autopsies.
Dooly County Sheriff Craig Peavy said shots were fired at at least 50 people in at least two locations about a block apart. At least 25 people were shot and taken to the hospital, and as many as 35 people may have been injured.
The Georgia Bureau of Investigation is assisting local authorities with the investigation.
An impromptu community prayer vigil was organized Sunday morning in response to the shooting. Around 100 people gathered at the courthouse in Vienna, Georgia, to pray for the victims and their families.

title: Reader wishes to connect with a teen for holiday giving
text:
DEAR SUN SPOTS: Are there any local programs to assist me in adopting a teen for Christmas? I know there are a ton of general programs where you can donate gift cards and such, but I’m specifically looking for a teenager who is interested in makeup and fashion as I am. I have no children of my own and would love to purchase gifts for a teen as I have learned they aren’t chosen for gift-giving as often as small children.
Whether it’s through an organization or just a local family, I’d love to know how I can help. — No name, no town
ANSWER: I’m touched by your thoughtfulness and for coming up with this idea as the holiday season approaches. I’m sure there are many teens who would appreciate your generosity.
Since you are looking to give specific gifts to a specific age group, try contacting: Big Brothers, Big Sisters (729-7736), a social worker in your area, your town office where there may be a local Santa Fund, local churches, high school guidance counselors, Maine Needs (send them a message at https://www.facebook.com/groups/MaineNeeds/), or contact 211 and ask them to help you track down a teen in need.
You may also want to consider spreading your gifts to more than one teen. Some middle school and high schools have special supply closets that are stocked with items teens can use.
Readers, if you know of an organization who could connect a teen to this benefactor, please write to me and I’ll put you two in touch with one another and of course, I’ll keep the identity of all involved confidential.

All lot owners are invited to attend. Please bring your chairs and dress accordingly for the weather. The meeting will be held rain or shine. If there are any questions, please contact me at 783-6839. — Joe, Lewiston

For more information, please contact the Drop-In Center at 200-4869 or visit https://www.thedrop-incenter.org/get-involved. Whether you can help regularly or occasionally, we’d love to hear from you. — Erin, Auburn

But by all means, give Erin a call and hear first-hand how you can lend your time and energy to this vibrant group who serves our community’s unhoused individuals. It’s a great opportunity to bestow kindness and caring upon those who can really use it.

title: Former US attorney to conduct review of botched execution of Christa Pike
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee’s Office announced Saturday that former U.S. Attorney Ed Stanton will be conducting the independent review of the botched execution of Christa Pike.
The governor’s office said the Tennessee Attorney General’s Office retained Stanton to conduct an “independent review of the Tennessee Department of Correction’s actions” during the failed attempt to execute Pike.
On Wednesday, Pike, who is the only woman on Tennessee’s death row, was set to be executed by lethal injection. Following some legal hurdles throughout the day, Pike was given two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital, but her attorneys said she was “alive and snoring.”
Pike remains alive and hospitalized in “critical condition,” according to her attorneys, marking the second failed execution in Tennessee this year.
“The independent review will seek to determine whether the protocol was followed and consider whether additional recommendations are necessary to ensure the State’s protocol continues to be lawful and effective,” the governor’s office said.
Lee has called off the remaining execution that was set for this year, pending the completion of the review. Gary Wayne Sutton was supposed to be executed on Dec. 3.
Stanton previously conducted an independent review of Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol following an oversight in the process’s testing. His review in 2022 prompted “the State and Attorney General’s Office to substantially rewrite the protocol before executions resumed.”

title: Foot and Paddle: Little Jackson

text:
Diego Gonzalez’s penalty kick right before the final whistle kept the Portland Hearts of Pine’s slim playoff hopes alive.
The Hearts of Pine nearly scored on a stoppage-time corner kick, but after the ball was deflected, Diogo Barbosa was fouled in the box in the 97th minute. That gave Gonzalez a penalty kick, which he buried in the back of the net to secure a 3-3 draw with Spokane Velocity FC in a USL1 soccer match Saturday in Spokane.
Hearts of Pine (7-12-10) now have 31 points, putting them eight behind Fort Wayne FC for the eighth and final postseason spot.
Heading into halftime, the Hearts looked headed for their 13th defeat of the season. Spokane scored three goals in a 10-minute spurt at the end of the opening half. Nil Vinyals netted the first goal and set up scores by Neco Brett and Andre Lewis.

The Hearts of Pine, ranked 13th in the league, next host fourth-ranked Athletic Club Boise, which has already clinched a playoff berth, Saturday at 5 p.m. at Fitzpatrick Stadium in Portland.

title: Patriots stun Buffalo with late game heroics
text:
ORCHARD PARK, N.Y. — Drake Maye threw three touchdown passes, including Efton Chism’s one-handed catch with 1:50 remaining, and the New England Patriots defeated the Buffalo Bills 29-26 on Sunday.
Romeo Doubs had touchdown catches of 2 and 14 yards, and Rhamondre Stevenson scored on a 1-yard run.
Though Maye’s turnover troubles continued with an interception and a lost fumble in the first half, the third-year starter was sharp in the final minutes after New England fell behind 26-21.
Maye’s 23-yard TD pass to Chism came on third-and-5, with the receiver bringing in the ball with his right hand and maintaining control in the end zone. Maye then hit Stevenson for the 2-point conversion.
Despite having a minute left and the ball at their 40, Josh Allen turned overly aggressive. On second-and-6, he spun out of Dre’Mont Jones’ sack attempt, stepped up in the pocket and went deep only to have his underthrown pass intended for Josh Palmer intercepted by Craig Woodson.
Taking over at the Patriots 19, Maye put the finishing touches on the win by rolling to his right and lobbing a 12-yard pass to Hunter Henry in allowing the Patriots to run out the clock.
The Patriots improved to 2-2 and for once put aside questions about a sputtering and turnover-prone offense.
The Bills, meantime, dropped to 3-1 in Buffalo’s first loss at its new Highmark Stadium, and first under new coach Joe Brady.
Maye finished 22 of 37 for 269 yards in overcoming the criticism he’s faced in opening the season by combining for six interceptions and a lost fumble in his first three starts. The lost fumble, recovered by the Buffalo at its 30, was on Maye, who lost the ball as Bills tackle Ed Oliver shoved an offensive lineman into him.
The interception, however, was on Doubs, who made the catch and in the process spun around and lost control of the ball, which sailed into the hands of cornerback Dee Alford.
The Bills had their sloppy moments, too, a week after committing five turnovers in a 24-16 win over the Los Angeles Chargers.
Receiver Khalil Shakir lost a fumble, in addition to Allen’s interception — his third of the season. Allen finished 23 of 33 for 253 yards, including a 34-yard go-ahead touchdown to Keon Coleman with 4:27 remaining. The touchdown put Buffalo up 26-21, but the 2-point conversion attempt failed when Palmer never looked for Allen’s pass directed his way.
Allen also scored on a 2-yard run, while James Cook scored on an 8-yard run.
The Bills were limited to 340 total yards and 19 first downs, both season lows, and resembled nothing like the high-powered unit that opened the season combining for 855 yards and 77 points.
The outing was a breakthrough for the Patriots’ slumbering offense, which posted season highs with 405 yards and 26 first downs. New England’s defense also rallied in containing the Bills despite missing its top cornerback Christian Gonzalez and starting defensive tackle Christian Barmore because of shoulder injuries.
ALLEN MILESTONES
Allen’s 2-yard touchdown run to tie the game at 14 with one minute left in the first half was his 88th career from scrimmage (rushing/receiving) to break the team record held by Hall of Famers Thurman Thomas and Andre Reed. It was also Allen’s 86th TD rushing, moving him into a tie with Priest Holmes for 16th place on the NFL’s career list.
INJURIES
Patriots: WR Mack Hollins hurt his calf.
Bills: WR DJ Moore did not return after hurting his shoulder attempting to make a diving catch in the second quarter. DT Ed Oliver left in the third quarter with a knee injury. And a secondary already missing Christian Benford (toe), lost Dee Alford to an ankle injury in the second half.
UP NEXT
Patriots: host the Las Vegas on Sunday.
Bills: at the Los Angeles Rams on “Monday Night Football” on Oct. 12

title: What to know about the investigation into Cornell University gang rape allegations
text:
(AP) - An intense, public outcry over a woman’s account of being gang-raped at a Cornell University fraternity house prompted New York’s governor this week to angrily yank control of the investigation away from the local prosecutor who didn’t initially see what happened as a crime.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has said Cornell police omitted key information that could have affected his decision whether or not to pursue criminal charges.
Now, the task of unraveling the case will fall to the state’s attorney general, Letitia James, who was appointed as a special prosecutor.
James, a Democrat best known for tangling with President Donald Trump, suggested at a news conference Friday that her investigation wouldn’t be rushed. She described it as a months-long process, with no predetermined outcome.
Here’s what we know and don’t know about the woman’s allegations and the investigations that followed:
A lawsuit shone a fresh light on the woman’s allegations
The woman sued Cornell and seven former students last month, alleging she was given ketamine and became completely incapacitated while members of the Chi Phi fraternity sexually assaulted her at their campus residence in October 2024.
She reported the alleged assault to campus police about three weeks later, giving investigators a detailed account over two days. She also spoke with Cornell’s disciplinary investigators.
But Van Houten quickly declined to pursue charges or further investigation after reviewing a police summary of her interview.
After the victim filed her civil suit, Van Houten said it contained allegations he had never seen. He contended Cornell’s police had withheld key information, including a transcript of the woman’s interview where she explicitly said she was “100% confident” she was raped.
Van Houten said the materials suggested she had consented to some sex with multiple men, hadn’t been forced into other acts, and was intoxicated, but not to the point of helplessness.
Under New York law, being too drunk or high to consent to sex isn’t necessarily enough to support a rape charge. The law distinguishes that from being physically helpless or incapacitated by drugs administered without consent.
Van Houten later reopened the investigation. “Seeking justice sometimes requires us to reconsider or reopen cases when we are provided with additional evidence,” he said.
The school’s investigation produced conflicting accounts
Only a fraction of the evidence collected by the school has become public, but the portions that have provided a fuller — though disputed — timeline of events, as well as a glimpse at how the men responded to being accused.
According to the records, the woman had been invited to the fraternity by a member for whom she had long held strong romantic feelings. Cornell’s disciplinary panel found that she initially consented to sex with that man and one of his friends, though she later alleged in her lawsuit that she had been pressured into taking drugs and alcohol and was too intoxicated to consent.
Later, other men started coming into the room, some drawn by a message one of the fraternity brothers sent to a Snapchat group at 1:42 a.m. using a vulgar term to advertise that a woman’s body was freely available.
The woman told investigators that her intoxication had rendered her partly defenseless. She said some of the men inhaled drugs off her unclothed body.
“I felt like bait. I felt like lions around me. It just was a totally debilitating place to be in,” she told investigators.
The records also show that she acknowledged that her memory of the night was spotty, due to her extreme inebriation, and had verbally acquiesced to some acts she later felt were sexual abuse.
Some of the accused men disputed her account when speaking to investigators, or said that the drug use and sexual activity were consensual.
Cornell hasn’t detailed the results of its investigation, but said it resulted in some students being expelled. The records show it also cleared at least some of the men of sexual assault allegations.
New York’s governor was outraged by the police investigation
Hochul said she appointed James because she had lost faith in Van Houten’s handling of the case. She said Van Houten should have asked Cornell for more information and interviewed the woman before closing it.
“This woman, this young woman, had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable,” she said. “And then at every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her.”
Van Houten said he supports James’ appointment but maintains that New York law didn’t allow him to prosecute based solely on the woman’s allegations that she was too incapacitated to consent.
The case sparks calls for change
At a Cornell Student Assembly meeting Thursday, students and other members of the university community spent more than 2 1/2 hours discussing the handling of sexual assault allegations. Some expressed fear, anger, and grief — while others shared their own experiences of sexual violence on campus.
Among them was Jane Wang, who said she had reported being sexually assaulted at Cornell a year earlier.
When she filed her Title IX case in the midst of “mental, physical and emotional recovery from the assault,” she said, “I was also met with an abundance of paperwork, very little instruction on how to navigate it and no follow-up from our Title IX office of an outcome.”
The presidents of every fraternity in Cornell’s Interfraternity Council voted unanimously to cancel social events this weekend in response to the allegations, according to The Cornell Daily Sun. Twenty student organizations are also planning a protest Monday to voice support for a promised independent review of Cornell’s handling of the case and advocate changes to its sexual assault policies, the newspaper reported.
In a video message Saturday, Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff pledged greater transparency amid the mounting outrage about how the school handled the case. He called the gang rape allegations “deeply disturbing” and said the case would weigh on the university for years to come.
The case has also renewed scrutiny of a New York sexual assault law that makes it more difficult to prosecute cases involving people too intoxicated to consent. New York is one of 19 states with such laws.
Hochul said Friday that she supports changing the law.
