title: Vassalboro event venue plan divides neighbors as final decision approaches
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
VASSALBORO — In a relatively quiet community on the west side of Webber Pond, a conflict common to communities across Maine is playing out among neighbors and at planning board meetings.
Families who live near Chuck and Debby Cabaniss’ old place see their neighborhood as peaceful. It’s home to a handful of businesses, including a golf course, some neighbors say are quiet. They enjoy listening to the sounds of the lake in the morning and wildlife in the evening.
So they were surprised when the Cabanisses sold their 53-acre property to Keith and Ratesha Rosell. The Cabanisses knew the couple planned to turn the lakefront parcel, formerly a gun range, photography studio and airstrip, into an event venue for everything from weddings to Mother’s Day brunches.
“I would have loved to have done something like that,” Debby Cabaniss said.
Both the Cabanisses and the Rosells were surprised when neighbors objected.
New businesses and developers often encounter neighbors who don’t want projects, large or small, in their backyards. Planning boards, who review development proposals to determine if they are appropriate for the town’s zoning, find themselves in the middle of disputes.
The Rosells have wanted to open an events venue for years. It’s their dream. But now that they’ve closed on the Webber Pond Road property and head toward what will likely be their final planning board site review, neighbors are asking: “What about our dream?”
NEIGHBORS’ CONCERNS
Many neighbors say the venue will disrupt a community they chose for its peace and quiet.
But that’s not the primary concern of Vassalboro’s planning board, which is charged with “ensur(ing) orderly, beneficial, and environmentally sound development and the most appropriate use of land in keeping with the purposes of the general area in which a development is proposed.”
Neighbors, who feel they have little recourse, are doing whatever they can to prevent the new venue. Some tried to dissuade the Cabanisses from selling and the Rosells from buying. One neighbor told the Rosells the water on their part of the lake was bad. Another said their business wouldn’t be successful.
The Cabanisses say they lost friends over the issue. At a recent planning board meeting, Debbie Cabaniss said when she introduced herself to a woman she recognized sitting next to her, the woman said she couldn’t sit next to her and moved.
Neighbors said they don’t know what else to do; they know the general public won’t take their side, but they feel their dream of a peaceful retirement or a peaceful childhood for their children is under threat.
When the Rosells first went before the planning board in July, they gave a thorough presentation, showing what they hope Rosewood Hills might become. That presentation included information about how they would handle up to 350 guests.
For now, what the Rosells are asking for is simple: they want to host 75-person events that shut down at 10 p.m.
They have no current plans to host such big events, but for neighbors, a can of worms was open. They imagined hundreds of guests, drunken parties and loud music playing into the night. Word spread quickly.
Before the next planning board meeting originally scheduled for Aug. 4, Chris Cote, a neighbor, circulated a letter describing a 300-person venue, encouraging people within a few miles of the venue to attend the meeting.
“It will be a nuisance,” Cote said in an email to the Morning Sentinel. “This venue will fundamentally destroy the quiet, peaceful character of the neighborhood, and adversely affect every abutting property owner in how they use their property.”
Cote said he and other neighbors sent letters to the planning board objecting to the new venue. They did the same at the Rosells’ next site review.
In a three-hour review of the Rosells’ proposal, neighbors repeatedly raised concerns about noise, traffic and visibility. Some issues were seriously considered by the planning board. Others were unrelated to town policies.
One of the chief concerns about the property came from an abutting neighbor, who had been clearing the buffer of trees and brush between the two properties to make space to build a house. Although she worried the buffer would be too small, Cabaniss said the neighbor cleared even more trees after that meeting.
The planning board requested the code enforcement officer measure noise levels and the buffer between the Rosells’ and neighboring properties. They also asked for a Department of Transportation assessment of the property’s driveway and road safety.
Code enforcement found the buffers were thick enough, and the DOT gave the green light. For the sound test, the Rosells hired a second code enforcement officer and a professional DJ.
The DJ played music at the loudest volume he deemed appropriate for the airplane hangar-turned-reception hall, the Rosells opened the door and both code enforcement officers measured the decibels from the property lines. The readings were all within the town’s limit.
Cote and neighbor Darlene Hineman said they could hear the test and sound at that level would negatively impact them.
“The Rosells think we will adapt and get used to this, but we won’t,” Hineman wrote in an email. “We bought this place for the ‘pond’ life not a party life.”
One neighboring couple, who did not want to be named, said their quiet evenings are a highlight of being on Webber Pond. Even the golf course closes at 8 p.m. They said the noise from Cabaniss’ air strip and gun range never disturbed them at night and was not as consistent as noise from a long party would be.
“I don’t want to be listening to the ‘Macarena’ every night,” the neighbor said. “Everybody would do the same thing if it was in their backyard. When people say ‘Oh, they’re typical ‘Not In My Backyard,’ that’s true. Ninety-nine percent of people don’t want it in their backyard.'”
NEXT STEPS
The Rosells, who have already moved to their new home with two of their adult children, said they’ve been called “flatlanders” who don’t understand Vassalboro. Keith Rosell has lived in Maine his whole life, and Ratesha Rosell has lived in central Maine for two decades.
Ratesha Rosell said she’s not going to let the opposition stop her. She said she grew up in an abusive household with addiction and poverty, and she saw it push her siblings down negative paths. She decided that wouldn’t happen to her.
“I’ve been through a lot to get to where I am right now,” Rosell said. “I decided I am my own person, I know my worth, I know what I can do … to go from having mayonnaise sandwiches for dinner to having a master’s degree and having businesses — I’m not the type of person who’s going to let somebody’s opinion sway my dream.”
Cabaniss said he knows two neighbors who support the venue, and plenty of people in town like the idea.
Among them is SarahBeth Grant, who has four children and has lived in Vassalboro for a decade. She doesn’t know the Rosells, but when she heard about the venue she immediately reached out.
In addition to weddings, the Rosells want to host community events, like a fright night, Santa’s village and a Mother’s Day brunch. They want to hire people with disabilities and make their events inclusive for their own children on the autism spectrum. They want to use local vendors, and have had support and interest from some of them already.
Grant said this would have a huge impact on the town and her household, which she described as a special needs home.
Grant said there aren’t many community spaces in Vassalboro and she’s spoken to many other excited residents.
“To actually have a space where we can invite the community?” Grant said. “I’m really rooting for them.”
While neighbors continue to push for the planning board to reject the Rosells’ application, Grant has started to rally people on Facebook, asking residents to show up to the next planning board meeting in support of the venue
The meeting will be at 5:30 p.m. Tuesday at 682 Main St.

WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The House and Senate are on recess until after Election Day as President Donald Trump campaigns for Republican candidates in the final weeks before the midterm elections.
Vice President JD Vance is headed to Alaska Monday, while Trump is set to kick off this week’s tour with a rally in Grand Island, Nebraska.
Nebraska, a usually red state, has a competitive Senate race this year. Incumbent Republican Pete Ricketts is facing independent Dan Osborn.
Trump is then heading back to Texas, hosting a rally in San Antonio on Wednesday.
Critical Republican candidates in Texas include incumbent Governor Greg Abbott and GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton, who is in a tight race with Democrat James Talarico.
With less than a month to go before the midterms, Republicans face pressure to perform as multiple Democratic wins could flip control of Congress.
Meanwhile in Washington, the Supreme Court starts its new term on Monday. In the coming months, the justices will hear cases involving gun rights, immigration and voting rights. It’s tradition for justices to begin taking up cases on the first Monday of October, this year: October 5.

title: Quality of life in Maine is high — why do people say it’s getting worse?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Maine Trust for Local News wanted to get a sense of how people feel about living and working in Maine. So, we commissioned a survey to find out. Over the next few weeks, we’ll be exploring the results and hearing from dozens of people who participated. You can read all about it here.
The ground was still frozen eight years ago when Maggie Hoffman’s husband came to Bangor for a job interview. They left a charmed and vibrant life in New York, just outside the city, and eventually landed in Hampden, an 18th-century town of 8,000 in Penobscot County with few sidewalks.
In some ways, life is good — the way it should be.
Hoffman marvels at the Cooper’s hawks and the red foxes and the bald eagles circling above the ever-nourishing Penobscot River.
“Look, I got to learn how to pee in the woods when I came to Maine,” she said.
The Maine Trust for Local News partnered with the Siena Research Institute to survey 824 residents and take a snapshot of life in Maine. Although three out of four respondents described an overall positive quality of life, only 20% said life in the Pine Tree State is getting better or much better.
And 38% said life is getting worse or much worse — that’s more than double the share of people nationally who said things are getting worse in their communities, according to polling Siena conducted last year.
Mainers are more likely to feel safe and secure in their home than the average American. The state’s outdoor spaces, as Hoffman noted, as well as its schools (particularly higher education) and sense of community scored highly.
But they say healthcare is hard to find, housing costs are high and the likelihood a young person will get a job with opportunity for advancement is low. All of that contributes to the disproportionately high number of people feeling that things are getting worse.
“I haven’t seen anybody really doing anything toward fixing any of those problems,” said Justin Crockett, who grew up in Franklin County and is worried about the high cost of living and the scourge of drug addiction.
It’s not surprising to Bill Nemitz, a retired journalist who for decades wrote a column for the Portland Press Herald/Maine Sunday Telegram, that Mainers are simultaneously fond about the place they live and yet pessimistic about its future.
“Maine has always had a really strong self identity of — the slogan says it all — ‘the way life should be.’ And I think Mainers have always taken pride in that,” Nemitz said.
It’s a state with a tempered resistance to change.
With the deluge of thousands of new-comers who have moved to Maine since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, change can feel inevitable.
And, Nemitz added, it’s difficult to look at the contours and trend lines of the world “and not feel a tinge of pessimism.”
“The fact that Mainers feel that way more strongly, perhaps, than other people in the country might be reflective of the fact that they value what they have so dearly,” he said.
It’s not all pine trees and soaring raptors for the Hoffmans either.
Their 38-year-old son, Jake, lives at home and has developmental and intellectual disabilities. He is a rock music aficionado and a dog whisperer, his mom said, but requires a high level of support. Finding caretakers who can help meet Jake’s needs is increasingly difficult. Maggie blames the high cost of living and childcare, and the lack of affordable housing.
“I believe that our scarcest resource are human beings, and that we’re really forgetting what we need to do to keep Maine alive,” she said. “What are we, 1.4 million people in this vastness of beautiful forestry and great waters, and people can’t live here?”
JUMPING TO HELP OUT
When his neighbor fell and broke her arm, Joel Katz brought over a healthy portion of potato leek soup.
That’s the way their community on the Blue Hill peninsula in Hancock County works, he said.
As Katz, 74, considers what he loves about living in Maine, his neighbors come to mind first. “The people we live around are just outstanding,” he said.
Down East, 52% of those polled said that quality of life, lifestyle and sense of community was the No. 1 best thing about their life in Maine, and 46% said the same statewide.
Katz moved to Maine full time when he retired a decade ago from a career leading performing arts centers, but has lived on and off in the state for 41 years. He was the first executive director of UMaine’s Center for the Arts, now known as the Collins Center for the Arts.
In the last decade, Katz and his wife have taken up some typical pastimes of the retired: they garden, for both flowers and food; on Mondays, he’s part of a team of that delivers soup to about a hundred residents of the peninsula; and on Thursdays he volunteers at the Tree of Life Food Pantry.
He’s found a community in Penobscot unlike anything he’s ever seen before.
The way life should be, for a long time, evoked the way in which life in Maine was different from other places, said Bill Green, the retired TV reporter who hosted “Bill Green’s Maine,” a program about Maine’s outdoors.
Mainers’ sense of community identity becomes “really the glue that binds this state together through thick and thin,” added Nemitz, the former columnist.
“Day to day, you can go to Hannaford, you can go to the hardware store, and, like, people really are nice to each other, and that’s something to celebrate,” said Hoffman, of Hampden.
Patricia Smith, a Lewiston resident, raised her son in Buxton and always appreciated the little things, like how neighbors check on each other during storms and power outages, or her landlord hiring the 8th grader down the block to mow the lawn.
“What we need is that type of community support,” Smith, 63, said.
NO SMALL PRICE: MAINE’S RISING COST OF LIVING
Katz is fortunate, he recognizes, to have stable housing and a reliable way to feed himself.
But with the costs soaring, he and his wife have opted to forgo some luxuries of retirement: a trip to Europe is off the table right now; the couple is waiting on a plan to add a second utility room to their 1,000-square-foot home; and they’ve put off adding solar panels to the house since the tax credits dried up.
“We don’t think it’s wise to spend our reserves,” Katz said. “We plan to live a little longer and we don’t know what’s going to happen, quite frankly.”
More than any other issue, Mainers surveyed said affordability was the worst thing about living here.
At the food pantry and thrift shop where he and his wife volunteer, there’s been a sharp increase in the number of people walking through the door.
“The rich have been doing very well, and the poor even worse,” Katz said.
Down East, the rising cost of fuel and bait has slimmed profit margins in Washington County’s $100-million commercial fishing industry, said Charles Rudelitch, executive director of the Sunrise County Economic Council.
Diminished services, the dearth of emergency medical care and specialists chief among them, makes the rural county a hard sell for those looking to settle long term. The median home price in Washington County has more than doubled in the last decade, while wages have only risen 54%. That said, it’s still one of the more affordable places to live in the state.
But what it giveth in housing, it taketh away in jobs, said Sean Thomas, who moved to Calais four years ago from Brockton, Massachusetts.
“It’s taken me a long time to get established in having enough work,” he said. “I was under-employed for a long, long time.”
Thomas was among those who said things were getting somewhat worse. He also quite likes living in Maine.
“Calais reminds me of when I was a kid,” he said, adding, “It’s a bit like stepping back in time.”
In Maine, 32% of those polled said a young person in their community was likely to find a job with opportunity for advancement and 27% said it was unlikely, while 39% said it was a tossup. Down East, a third of respondents thought it was unlikely.
Now, Thomas works as a janitor cleaning a supermarket and office buildings a few nights per week. He got another part-time job, but it meant his Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits were cut “down to nothing.”
At 57, starting over in a small town, it’s hard to see how he might move up, professionally speaking.
The Woodland Pulp Mill, in Baileyville, is Washington County’s largest employer and is considered the county’s economic anchor. It’s the kind of place where employees can work for decades.
But those large-scale economic development projects are few and far between these days, Rudelitch said, given that political opposition can threaten a project and scare off investors. It’s hard to find the community consensus needed to swallow the downsides of something like that — the blows it could strike to quality of life and the environment, for example.
Rudelitch can envision a world in which rural Maine resembles something of its past: a place with economic opportunity where people want to move to start a family.
“But it’s hard to really imagine how that would actually happen right now,” he said.
NATURE: ‘THE GREATEST THING EVER’
Justin Crockett’s ancestors landed in Kittery in the mid-1600s and they never left.
“Every grandfather I ever had from that time until present day lived and died in the state of Maine,” he said.
Now 44 with two teenage kids of his own, Crockett isn’t sure he wants his grandchildren to grow up in Maine.
He was raised in a small town in Franklin County and now lives in central Maine. Crockett left 25 years ago to join the Air Force and returned in 2022, stunned by what he described as the state’s 180-degree turn for the worse.
Four childhood friends have died from drug overdoses, including one last winter. The sawmills buzzing in his hometown when he left are all gone and the quality of public education has dropped precipitously.
“How much worse is this drug problem going to get? How much worse is the housing crisis going to get?” Crockett said.
He, along with Smith, the Lewiston resident, were among the small minority of poll respondents who felt that crime and public safety were major problems in Maine, and it contributed to their perception that things were getting much worse.
It’s when he’s alone in the woods, hunting and watching the seasons change, that Crockett is reminded of why he loves Maine.
He and Hoffman, the New York transplant, are unlikely to agree on much, at least politically. But on this, they, and many others, stand on common ground.
Some 69% of respondents said the quality of the environment was better than in other places they’ve lived or know. Nature and the environment was the second-most popular pick (22%) when respondents were asked about the best thing in their community.
“If you want to go out and grasp the goodness of Maine, you can still do it,” said Green, the retired local TV personality.
Maine has vast forest lands and craggy coastlines, and ample opportunity to play and hunt and even make a living.
“It’s just the greatest thing ever, being out in nature,” Hoffman said.
Mainers say it’s a large part of what makes life here the way it should be.
And because Maine is a place where your neighbors will bring you soup.
Reuben M. Schafir is a Report for America corps member who writes about Indigenous and rural communities for the Portland Press Herald.

title: Why stink bugs invade your home in fall—and how to stop them
text:
Why stink bugs invade your home in fall—and how to stop them
Fall is stink bug season. Here’s how to get rid of them and keep them from coming back.
Why stink bugs invade your home in fall—and how to stop them
Fall is stink bug season. Here’s how to get rid of them and keep them from coming back.
If stink bugs are suddenly appearing on your windows, walls, or curtains, fall is probably to blame. As temperatures drop, these pests look for warm places to shelter through winter. Here’s how to remove the ones already inside, keep more from coming in, and avoid the mistake that can make the problem worse.
To sort out fact from fancy, we reached out to Dr. Chris Hayes, director of the Hayes Structural Pest Research Lab at NC State.
Why Stink Bugs Suddenly Appear in Fall
Stink bugs are usually outdoor pests during the spring and summer. They feed on plants, including garden vegetables and crops, but they become more noticeable indoors when nights begin to cool.
“Starting in September, they start moving inside, into structures and anywhere they can find warm shelter,” says Hayes.
As soon as you start to get a few cold nights, stink bugs enter a phase that's called "diapause." This is when, according to Chris, they would naturally tend to cluster in hollow logs or trees, out of the way of predators and frost. "Then they slow their body way, way, way down. They stop feeding. And that allows them to survive until spring."
The timing varies depending on where you live, but stink bugs may begin moving indoors in late summer or early fall and remain hidden through winter.
What Do Stink Bugs Look Like?
Stink bugs have a distinctive shield-shaped body. The brown marmorated stink bug is usually mottled brown and gray, with lighter markings along the edges of its abdomen.
There are many native stink bug species, but the brown marmorated stink bug is invasive and can be especially troublesome because it has few natural predators in the United States. Stink bugs generally do not bite or sting people, but they can damage plants outdoors.
What Attracts Stink Bugs to a Home?
In late fall, they are primarily looking for a place to shelter. They may be drawn to warm, sunny sides of a home, then gather around windows, eaves, soffits, attics, and other upper areas. Bright lights can also attract them, which is why you may notice them around exterior lighting or windows at night.
Fortunately, they're not typically there for food, so you don't have to worry about leaving food out, as you would with other pests. "I don't want to say you'd never see a stinkbug eat a fruit," says Chris. After all, that's what they eat outside. "But most of the time, by the late fall, they’re they’re not concerned with feeding, just surviving."
How Do Stink Bugs Get Inside?
Stink bugs can enter through small openings around windows, doors, vents, soffits, utility lines, and other exterior penetrations.
"Typically, stink bugs try to go up and in, so they look for windows, eaves, soffits, and will try to cluster in attics and higher levels," says Chris. The good news is that they're not typically doing damage. "A few on your window could mean you have a small number, or you could have hundreds up there and you wouldn't know. When the spring comes, they're gone and you'd never know they were there."
What’s the Best Way to Get Rid of Stink Bugs?
If you're only dealing with one or two stink bugs—say a few on the window—then you can simply grab it and dispose of it. Because of the cold, they tend to be especially sluggish. "I recommend just picking it up with a tissue or paper towel and flushing it," says Chris. "You could put it outside, but it would just come back in again."
For larger groups, use a vacuum cleaner. "But don't just leave them in there. They'll crawl right back out. You'll want to freeze them, or drown them in a bucket of soapy water."
Don’t Crush Stink Bugs in Large Numbers
Despite their name, stink bugs do not always smell strongly. They release an unpleasant odor when crushed or disturbed, however.
Chris says that it is probably fine to crush one or two, but there are reasons to avoid crushing them when dealing with larger numbers. "When they release their odor, it's a chemical defense system," he explains. "And it's very likely releasing an alarm pheromone for other stink bugs. Crushing one alerts the others."
In a situation where you've got a lot of them clustered together, then, crushing one or two could cause the others to scatter throughout your home, making them much harder to get rid of.
5 Ways to Keep Stink Bugs Out of Your House
1. Repair Window Screens
Look for tears, loose edges, or gaps around window screens. Replace damaged screens and make sure they fit securely in their frames.
2. Replace Worn Weatherstripping
Check the weatherstripping around exterior doors, garage doors, and windows. If you can see light around a closed door, insects may be able to get through the same opening.
3. Seal Cracks Around Windows and Trim
Use an appropriate exterior caulk to seal small cracks around window frames, door frames, siding, and trim. Pay particular attention to sunny sides of the house where stink bugs may gather.
4. Inspect Utility Openings and Upper Levels
Check areas where pipes, wires, and cables enter the house. Also inspect attic access points, eaves, and soffits for gaps. Do not block active vents, since proper attic ventilation is important.
5. Ask a Pest Professional About Exterior Treatment
If stink bugs return every fall or gather in large numbers, a licensed pest professional can inspect the structure and treat likely entry points with an appropriate residual insecticide.
When Should You Call a Pest Professional?
Call a licensed pest professional if:
- Stink bugs are appearing in several rooms.
- Large clusters are gathering in an attic, wall void, or upper story.
- The bugs return every fall despite sealing obvious gaps.
- You cannot safely remove the infestation with a vacuum.
- Someone in your household has respiratory sensitivities or concerns about pesticide exposure.
Per Chris, "You may want to involve an insecticide. There are aerosols that are knockdown products, that will kill any insect that breathes it in almost immediately. But don't do it yourself. You want to try someone who has the training to use it."

title: Christa Pike’s lawyer says she has not regained consciousness since her failed Tennessee execution
text:
(AP) - Christa Pike has remained unconscious and on a ventilator at a hospital in the four days since her failed execution in Tennessee, and her prognosis might not be known for days more, one of her lawyers said Sunday.
Little has been released about Pike’s condition since Wednesday night’s execution attempt. She has since remained hospitalized under guard as doctors try to get the massive dose of the barbiturate pentobarbital out of her system.
When asked whether she ever regained consciousness after the execution attempt, Assistant Federal Defender Stephen Ferrell, Pike’s lawyer, said on CNN’s “State of the Union”: “Not that I am aware of.”
Lawyer says Pike’s medical decisions are being decided by someone else
Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in a jealous rage in 1995. She became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row.
Tennessee prison officials gave Pike two doses of the lethal injection drug on Wednesday night. The pentobarbital didn’t kill her, but her lawyers said her arms were burned and blistered from the caustic drugs.
Pike gave someone her medical power of attorney and that person is protecting her privacy, Ferrell said.
“I’m not sure what all they may have told that person,” Ferrell said.
Pike’s attorneys have not identified who is making Pike’s medical decisions. They said they may not know for several more days whether or not she can recover.
“We don’t know right now, and we may never know what sort of torture she endured during that process, where her consciousness was, what physical pain there was — what mental torture she went through,” Ferrell said.
A spokeswoman for Pike’s defense team said in a statement early Sunday that “we appreciate all respect for Christa’s rightful privacy.”
Pike’s lawyer says Tennessee needs to be more open about executions
Pike’s execution was delayed for more than eight hours Wednesday as the U.S. Supreme Court considered, and ultimately overturned, a federal appeals court ruling to halt her lethal injection so judges could thoroughly review whether the jury that sentenced her to death should have considered sexual abuse she said she suffered as a child.
Her attorneys asked a court Friday to order Tennessee prison officials to preserve any written records, communication, images or video from the execution.
Tennessee, like many other states with capital punishment, keeps many details about executions secret from the people involved to details about how the drugs are manufactured or obtained or any tests done on their quality.
“The state of Tennessee has got to start telling its people exactly what it is doing so that in the democratic process, the people of Tennessee can decide if that’s what they want to be done in their name,” Ferrell told CNN.
Tennessee has struggled with executions before
This was the second time this year Tennessee has not been able to execute a prisoner who was seemingly moments away from death. In May, Tennessee stopped the execution of Tony Carruthers after staff placed an IV into his right arm but couldn’t get a secondary IV line.
Commissioner of the Tennessee Department of Correction Frank Strada announced Saturday he was resigning.
Gov. Bill Lee has ordered an independent investigation into the state’s capital punishment system conducted by former U.S. Attorney Ed Stanton. He also reviewed Tennessee’s execution procedures after Lee called off a different execution in 2022 and found the state did not comply with its own lethal injection process.
Prison officials and the Tennessee Attorney General’s Office have said little since Pike was taken to the hospital.
Future of Pike’s death penalty case is unclear
It is unclear what will happen in her death penalty case. Pike’s lawyers have asked the governor to commute her punishment to a life sentence.
“If she recovers, she may not fully recover. And there may be issues about her competence,” Ferrell said.
Pike didn’t deny she killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in 1995. The two were classmates at Knoxville Job Corps.
Prosecutors said Pike feared Slemmer was a romantic rival and lured her to a secluded area where she and her boyfriend slashed Slemmer with a box cutter and beat her with a large chunk of asphalt. The case got widespread attention because of the brutality of the killing, the ages of the people involved and because a satanic symbol was carved into the victim’s body.

title: Maine Marathon winners soak in atmosphere, experience
text:
PORTLAND — Dylan Stoltzfus made a heart shape with his hands as he made his way to the finish line.
It was evident how much winning the 35th annual Maine Community Bank Maine Marathon meant.
“I spent a really long time with an injury in college,” said Stoltzfus, 24, a Portland resident. “I thought I would never run again, never race again. This is the first big race I’ve ever won. It feels like years in the wilderness and this is like coming out.”
Stoltzfus finished with a time of 2 hours, 23 minutes, 59 seconds, easily out-distancing runnerup Steven Fritzsche of Kennebunk (2:31.12). Will Faden of Somerville, Massachusetts (2:32.02) placed third.
Betsy Burke, 42, of Rye, New York finished first in the women’s field with a time of 2:54.08.
This was her second time running the race.
“I was really surprised,” Burke said. “It was fun. I had people to run with and felt pretty good until about (mile) 21 and then just tried to turn my brain off.”
Burke’s husband and his family are from Blue Hill, so she visits Maine often.
“I felt really good in the hills, like (miles) 12 to 18, then started feeling much worse,” Burke said, laughing. “But I felt good for a while and was like, ‘this is great,’ and then I knew I could just get to the end.”
Alyssa Carreau of Old Lyme, Connecticut (2:55.39) and Linnea Maynard of Portland (2:57.32) followed in second and third places, respectively.
On the half marathon side, winners JP Flavin and Megan O’Neil broke new ground.
As teammates who train out of Rochester, Michigan, not only was this the pair’s first time in Maine, but they earned course records in the men’s and women’s half marathon races.
“Oh my gosh, it’s gorgeous,” O’Neil said said of Maine. “I’m from Michigan. All my friends are super jealous I got to go to Maine in October. … Beautiful day for running, perfect temperature, not too windy.”
O’Neil, 30, finished in 1:14.34. Her time was 32 seconds faster than Cliodhna O’Malley’s record-setting run last year.
Flavin, 28, finished with a time of 1:03.00, beating previous record holder Colin Cernik’s 2025 time by 1:39.
“I’m in the middle of preparing for (the) New York City Marathon, so it’s kind of more of a workout, but it was fun,” Flavin said. “It was (a) good group of guys to work with for 10 miles and I was going to pick it up the last 5K and got rolling down those hills. The crowd was awesome, running past everyone was so much fun, so it was a blast.”
Next to finish were two Massachusetts runners — Cameron Dickson from Jamaica Plain (1:03.30) in second place and Ned Farrington of Cohasset (1:03.48) in third.
Heather Gallant of Wayne (1:15.38) and Isabel Seay of Hanover, New Hampshire (1:16.28) joined O’Neil on the podium in second and third place, respectively.

title: A frosty start today, then mainly sunny. Clouds and showers for Monday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - It was a chilly start to the morning with most people seeing temps in the 30s to start the day which will quickly transition to sunny skies and then some high clouds as the day goes on. It will not be as cold tonight with lows mainly around 50. A front will march its way across the state tomorrow and bring some showers with it. It will also bring some gusty winds behind it into Tuesday as the pressure gradient tightens because of a low to our north. Then yet another comfortable fall week.
Today: Frosty start, but another great finish
The spots that see frost this morning will likely rebound quickly as the sun comes out quickly and warms things up comfortably. Some high clouds will work their way in by the afternoon as highs top out around 60 for most. Today will be another great day to get outside and enjoy the leaves or some other outdoor activity!
Sunday night: Clouds arrive ahead of next system
It will cloud up and stay relatively warm on Sunday night ahead of our next system which will arrive on Monday, some light showers may also work their way in. Winds will also pick up out of the SW at 10-15 mph overnight.
Monday: Rain crosses state west to east, then gusty winds
Rain may arrive in the early morning on Monday especially in western regions. It will quickly move across the state with less than a quarter of an inch for most. It will be clear by the evening hours more than likely.
Tuesday and beyond: Windy Tuesday then another nice fall week
Following the rain it will likely get gusty Tuesday. It may gust over 40 mph for places up in the county with gusts over 35 across much of the rest of the region. This will knock a large number of leaves off the trees and being some colder temps as well.
Sunday: Mainly sunny. Highs near 60. Winds NW at 5-10 mph
Sunday night: Not as cold and clouds arrive. Lows near 50. Winds SW at 10-15 mph
Monday: Showers arrive with general cloudiness. Highs near 60. Winds SW at 10-15 mph.
Monday night: Mainly clear. Lows in the 30s and 40s. Windy with winds W at 15-20 mph.

title: Skateboarders shred Exchange Street during Portland’s Cobble to Cobble event
text:
PORTLAND — Henry Elias came to Exchange Street on Sunday with a skateboard and a mission: to land a perfect 50-50 kickflip.
“My favorite part about skating is landing the trick,” said the 12-year-old, staring down the track at scuffed rails and freshly waxed ledges.
Beside him, a dozen other skaters gathered, plotting their own runs and preparing for their turn to jump the cobblestone gaps in the pavement at the second annual Cobble to Cobble skateboarding event downtown.
Presented by independent Portland skateboard business Mocean and Portland Old Port, the free event celebrates the skating community by shutting down the iconic Portland street for an afternoon of skating.
“It’s very unofficial. There’s no rules as to what you can and can’t do on a skateboard, so everybody’s happy to just show up and do what they can and have fun,” self-proclaimed unofficial Cobble to Cobble consultant Nathan Keen said before setting off to capture some b-roll as an unofficial videographer.
Last year, Cobble to Cobble drew over 2,000 attendees. Despite a weeklong delay for weather this year, organizers said they were confident the crowd would exceed that.
By the time the event started at noon, Exchange was already packed with skaters eager to ride the brand new custom ramps, and spectators waiting to hear who’d be crowned the winner of a $5,000 cash prize.
The open jam format meant anyone could skate, brave newbies and seasoned veterans alike. They bombed down the track, dodging the cobblestones, unafraid of eating pavement in front of the crowd. Skaters and onlookers watched with “oohs” and “ahhs”— a reaction seemingly fit for both the cleanest skates and the gnarliest wipeouts.
Henry and his friend Xavier Parkhurst, who is also 12 years old, stood a couple feet shorter than the rest as they prepped for another fearless ride down the street. They’ve been skating for eight years and three years, respectively, and said coming to the event gave them the chance to learn from some older skaters.
“My dad teaches me a lot,” Xavier said as his father returned from his own run with a skateboard in hand.
Keen described Cobble to Cobble as a big block party — one that could help fill in for the long gone Old Port festival, and one that could be bigger than just skateboarding.
A few yards away, an artist dipped a brush into a blob of red on a palette and painted it onto a canvas in the middle of the crowd. DJ’s kept the energy high, adding to the soundtrack of wheels on metal, and at the top of the hill, local business owners sold vintage clothes and art.
“It’s nice to have a big party downtown,” Keen said, adding that this year, it was easy to get the city on board and celebrate the skate community after the success of the inaugural Cobble to Cobble last year.
At the bottom of Exchange Street, Gabbi Perry began rolling up the hill with a smile after a turn on her roller skates. As the only skater with wheels fixed to her feet, she said she was intimidated. Being a woman in a male-dominated environment also made her a little nervous.
“But the Portland crew, is, like, one of the best crews of skaters I’ve ever met. Very welcoming, very encouraging,” Perry said.
Last year, she was the only girl. This year, as she tried to nail the rainbow rail, she was proud to see more joining in and finding a way to celebrate the community.

title: ‘Digger’ Is One of Tom Cruise’s Biggest Flops Ever
text:
‘Digger’ Is One of the Biggest Flops of Tom Cruise’s Career
Tom Cruise has dug himself quite a financial hole.
His new comedy Digger has flopped in a way that few Tom Cruise movies have ever flopped before. It’s estimated to have earned $8 million in its opening weekend. Prior to release, Warner Bros. had reportedly projected the film would earn in the $12-15 million range over its opening weekend. Those estimates would have already been bad for a big-budget movie — and Digger’s final tally is closer to half of the high-end of that range.
The last time Cruise had a movie open that weakly was 2007’s Lions for Lambs, which grossed $6.7 million in its first few days of release. But that was a relatively small-scale drama about politics and the war in Afghanistan. (Wikipedia claims its budget was $35 million.) Digger cost $125 million according to The Hollywood Reporter. Even if Digger had exceeded Warners’ expectations, it would have been unlikely to turn a profit — especially since it’s a broad, audience antagonizing satire about climate change and corruption, with Cruise playing a cocky oil barron whose reckless drilling causes an environmental calamity the alternately attempts to fix and deflect blame for onto others.
READ MORE: Tom Cruise’s Most Extreme Onscreen Transformations
The top film of the weekend was Verity, based on the novel by Colleen Hoover (It Ends With Us). It grossed $32.7 million in the U.S. — roughly four times what Digger earned — against a reported budget of $40 million.
Meanwhile Avengers: Endgame sold enough tickets in its new Encore cut to nudge it past Avatar and once again make it the top-grossing film in the history of movies. (It passed Avatar once before, but 20th Century Studios put James Cameron’s sci-fi film back in theaters in the run-up to Avatar: The Way of Water, and it grossed enough in re-release to reclaim the #1 all-time post.)
As for Tom Cruise, well, it sure makes a lot of sense why he announced Days of Thunder 2 before Digger opened in theaters, huh? He’s already got his next project lined up. And there’s no way it doesn’t gross more than this one.

title: LIHEAP heat benefits may fall short as winter bills jump, new data shows
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
With rising home energy prices, LIHEAP heat benefits may fall short this winter
Nearly 5 million U.S. households receive heating assistance through the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program. But this winter, these households could struggle to afford their heating bills and risk falling behind on utility bills.
U.S. households are projected to spend an average of $1,030 to heat their homes this winter, an $82 increase from last winter, according to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association. NEADA released its initial winter heating projections in mid-September and revised its heating oil cost estimate in late September. The $1,030 figure comes from the initial projection.
The average heating benefit households received in fiscal year 2025 was $467, according to the latest LIHEAP data.
If benefits average about the same as they did in 2025, families could be left to figure out how to cover more than $500 in additional heating costs. 
NEADA is urging Congress to increase LIHEAP funding from $4 billion to $7 billion to help families manage rising home-energy costs.
Higher heating and electricity bills could leave families with less money for food, housing, transportation and other necessities, according to NEADA.
“This is a warning that too many families are entering winter with no room left in their budgets,” said Mark Wolfe, executive director of NEADA.
The projected cost increase comes as crude oil keeps trading above $100 a barrel as the conflict in the Middle East continues to disrupt global oil supplies. Households that primarily rely on heating oil will see the sharpest increase, with costs estimated to rise by 50% because of the war in Iran.
Share of households receiving LIHEAP heating benefits
About 14% of households in New York received LIHEAP heating benefits in fiscal year 2025, more than any other state, according to a Get the Facts Data Team analysis.
Vermont and Michigan each have nearly 8% of their households enrolled in the program. 
The average benefit per household varies by state. Each year, all states and territories submit applications to receive funds, and the states decide how to distribute funds.
Alaska’s average household heat benefit was $1,554, the highest among the states. New Hampshire’s average benefit was the second highest at $1,045. Households in New Hampshire primarily rely on heating oil to heat their homes.
Households in the Northeast are projected to spend nearly $2,627 on heating oil from mid-November through mid-March this winter. That could leave families scrambling to cover more than $1,000 after receiving heating assistance.
“Winter is almost here, and families have very little time to prepare,” Wolfe said.

title: US Marine arrested for alleged murder of a woman on Okinawa, triggers outrage from Japan
text:
TOKYO (AP) — Japanese police arrested a U.S. Marine in the alleged robbery and murder of a woman on Okinawa, officials said Sunday, the latest criminal case on the southern island where the heavy American troop presence has remained a sensitive issue.
The Okinawa prefectural police said they arrested a 20-year-old Marine stationed at the Futenma Air Station on suspicion of killing a 39-year-old local woman at a hotel in Naha, Okinawa’s capital city, and taking her wallet and backpack in the early hours of Saturday.
Kyodo News agency, citing the police, reported the woman’s body was found in her hotel room and she appeared to have been strangled to death.
Police said security camera footage showed the man believed to be the suspect entering the hotel with the victim and coming out alone. An officer arrested the suspect after spotting him walking alone on a street in Naha’s entertainment district late Saturday, Kyodo said.
“The case deals a major shock and adds fear to the Okinawans who have already been forced to live next to U.S. bases,” newly elected Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja told reporters. “It is absolutely unforgivable and we are outraged.”
“I must say, discipline and troop education are not working at all,” said Koja, referring to the U.S. military’s measures taken in response to past criminal cases.
Some 50,000 U.S. troops are deployed in Japan under a bilateral security pact, about half of them on Okinawa, whose strategic role is seen as increasingly important for the Japan-U.S. military alliance amid growing tensions with China. Japan’s southwestern shift in its military focus centers heavily on Okinawa and its nearby islands.
Okinawans have long complained about noise, pollution and crime related to U.S. bases, with crimes involving U.S. service members on Okinawa complicating ties between Japan’s central government and the Okinawa administration. The latest case comes as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s cabinet pushes to further fortify its Japanese military presence on Okinawa and work more closely with the U.S. military.
“The occurrence of the heinous crime is extremely regrettable,” Takaichi said in her message on X. She said her government has strongly protested to the U.S. side and demanded maximum cooperation with the Japanese authorities in the investigation, as well as tougher discipline for U.S. service members and preventive measures.
Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi summoned U.S. Ambassador to Japan George Glass to his office and conveyed “outrage,” the ministry said in a statement.
Glass, on X, expressed condolences to the victim’s family, adding that the United States is cooperating with the Japanese national and local governments.
The U.S. Marine Corps said in a statement the suspect is assigned to the III Marine Expeditionary Force on Okinawa and that it is fully cooperating with Japanese authorities. “The Marine Corps takes these allegations very seriously and expects every Marine to adhere to the highest standards of behavior.”
Futenma base, located in a densely populated area in central Okinawa, has been a sore spot for many Okinawans for decades, who demanded its relocation. Despite protests, the central government greenlit construction to relocate the base to Henoko on Okinawa’s eastern coast, though the project has faced massive delays.
A high-profile 1995 rape of a 12-year-old girl by three U.S. service members sparked massive protests against the heavy U.S. troop presence on Okinawa. The number of arrests related to U.S. service members and their families exceeded 100 last year, according to prefectural police. Repeated occurrence of sexual crimes and some of their delayed disclosures have also sparked outrage on Okinawa in recent years.

title: Trump announces leadership of new federal AI task force
text:
Trump names national intelligence director Jay Clayton to lead a new federal AI task force
President Donald Trump on Sunday tapped Jay Clayton, his director of national intelligence, to lead a new government task force on artificial intelligence.
Related video: Trump unveils voluntary AI safety accord with tech leaders
Trump is calling it the "Super Intelligence Force," because he has tried to rebrand AI as "super intelligence." The announcement comes after Trump hosted top executives of AI companies at the White House last week and said they had signed a voluntary accord that would effectively self-police the development of the technology.
The task force will coordinate the federal effort "to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans," Trump in a post on social media Sunday.
The task force will reach out to consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers and AI companies, the Republican president said.
Others on the task force include the Federal Trade Commission's chairman, Andrew Ferguson; Emil Michael, the Pentagon's chief technology officer; and Scott Kupor, the director of the Office of Personnel Management.
The group will report to Trump and his chief of staff, Susie Wiles.

title: Squishy toys recalled over potential hazards for children. Here’s how to get a refund
text:
(Gray News) - About 37,000 popular squishy toys sold nationwide were recalled because they potentially pose a deadly hazard to children, according to the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission.
The water beads inside the recalled squishy toys expand larger than permitted by the mandatory safety standard for toys. If a water bead is ingested, it can pose a choking or obstruction hazard inside a child’s body, which can cause severe discomfort, vomiting, dehydration or death.
The recalled squishy toys are dumpling and crazy squib ball toys.
The recalled squishy dumplings are model 3655 and come in multiple translucent colors containing glitter and water beads. The toys have a cartoon face and are packaged in a tan plastic container shaped like a bamboo steamer. “SQUISHY DUMPLING” is printed on the front of the removable package label. There are no markings on the product, other than the cartoon face.
The recalled crazy squib balls are model 3984 and come in multiple translucent colors containing glitter and water beads. The toys are individually wrapped in a white netting. “CRAZY SQUIB BALL” and “Squeeze it! Throw it!” are printed on the front of the package labeling.
Anyone with the recalled squishy toys should stop using them immediately and contact ABC Trading for a full refund.
The recalled toys were sold at ABC Trading stores in Los Angeles and other stores nationwide from April through June 2026 for between 41 cents and $1.25.

title: Death Notice: Cecile Juliette Chenard
Christa Pike's lawyer says she has not regained consciousness since her failed Tennessee execution
text:
Christa Pike has remained unconscious and on a ventilator at a hospital in the four days since her failed execution in Tennessee, and her prognosis might not be known for days more, one of her lawyers said Sunday.
Little has been released about Pike’s condition since Wednesday night’s execution attempt. She has since remained hospitalized under guard as doctors try to get the massive dose of the barbiturate pentobarbital out of her system.
When asked whether she ever regained consciousness after the execution attempt, Assistant Federal Defender Stephen Ferrell, Pike’s lawyer, said on CNN’s “State of the Union”: “Not that I am aware of.”
Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in a jealous rage in 1995. She became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row.
Tennessee prison officials gave Pike two doses of the lethal injection drug on Wednesday night. The pentobarbital didn’t kill her, but her lawyers said her arms were burned and blistered from the caustic drugs.
Pike gave someone her medical power of attorney and that person is protecting her privacy, Ferrell said.
“I’m not sure what all they may have told that person,” Ferrell said.
Pike’s attorneys have not identified who is making Pike’s medical decisions.
A spokeswoman for Pike’s defense team said in a statement early Sunday that “we appreciate all respect for Christa’s rightful privacy.”

title: Former US attorney to conduct review of botched execution of Christa Pike
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee’s Office announced Saturday that former U.S. Attorney Ed Stanton will be conducting the independent review of the botched execution of Christa Pike.
The governor’s office said the Tennessee Attorney General’s Office retained Stanton to conduct an “independent review of the Tennessee Department of Correction’s actions” during the failed attempt to execute Pike.
On Wednesday, Pike, who is the only woman on Tennessee’s death row, was set to be executed by lethal injection. Following some legal hurdles throughout the day, Pike was given two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital, but her attorneys said she was “alive and snoring.”
Pike remains alive and hospitalized in “critical condition,” according to her attorneys, marking the second failed execution in Tennessee this year.
“The independent review will seek to determine whether the protocol was followed and consider whether additional recommendations are necessary to ensure the State’s protocol continues to be lawful and effective,” the governor’s office said.
Lee has called off the remaining execution that was set for this year, pending the completion of the review. Gary Wayne Sutton was supposed to be executed on Dec. 3.
Stanton previously conducted an independent review of Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol following an oversight in the process’s testing. His review in 2022 prompted “the State and Attorney General’s Office to substantially rewrite the protocol before executions resumed.”

title: How Maine’s schools need to be approaching AI
text:
Joseph Hennessey, MSEd, is an educator who has served in classroom and building-level leadership roles, most recently in central Maine. He was the 2018 Piscataquis County Teacher of the Year, the 2019 Maine Teacher of the Year, the 2020 National University Teacher of the Year for Maine and is currently an American Service Fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School of Government.
Toward the end of the last school year, I sat with a middle school teacher and her student in the classroom to address misuse of AI on an important assignment. Were Google and Gemini (Google’s AI assistant) really different forms of sources? How much “assistance” from AI qualified as too much, at this developmental level, in this content area, at this juncture in history?
Our district’s acceptable use policy had been provisionally updated, but we had not yet had time to share the changes with students. The teacher did not want to penalize the student unfairly; the student did not want to receive an “incomplete” for the assignment; and I did not want to establish a precedent that would be difficult to maintain.
In the end, we used this meeting as an educational opportunity for the student, and the teacher and I revised plans to deliver even more digital literacy to all middle school students in the coming year — this was a positive result in the face of complex circumstances.
***
Public education has been grappling with the AI issue for several years. As Kate Meyer and Nicole Davis reminded me in their recent book “EduProtocol Field Guide: AI Literacy Edition,” however, we are only limited in our use of AI by the constraints of our imaginations.
There are many reasons one could be optimistic about AI’s application in public schools, but students’ and schools’ relationships to this emerging technology are still very unclear, as evidenced in my anecdote above.
What’s undeniable, though, is that artificial intelligence affects the environment much more than it should. Schools should thus treat AI as what it is: a very expensive, very precious commodity that is not to be misused, squandered or discarded. Casual use of AI in education at this stage is careless use of AI that we can ill afford.
In 2024, the Berkeley Lab projected that AI “hyperscale” data centers would consume 98% of all water used by the sector by 2028. New Yorker contributor Steven Witt noted in his 2025 article that each new AI data center built in the United States is expected to use one gigawatt of electricity per year, which is more than the entire annual energy use of Philadelphia.
According to Noman Bashir of MIT and his colleagues, the global electricity consumption of data centers is expected to reach 800 terawatt hours in 2026, which is more than three times the annual energy use of California.
And while this is a small portion of the overall environmental demands of the United States and globe (according to CBS News, more water is needed to produce one hamburger than to conduct hundreds of AI queries), it is very important to consider. AI and its natural resource usage is part of a critical context concerning energy behaviors. And if there are popular movements to limit red meat consumption (i.e., Meatless Mondays addressing the hamburger problem), a similar standard should be applied to AI in general and in education in particular.
Schools already teach about natural resource conservation and climate change. AI must be a distinct part of that discourse precisely because we do not know how large it will be. When the student described above had used AI so frequently and inefficiently to complete a single assignment, they likely had not considered their environmental impact as much as their desire to produce excellent work.
Our colleagues and communities expect that schools will embrace AI in a manner that is net productive and equips our students with the knowledge and skills to confront a rapidly evolving society. These are large tasks along an uncertain path. In response, we should tread conscientiously on that path, not fearfully.
In accordance with the federal and various worthy state-level AI frameworks on offer, three questions guide my use:
- Am I producing something concrete that will make sense to others and mean something to others?
- Am I producing something durable that will stand the test of time rather than become immediately irrelevant?
- Am I producing something reusable that can be taken offline and into the real world with necessarily needing more AI?
If the AI task satisfies those criteria for me, then the product will satisfy the different human forward frameworks. For students, this means putting in the real work of learning, whether AI is used in the beginning, middle or end stages of a task. No machine or algorithm should be doing the thinking for you.
For teachers, this means generating the core materials (lesson plans, supplemental handouts, differentiated readings), and then using your own professional judgment to create replicable learning experiences for students. Teachers are still the experts; AI is a tool.
For administrators, this means crafting queries carefully the first time and working with colleagues to polish the message. Use efficient prompting to get it right the first time and do the important refining work offline.
And for all of us in public education, this means not demanding pristine, symmetrical perfection from student work. We should be far more interested in work that looks like a young person made it with an authentic combination of time, effort and risk-taking. Let’s let children express themselves through their assignments, even if it involves occasional smudges, curved lines or wrinkled edges.
***
The student whom I met with in that classroom in June had dutifully participated in class, had worked with their peers every day and had wanted to do exceptionally well when they turned to Gemini.
Yet what they learned in that unit overall is of far more importance to me than whether or not the end product sounded like it was written by a generic college student. That polish was worth far less, pedagogically, to their teacher or our school than what it cost to produce environmentally.
AI will become more efficient, and scale will help, but good habits should be developed now. As educators, we must model more effectively as the technology and its potential emerges. Let’s use AI more conscientiously to preserve cognition and the environment at the same time.

title: Sunday Photos: October 4th, 2026
Obituary: Sharon Lee Davis
text:
CHARLESTON, S.C. – Sharon Lee Davis, 75, passed away peacefully on May 28, 2026.
Born and raised in Windsor, Vt., Sharon developed an appreciation for hard work, beauty (of art/craftsmanship), and the wider world from an early age. Though she always held a special place in her heart for New England, she dreamed of seeing beyond its borders and embraced a life filled with travel and discovery.
Her career in healthcare administration and management provided opportunities to lead in hospitals and medical practices in New Hampshire, Maine, Michigan, Texas and South Carolina. She loved experiencing new communities but especially cherished Maine for its beauty and family heritage.
She loved traveling throughout the globe, visiting countless countries and exploring art, culture, connecting with people and enjoying local cuisine and fine wine. She shared her passion for travel with her sons and grandchildren.
Above all else, Sharon loved her family and friends. She was a devoted mother and a proud grandmother, choosing to settle in Charleston, S.C. to be near them. Her love and support were unwavering. Memories of countless laughs over dinners, days at the beach, adventures, cherished gifted Pooh Bears, trips to the aquarium, concerts and overnights with “Nonna” are a lasting gift.
Sharon will be remembered for her strength, quick wit and a wry sense of humor with a knowing smile.
“SLD” will be deeply missed and lovingly remembered by her sons, Jason Davidson (spouse Noël) and Benjamin Davidson (spouse Leslie); her grandchildren, Evelyn Davidson, John “Jack” Davidson, Miles Davidson, Lyla Davidson and Nia Davidson; her brother, Lee Pudvah (spouse Crystal), sister-in-law, Phyllis Olson; and many nieces, nephews, cousins, extended family and many dear friends.
Sharon was preceded in death by her parents, Harold and Evelyn Pudvah; brothers, Richard Olson and Gary Pudvah.
Her family takes comfort in knowing she is at peace and will forever cherish the memories, love and appreciation for the beautiful world and legacy she leaves behind.
A memorial will take place on Sunday, Oct. 11 at the Windsor, Vt. Welcome Center, 3 Railroad Ave., Windsor, Vt. 05089 from 12 p.m. to 2 p.m.
In lieu of flowers or gifts, please support the World Wildlife Fund, as Sharon did for much of her life

title: Archaeologists found 11 silver coins buried 2,000 years ago
text:
Archaeologists found 11 silver coins buried 2,000 years ago
The 11 quinarii are the largest group ever found, but where they were minted remains a mystery.
Archaeologists found 11 silver coins buried 2,000 years ago
The 11 quinarii are the largest group ever found, but where they were minted remains a mystery.
Ahead of the construction of a fire station on land that formerly housed a sports field, archaeologists made a discovery that set off some alarms of its own, so to speak.
The field sits in Singen, in the German state of Thuringia. Digging there, archaeologists recovered 11 rare silver coins known as quinarii that were made by an ancient Celtic culture. The coins were likely buried together in the first century B.C.E. in an area that was heavily populated by the Celts roughly 2,000 years ago. The silver coins were slightly scattered through the field thanks to plowing over the years, but now they’ve been reunited.
All 11 coins represent the Prague style of a silver quinarius. Having once been buried together, likely in an organic container that has since degraded, the coins could help experts better understand regional mints and the movement of goods in the Celtic-dominated region, according to the Thuringian State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology as reported by Arkeonews.
Archaeologists called the discovery, located in an area of about 20 feet by five feet, a “closed find,” an example of coins that were buried together at a single point in time. While archaeologists discovered other artifacts at the site — including a Roman denarius minted sometime between 164 and 169 C.E., a different silver coin from later in history, and additional beads and buttons — no additional clues surfaced about the person who buried the 11 quinarii, or how the coins got there in the first place.
An initial search in 2025 discovered the first coins in the field, and further excavation dug up the rest in 2026. Archaeologists now believe they’ve found all the quinarii present at the site. While the state office didn’t release additional details about the coins, numismatists — coin experts — said they believe the coins were produced in the Gotha region northwest of Singen, where there was a heavy concentration of Celtic settlements.
Despite the name, “Prague style” coins have nothing to do with Prague beyond the fact that the first discovery of this type of coin was made there. They were struck in Thuringia. The quinarius was a Roman silver coin valued at half of a Roman denarius. The Celtic version mimicked the size and weight of the Roman quinarius and was often designed with Celtic abstracts. They commonly included a stylized horse or Greco-Roman designs and circulated throughout Central Europe.
Archaeologists learned at Singen that one pass is rarely enough — a follow-up search is always a good idea. Switzerland offers another, similar lesson. In Switzerland, coins dating from 2,100 to 2,300 years ago were found in the Bärenfelser bog near Arisdorf multiple times. Two coins found in 2025 are the oldest ever unearthed in Switzerland, both dated to the middle or second half of the third century B.C.E. But before that, in 2023, archaeologists found 34 Celtic silver coins dated to roughly 80 B.C.E. It can really pay to give things a second look.

title: Husson becomes 1st Maine Division III football team to win a game this season
text:
Husson University became the first of Maine’s six Division III college football teams to earn a win this season as the Eagles had four interceptions, including one for an 85-yard touchdown return by freshman Melvyn Telisca, and posted a 26-21 victory over Western New England on Saturday at the Winkin Sports Complex in Bangor.
In the other games involving Maine teams, Nichols College dealt Maine Maritime Academy its 36th consecutive loss, 38-20; nationally-ranked Endicott College outscored the University of New England 55-27; Tufts edged Bates 22-21; Amherst topped Bowdoin 22-13; and Middlebury clobbered Colby 32-2.
In Bangor, Daniel Ruiz Cantu scored on runs of 3 and 5 yards, Brody Gibson tossed a 17-yard touchdown pass to Jacob Lenz, and Telisca’s second interception of the game and his 85-yard return proved to be the game-winner.
It gave Husson a 26-7 lead and the Eagles withstood a Western New England fourth-quarter rally that saw Paul Gorry throw a 34-yard touchdown pass to Kevin Acosta, whom he had connected with on a 22-yard TD reception in the first half, and a 29-yard pass from Corey Kilroy to John De Camps with 2:17 left.
Husson is now 1-4 overall and 1-1 in the Conference of New England while Western New England is 2-3 and 1-1.
Husson’s Gibson completed 16 of 26 passes for 143 yards and a touchdown and Caden Crocker had seven catches for 50 yards. Lenz had four for 55.
Brett Davis had an 88-yard kickoff return to set up a touchdown.
Ruiz Cantu had 20 carries for 65 yards and two TDs. Cooper McNamara had a game-high 11 tackles for Husson and he also had an interception. Erik Menger and J.T. Wright had 10 tackles apiece and Brayden Trombly had an interception.
The four interceptions is the most since Husson had five against Nichols in 2023.
Gorry completed just seven of 24 passes for 114 yards and two TDs with four interceptions for Western New England. Kilroy completed five of nine passes for 75 yards and a touchdown and he also carried the ball 12 times for 58 yards. Acosta caught six passes for 107 yards. Matthew McGuire had 15 carries for 62 yards for the Golden Bears and the defense was led by Michael Canavatchel’s eight tackles.
In the matchup between Nichols and Maine Maritime Academy in Dudley, Massachusetts, Nichols quarterback Will Migliaccio completed 21 of 23 passes for 270 yards and three touchdowns and he also ran for a touchdown as Nichols improved to 2-3 and 2-0 in the Conference of New England.
Maine Maritime Academy fell to 0-4 and 0-2.
Migliaccio tossed TD passes of 24 and 17 yards to Brett Lato and 40 yards to Kahlil Talley and he added a three-yard TD run. Teyshon McGee scored on a two-yard run and rushed for a game-high 83 yards on 12 carries.
Lato, Ethan LaGuardia and Noah Gincastro each had four receptions for the winners and Mike Orvil and Nat Cook had six and five tackles, respectively, to spark the defense. Orvil also had an interception.
Harris Stone completed 19 of 33 passes for 228 yards for the Mariners. He threw 43 and 14-yard TD passes to Evan Flowers and a six-yarder to Aiden Sullivan.
Auston Harris carried the ball 12 times for 63 yards and caught six passes for 91. Flowers had five receptions for 67 yards.
Lucas Houghton had a game-high 12 tackles and Matt Gagin had nine.

title: Skowhegan teacher running Maine Marathon with a simple message: Never give up
text:
Skowhegan teacher running Maine Marathon with a simple message: Never give up
Richard Drown of Skowhegan was diagnosed with autism at a young age. Now, he uses running as his anchor and hopes to inspire others with autism to do the same.
Skowhegan teacher running Maine Marathon with a simple message: Never give up
Richard Drown of Skowhegan was diagnosed with autism at a young age. Now, he uses running as his anchor and hopes to inspire others with autism to do the same.
Richard Drown was just 7 years old when he was diagnosed with autism. Thanks to years of treatment and support from his family, he is now a special education teacher at Community Region Charter School in Skowhegan. But he is also a five-time overall marathoner, and will add a sixth to his list on Sunday when he completes the Maine Marathon. He has been raising money for the Autism Society of Maine.
"As someone with autism, I need a lot of structure in my day and running provides that structure," said Drown.
Drown is up almost every day before the sun at 4:00 to train. He said running helps him to remain disciplined before he heads to the classroom to help students. He started running in college and joined the Cross Country team at Thomas College. He hopes to be an inspiration to others who have autism that you can do whatever you set your mind to.
"I am here to serve others, and I want to make sure that people are being treated fairly, and people are getting after it by being their best selves every day," said Drown.
On Sunday, he will run to earn a qualifying time for the Chicago Marathon, which he hopes is the next one he can check off his list. But more than anything, he is running for all Mainers with autism.

title: US Marine arrested for alleged murder of a woman on Okinawa
text:
TOKYO (AP) — Japanese police arrested a U.S. Marine accused of robbing and killing a woman on Okinawa, officials said Sunday, in the latest criminal case involving U.S. military personnel on the southern island where the heavy American troop presence is a sensitive issue.
The Okinawa prefectural police said they arrested a 20-year-old Marine stationed at the Futenma Air Station on suspicion of killing a 39-year-old local woman at a hotel in Naha, Okinawa’s capital city, and taking her wallet and backpack early Saturday.
Kyodo News agency, citing the police, reported the woman’s body was found in her hotel room and she appeared to have been strangled.
Police said security camera footage showed a man believed to be the suspect entering the hotel with the woman and leaving alone. An officer arrested the suspect after spotting him walking alone on a street in Okinawa City’s entertainment district late Saturday, Kyodo said.
“The case deals a major shock and adds fear to the Okinawans who have already been forced to live next to U.S. bases,” newly elected Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja told reporters. “It is absolutely unforgivable and we are outraged.”
“I must say, discipline and troop education are not working at all,” said Koja, referring to the U.S. military’s measures taken in response to past criminal cases.
Some 50,000 U.S. troops are deployed in Japan under a bilateral security pact, about half of them on Okinawa, whose strategic role is seen as increasingly important for the Japan-U.S. military alliance amid growing tensions with China. Japan’s southwestern shift in its military focus centers heavily on Okinawa and its nearby islands.
Okinawans have long complained about noise, pollution and crime related to U.S. bases, with crimes involving U.S. service members on Okinawa complicating ties between Japan’s central government and the Okinawa administration. The latest case comes as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s cabinet pushes to further fortify its Japanese military presence on Okinawa and work more closely with the U.S. military.
“The occurrence of the heinous crime is extremely regrettable,” Takaichi said in her message on X. She said her government has strongly protested to the U.S. side and demanded maximum cooperation with the Japanese authorities in the investigation, as well as tougher discipline for U.S. service members and preventive measures.
Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi summoned U.S. Ambassador to Japan George Glass to his office and conveyed “outrage,” the ministry said in a statement.
Glass, on X, expressed condolences to the victim’s family, adding that the United States is cooperating with the Japanese national and local governments.
The U.S. Marine Corps said in a statement the suspect is assigned to the III Marine Expeditionary Force on Okinawa and that it is fully cooperating with Japanese authorities. “The Marine Corps takes these allegations very seriously and expects every Marine to adhere to the highest standards of behavior.”
Futenma base, located in a densely populated area in central Okinawa, has been a sore spot for many Okinawans for decades, who demanded its relocation. Despite protests, the central government greenlit construction to relocate the base to Henoko on Okinawa’s eastern coast, though the project has faced massive delays.
The rape of a 12-year-old girl by three U.S. service members in 1995 sparked massive protests against the heavy U.S. troop presence on Okinawa. The number of arrests related to U.S. service members and their families exceeded 100 last year, according to prefectural police. Repeated occurrence of sexual crimes and some of their delayed disclosures have also sparked outrage on Okinawa in recent years.
___
This story corrects the location where the suspect was spotted after the alleged crime to Okinawa City, not Naha.

title: Obituary: Raymond P. Loubier
text:
WINSLOW – Raymond P. Loubier, 84, of Winslow passed away on Sept. 26, 2026, in the home he built, surrounded by family after a long and determined battle with Parkinson’s Disease.
He was born on Oct. 25, 1941, the son of Paul E. and Fernande (Fortin) Loubier. Ray was a 1960 graduate of Winslow High School where he excelled in Industrial Arts and received First Place in the state for his senior project of a grandmother clock which earned him a four-year machinist apprenticeship at Keyes Fibre Co. in Waterville. A talented woodworker and machinist, he built a 43-year career there through two changes of company ownership, finally retiring in 2003. During that time he furthered his education in machine tooling at the International Correspondence School as well as earning credits at both Thomas College and the University of Maine.
He joined the Air National Guard in 1963 and served six years as a jet engine mechanic. He also enjoyed being part of the Winslow Area Jaycees where he served in many roles including as president in 1971-’72. Never one to rest, when he wasn’t accepting offers of free wood in exchange for cutting it down, he started his own company, Multi-Craft Products where he produced custom items requiring his machinist savvy
He enjoyed his retirement as an antique car enthusiast restoring corvettes and dabbling in side gigs as a home machinist, sailboat builder, floor monitor at Julia’s auction house, packaging specialist at Winslow Gun Shop, and antique corvette parts dealer travelling often to Corvette Carlisle.
He is survived by his children, Andrea Loubier, and Stephanie Weiss and her husband Carl; his grandchildren Winry and Benjamin Devenport, and Elizabeth, William, and Nicholas Weiss; his nephew, Clyde B. Arnold III of Florida; and close cousin, Carroll LaFlamme.
He was predeceased by his parents; sister, Anne Arnold; special aunt, Florence Loubier; and several cousins.
A Mass of Christian Burial will be celebrated on Thursday, Oct. 8 at 10 a.m. at St. John the Baptist Catholic Church, 26 Monument St., Winslow.
Arrangements are under the direction and care of Gallant Funeral Home, 10 Elm St., Waterville. An online guestbook may be signed, condolences and memories shared at http://www.gallantfh.com
